#9013. The Latest and Greatest Sunglasses for Triathletes, Tested in Training and Racing

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Sunglasses and triathletes go hand in hand. With not one but two sports calling for a good pair, and after so much time spent nitpicking over the perfect goggles, we can’t settle for less when it comes to shading our eyes through the bulk of our training and racing.

It’s not just about UV protection and keeping bugs and debris out, because, let’s be honest: style matters, too. And today’s saturated performance sunglasses market offers a nearly unlimited selection of styles, with many pairs more high-tech and often higher-priced than ever before.

We wanted to get a clearer, less-tinted picture of the triathlon-worthy sunglasses landscape in 2026, so we combed the internet to see what was on the cutting edge and spent the summer testing a wide range of pairs while running and cycling across different terrains and climates.

Along the way, we explored the latest tech, picked out standout features, and figured out what felt worth the money – and what wasn’t quite there yet. From light-shifting photochromic lenses and video-recording AI smart glasses to everyday pairs that won’t break the bank, here’s our roundup of the best sunglasses for triathletes in 2026.

In the Pacific Northwest where I live, it can be raining one minute and sunny the next. A ride might take you from wide-open roads into dense, dark forests, sometimes around a single corner. For that reason, I’ve found light-shifting lenses incredibly useful. But even if you don’t live where I do, these glasses are practical in plenty of other changing light conditions, such as an early-morning long ride that starts before the sun comes up and ends well into the day.

One of the biggest drawbacks of traditional photochromic sunglasses is that the lenses don’t always adjust as quickly as the light changes. Their tint range also has limits, and they don’t always get as clear or as dark as you’d like. Most rely on UV light to darken, which means they may not respond as you’d expect behind a UV-blocking windshield in your car or when you’re testing them by a window before heading outside.

That’s a perfect segue into where we’ll start, as the first pair on our list looks to address these issues by taking a different approach: tint you control with a swipe.

One of the most intriguing pairs on this entire list comes from a new brand called Povec. Rather than waiting for the lenses to react to changing light, these glasses allow you to swipe an interface on the temple to change the tint in about a second.

Sure enough, I was surprised by just how quickly, and how dramatically, the tint changed. It started shifting as soon as we swiped the temple, so naturally, we spent the next several days playing with it back and forth. The electrochromic tech, as it’s called, worked so well that the glasses quickly became a showpiece for impressing friends.

These glasses ironically shone in dimmer conditions, especially when we went off-road or deep into the forests and needed to change the tint quickly. When mountain biking, being able to change the tint almost immediately as we rounded a corner into a dense forest descent felt invaluable.

At the same time, we were slightly less impressed with the optical quality in harsher light. There are subtle but apparent reflections, and the clarity is just a little off. It’s nothing dramatic, but it is noticeable, especially compared with the crystal-clear optics of some other glasses on this list.

Our favorite everyday pair of photochromic sunglasses, especially for spring and fall days in the PNW forests, was the SunGod Velans 2.

This ultralight pair offered some of the best optical clarity, field of view, and comfort of any glasses on this list, even before the added bonus of photochromic lenses. They shifted from light to dark quickly enough for our normal riding, although they couldn’t match the on-demand tint changes of the Povecs.

SunGod has become increasingly visible in triathlon thanks to athletes such as Hayden Wilde and Chelsea Sodaro donning them, but also because of a few appealing extras not often found elsewhere in the market. An array of customization options, an emphasis on durability, repairability, and recycled packaging, and a lifetime guarantee that includes repairs for accidental breakage make the higher price easier to digest. Furthermore, features such as replacement lenses and screwless hinges make the price more logical and suggest this pair will likely last you for the long term rather than just a couple of seasons.

Tifosi consistently makes it into our roundups for offering quality sunglasses at some of the best prices, and its light-shifting options are no exception.

We tried the Rail XC with Clarion Blue “Fototec” lenses, which offer a stated light-transmission range of 12% to 46%.

Compared with the SunGods, these felt like only a small step down in optical quality and fit during our testing. We did notice more glare from sunlight at certain angles and slightly more fogging during humid runs. At 31 grams, they were also a little heavier.

But beyond that, there’s little else to nitpick. They’re comfortable, clear, and transition smoothly and quickly, with nose pads and temple tips that adjust on the fly, offering plenty of room to dial in comfort.

Perhaps the most controversial pair on this list, these smart glasses have divided opinions about where this technology belongs in triathlon. From Ironman banning their use at its events to T100 welcoming them through a partnership, it’s a hot topic.

After training and racing in them twice, my own mixed opinion comes down to something simpler: I thoroughly enjoy wearing them and appreciate their practicality, but I’m still struggling with the bulky styling of the Vanguard. Enough so that I often intentionally leave them behind so I’m not the guy with the video sunglasses when running or cycling with friends.

That functionality, on the other hand, is hard to argue with. Being able to capture hands-free video and photos, listen to music, take phone calls, and ask Meta questions — among many other features — makes these glasses useful in ways a regular pair simply can’t match.

The Oakley Prizm lenses offered the clarity we expected, although the bulkier frame slightly restricted the field of view. Even after keeping them in their case and using only a microfiber cloth to clean them, I also noticed tiny scratches under close inspection after a few months of use. They weren’t noticeable while wearing the glasses, but they were there.

At 66 grams, you’ll notice the weight, too. If you have one of the lightweight alternatives on this list sitting next to them, you might think twice before grabbing these for an everyday session.

Where these really earned their place is in documenting your triathlon experiences. At SOS Triathlon and Escape from Alcatraz, capturing moments before, during, and after the race felt almost effortless. I could quickly tell Meta to take a photo or record a video, then download the footage to my phone through the app afterward, and I was set. Compared with previously having to bring GoPros, set up shots, and worry about batteries and SD cards, it makes it all too easy.

On the way to the SOS check-in tent, I even asked Meta to help me remember the different stages of this unique multi-stage race (read more about the SOS here).

Like it or not, smart glasses are likely to become an increasingly familiar sight around triathletes. After using them, I can understand the appeal.

Read a full Oakley Meta Vanguard review here.

The award for the most pleasantly surprising sunglasses on this entire list goes to this Oakley Meta rival, which packed in enough features to put the Vanguard on the ropes.

I’ll admit I went into testing the Rover sunglasses with the preconceived notion that these wouldn’t compete with the powerhouse name above. But I was taken aback by both the quality and functionality.

The first things I noticed were the weight, more than 10 grams lighter than the Vanguard, and the lenses. I hadn’t expected optics this good from a brand I had never heard of.

Then it only got better. The Rovers offer both landscape and portrait recording, plus a tiltable camera that helps you adjust the shot. The video resolution was also better than I expected at 3K and 60 fps – all capabilities the Vanguard doesn’t offer.

One of the standout features was the intercom function, which lets the glasses act like a walkie-talkie with fellow cyclists using the BleeqUp app. Being able to talk to each other more easily is something I’ve always wanted on small group rides, and hearing everyone clearly through the sunglasses themselves takes away the hassle of phone calls or dealing with headphones.

They’re marketed as AI sunglasses, with tools for quickly editing captured footage and adding ride-data overlays. If you’re feeling extra AI-adventurous, you can also generate a third-person view of your ride using mapping data and an uploaded photo of yourself and your bike. The results were interesting, to say the least.

Where the Rovers fell slightly behind the Vanguards was in the polish. The interface, AI assistant, and connectivity didn’t feel as refined as Meta’s. The feedback sounds weren’t as distinct, and connecting the glasses could be a little confusing, with frequent requests to reconnect to their Wi-Fi.

The Vanguard also comes with a charging case, which simplifies things, while the Rover uses a magnetic USB charger. Finally, having to say “Hey Bleeker” to activate the assistant just felt super weird.

One final gripe: The temples could rub against the lenses when folded, which felt like a small but frustrating design oversight.

In contrast to the pleasant surprise of the BleeqUp Rovers, these heads-up display sunglasses fell well short of my expectations.

I was excited to see whether technology similar to what we’ve enjoyed in Form’s smart swim goggles could bring the same benefit to running and cycling. Unfortunately, I was disappointed from the moment I unboxed them.

The idea is great, but the execution wasn’t there. The fit was the least comfortable of any glasses on this list, sitting unusually high on my face, and the secondary inner lens that houses the HUD projection compromised the view.

The bright green data displayed on the inner lenses is intended to keep cyclists from having to look down at their bike computer so they can focus on what’s ahead. In practice, however, I found the view even more distracting, sometimes struggling to adjust my focus from what I was reading on the glasses back to the road.

It was less of an issue while running, and thankfully, you can adjust the brightness and make some changes to the display position to keep the data less intrusive, but that was little consolation.

The app also felt unfinished, and we experienced several issues trying to connect our devices. Top it off with the worst-sounding built-in speakers and most robotic voice assistants I’ve heard in a while, and I’ll sadly be leaving HUD glasses out of my periphery for a while.

If I had the budget and could choose just one everyday pair to wear everyday or bring on a trip, like our recent all-in Ironman World Championship coverage, I’d choose the Oslo 2.0.

The blend of aesthetics, lens quality, and fit is hard to beat. Grippy temple tips and a very grippy nosepiece (which comes in various sizes) help it transition easily from casual use to training. Although it doesn’t look like it’s meant for running, it performs as well as a pair designed specifically for the sport.

For cycling, though, I prefer a little more lens coverage. That’s where I’d reach for Roka’s San Remo Air, which offers a similarly understated cafe style, but with more coverage and a vented lens for hot days.

Both were pairs I could happily wear all day, and all night if I had to. They also had some of the fewest fogging issues while running in the heat and humidity of a Washington summer and felt among the most premium of the bunch — from the finish of the frames to the cases they came in.

Our favorite mid-priced everyday pair was the Adidas Kaphiros, which came surprisingly close to the Rokas in overall performance. It also became the pair my wife consistently stole – sorry, “borrowed” – before we headed out for a ride together.

These are truly glasses you forget you’re wearing. They almost feel like they float above your ears. If pressure around your ears is something that regularly bothers you — as it has for me in the past — this is the pair I’d recommend.

The lenses offer generous coverage for cycling protection, and the optical quality impressed me. Small openings in the temples let air through while riding, although the glasses tended to fog during hot, humid runs — likely due to the size of the lenses.

Tifosi makes this list for a second time, beating out plenty of other running and cycling sunglasses as our favorite budget everyday pair.

The Vogel XC is lightweight, has proved durable enough to survive a couple of seasons with me, and offers a rimless, vented design that’s hard to beat at this price.

The lens tint we tested hit a useful middle ground for the varied conditions we wore it in. And the size and shape don’t scream “I’m a triathlete” every time you wear them out in public.

#9012. The Swedish Sport of Swimrun Is Spreading Across the U.S. I Tried It and Chaos Ensued.

Outside features editor Frederick Dreier participated in the October 4 Ötillö Swimrun race at Horsetooth Reservoir, Colorado. Dreier has competed in triathlons, bicycle races, and other endurance sports for 25 years.

A few memories come to mind from my recent Ötillö Swimrun, the endurance race that combines open-water swimming with trail running.

In one, I flounder in the chilly waters of Colorado’s Horsetooth Reservoir near Fort Collins, my arms feeling heavy as concrete as I struggle to swim in a straight line. In another, I sit by the side of a rocky trail plucking cactus spines out of my backside, moments after a clumsy toe-strike sent me tumbling into a clump of prickly pear.

Both of these scenes, however, are superseded by a memory with an altogether different vibe. That, of course, is crossing the finish line and exchanging a flurry of high-fives and hugs with a bunch of random sweaty strangers, all of us clad in wetsuits, goggles, and running shoes.

You see, I had a blast racing my first Ötillö Swimrun race despite the dead-tired arms and cactus butt.

If you have never heard of the swimrun racing format, here’s a quick primer. Picture a triathlon, minus the biking. Now, chop up the swimming and running portions, stitch them together in smaller portions, and spread the whole event out on a point-to-point course. You run, then swim, then run again, then swim, and so on. The event I did was a “sprint” distance event, comprised of five swims and six runs spread out across 12 miles of trails and lake.

It took me nearly three hours to complete, and at no point was I sprinting.

Unlike triathlon, where you abandon your gear after each portion, swimrun requires you to carry all of your stuff from start to finish. Thus, you must swim while wearing your running shoes, run while clad in your wetsuit, and carry your pull buoy, hand paddles — swimming gear that is allowed — for the entire journey. This makes for some hilarious blunders along the way (more on this later).

Within the swimrun world, Ötillö is the proverbial Ironman — the most recognizable brand of events. Outside has a somewhat rich history of chronicling the Swedish company, first in 2013, then in 2014, and also in a 2017 Brad Stulberg column. In 2019, longtime contributor W. Hodding Carter wrote an Outside feature story about his foibles at the Ötillö world series race in Cannes, France, where he and his partner paddled across the green-blue Mediterranean and jogged through the French Riviera.

In all of those stories, Ötillö swimrun races come across as grueling, fun, and distinctly European. The racing format, after all, was developed in Sweden and first held on the chain of islands just east of Stockholm, which is still the site of the annual Ötillö world championships. The name “Ötillö” is a Swedish word that loosely translates to “island to island.”

Good news for Americans: Ötillö is no longer just for the Euros. In 2023, the series expanded to North America after it purchased a budding collection of U.S. swimrun races called the Odyssey series, that were co-founded by a guy named Lars Finanger. Finanger and I were roommates in Boulder 20 years ago, back when we were both dirtbag triathletes chasing a daily endorphin high.

Now, Finanger is trying to spread the Swedish swimrun gospel in the U.S., where jogging trails while wearing a wetsuit is about as popular as pickled herring.

“We started out with a lot of triathletes, Ironman finishers, Eco-Challenge racers — it was a really eclectic group of endurance athletes,” Finanger told me. “Now we have a small but dedicated following of athletes who see themselves as Swimrunners first, even though they might do a triathlon or a bike race, too.”

Finanger first learned about Ötillö from the 2013 Outside story. He was burned out on triathlon and road bike racing and was looking for a new challenge, so he signed up for the world championship event in Stockholm, which is comprised of 38 miles of running and 5.7 miles of swimming, and requires participants to compete in teams of two. It’s a grueling test of endurance and grit that takes many teams upwards of 10 hours to complete.

“I had this big grin on my face throughout the whole thing, even though the water was so frickin’ cold and the trails made you feel like you were running through the hobbit scene from Lord of the Rings,” Finanger told me. “I realized we didn’t have anything like it in the USA.”

Finanger wanted to start his own race but didn’t know how. As luck would have it, he wasn’t the only person intrigued by the format. Jeffrey Cole, a veteran of the endurance sports industry and a longtime triathlon race director, emailed Finanger about the swimrun format. Cole said that Casco Bay, Maine, near his home in Kennebunkport, was a perfect place to recreate the island hopping of Sweden’s Ötillö. In 2016, they started the inaugural Odyssey event along the Maine coast.

“I think about the history of triathlon, where athletes raced in Kona and then went back home to put on their own races where they lived,” Finanger said. “We wanted to produce a swimrun that we’d have wanted to do ourselves.”

Their model was a success. Finanger and Cole started other swimrun races in the U.S.: Orcas Island, Washington; Cedarville, Michigan; Austin, Texas; and even one on California’s Catalina Island. These events are held annually, and the participation numbers now surpass 400 at some races.

Cole died in 2018, and Finanger kept the business going alongside a handful of new partners. In 2023, Ötillö approached them about purchasing the Odyssey series and bringing it under the corporate umbrella. Finanger said it was a no-brainer.

“It meant partnering with the gold standard in our sport,” he said.

These days, the former Odyssey races award points to elite athletes that help them qualify for the world championships race in Stockholm. But they also boast shorter distances, solo categories, and a laid-back vibe. Because the purpose of the events, Finanger told me, is to attract newbies like yours truly to the format.

“We are still this meeting ground for all of these different types of athletes — swimmers, cyclists, triathletes,” he said. “The one they have in common is they are adventure-minded.”

Qualifying for a race in Europe was not on my mind as I prepared for the 2026 Colorado Ötillö. The shorter sprint distance did not offer qualification points toward the Ötillö World Championship; however, the much longer World Series race in Colorado (23 total miles) did.

When I asked Finanger for strategic advice, he just laughed me off. “Just have fun out there, dude,” he said. He reminded me that the whole point was to have a personal adventure while swimming and jogging my way around the lake.

The laid-back atmosphere at the start line reinforced Finanger’s advice. Over the years, I’ve nervously waited for the start of Ironman triathlons, marathons, and almost every type of bike race out there. At Ötillö, the vibe was extremely chill — like what you’d expect at the start of a 5K color run or a boozy bicycle parade and not a three- to five-hour test of stamina.

Still, I had to remind myself to have fun more than a few times during the early moments of the race. Following a fast one-mile run to start the race, we plunged into Horsetooth Reservoir for the first swim.

I’m a former NCAA Division III swimmer and multiple Ironman finisher, and I’m accustomed to swimming in choppy water filled with thrashing arms and legs. But I struggled to find my groove with the swimrun gear, and I had to stop a few times to position my pull buoy between my legs and learn to swim while wearing sneakers. An even bigger challenge hit when I exited the water.

I stepped onto the clay beach and immediately stumbled around like a newborn fawn. I felt like I’d just gulped a tequila shot or three. I lumbered toward the trail and zigzagged my way up a hill like a punch-drunk boxer.

Upon exiting the water, seasoned swimrunners fastened their pull buoys to their waists with a cord, tucking the apparatus to their lumbar sections like a fanny pack. I fumbled to secure mine as I trotted along, the buoy bouncing off of my butt. As I twisted and twirled the buoy, one of my plastic swim paddles slipped from my hand, and I heard it crash into a bush. Should I stop to look or keep going? I wondered. I chose to stop.

The short pause allowed my thumping heart rate to chill. Soon, my brain fog cleared, and I was able to focus. I found the paddle, and as I jogged along the trail, I familiarized myself with the goofy gear. I practiced tucking and untucking my pull buoy into its tether. I threaded the fingers of my right hand through the elastic loops on my hand paddles to keep them secure.

During a triathlon, you’re constantly using products that are over-engineered for the specific modality of the moment: aerodynamic bike stuff, cushioned shoes, high-visibility swim goggles. Part of the fun quirk of a swimrun is learning to manage the wrong gear when it’s not used for the right job.

My confidence increased, and I picked up the pace, jogging past swimrunners and moving to the side as others jogged past me. People seemed stoked to be on the trail. Nobody seemed so caught up in their own struggles as to skip the customary “Lookin’ good!” or “Go get ’em!” during a pass.

The sprint course deviated from the World Series route near the five-mile mark, and I bid adieu to the athletes who were tackling the longer distance. I saw a handful of sprint racers up ahead of me and decided to push my pace on a long switchback ascent to try and catch them.

Perhaps it was my soaring body temperature inside my wetsuit, or my lingering buzz. But as I closed in on the guy ahead of me, my mind wandered, and I tripped on a rock, completed a somersault, and landed in the cactus. Bewildered, I made a mental note about swimrun: shit can hit the fan if you don’t pay attention.

The fall meant that I had to spend a few minutes plucking spines from my backside once I crossed the line. But the ordeal delivered one of my lasting takeaways from the race.

Perfection does not exist during a swimrun. Even during a shorter distance race, you’re bound to inhale water, drop your gear, battle through exhaustion, or trip and stumble. How you deal with these setbacks defines your experience out there.

I’ve spent the last 25 years trying out different endurance sports. And I’m familiar with the progression that most athletes follow with these sports. You try out a sport and fall in love with the adventure, camaraderie, and community. Then, as the years go by, you focus more on your results, and before you know it, you’re completing a training regimen, following a performance-oriented diet, and dreaming of a top-10 finish.

I will absolutely compete in another Ötillö Swimrun event, but I don’t envision myself ever getting too hardcore about the format. Simply doing a swimrun gave me enough feeling of adventure and carefree silliness, without an ounce of self-seriousness. Sucking at the format provided half of the joy. And I’m more than happy to chase that feeling again.

#9011. Hawaiian Interisland Awards — Hop Between Islands

Picture this: you've just landed in Honolulu after a long transcontinental flight. You've got four days on Maui planned, and then a few nights on Kauai before heading home. The problem? Those interisland flights add up fast — Hawaiian Airlines will gladly charge you $150–$250 *per person* for a 20-to-40-minute hop between islands. For a family of four, that's easily $600–$1,000 in airfare just to island-hop, on top of everything else you've already spent to get to Hawaii. Now imagine paying 7,500 HawaiianMiles per person instead — miles you transferred from your American Express Membership Rewards account at a 1:1 ratio just a day or two before booking. Suddenly, that $150–$250 ticket costs you points worth less than a nice dinner. At 3.3 cents per point on the high end, you're extracting extraordinary value from miles that most people leave sitting in an account doing nothing. This is what the ChooseFI community means when we talk about finding pricing inefficiencies in loyalty programs. Hawaiian Airlines prices these interisland segments on a dynamic award chart — but because these are short, regional hops operated almost entirely on 717s and A321s between islands most people aren't cross-shopping for redemptions, the program hasn't inflated the price the way major international carriers have. The sweet spot holds. The math is simple and satisfying: a cash ticket from Honolulu (HNL) to Kahului, Maui (OGG) or Lihue, Kauai (LIH) typically runs $100–$250. You're redeeming 7,500 miles to cover that cost, which means you're getting **1.3 to 3.3 cents per point** in value — above what most programs deliver on domestic redemptions. And because Hawaiian charges **zero fuel surcharges** on its own-operated flights, every mile goes toward the ticket price, not toward fees. For the FI-minded traveler who planned a multi-island Hawaii trip anyway, this redemption doesn't just save money — it reframes how you think about points. These aren't bonuses. They're a currency, and knowing where to spend them is the skill.

The core insight here is deceptively simple: HawaiianMiles prices interisland flights at a flat 7,500 miles in economy, and that price is shockingly stable relative to what these tickets actually cost in cash.

Here's why this works as a pricing inefficiency. Hawaiian Airlines operates a near-monopoly on interisland travel in Hawaii. There's limited true competition for these routes (go! Mokulele operates turboprops on some routes, but Hawaiian dominates the jet service). Because cash demand is inelastic — visitors need to get between islands — Hawaiian charges a premium in cash. But the HawaiianMiles award program hasn't kept pace with those cash price increases in the same aggressive way that programs like United MileagePlus or Delta SkyMiles have. The result: 7,500 miles per segment, consistently, while cash prices climb.

Now let's talk about how you actually get those miles into your account.

The primary transfer path the ChooseFI community uses is American Express Membership Rewards → HawaiianMiles at a 1:1 ratio. If you have the Amex Gold, Platinum, or a no-annual-fee Amex Everyday card earning MR points, you can transfer directly to Hawaiian. Transfer speed is 1–2 days — not instant, so plan accordingly and don't wait until the last minute.

Two other paths exist if you're working with different currencies:

One critical nuance: HawaiianMiles are earned primarily through flying, not credit card spend. Hawaiian does have a co-branded credit card, but it's not a top earner for most people's daily spend. This means your primary accumulation strategy is transfer partners — Amex MR and Bilt are your best levers.

Another key detail: Hawaiian miles never expire. This matters because you can slowly accumulate miles across multiple statement cycles, transfer when you're ready to book, and not feel rushed. There's no expiration clock running against you.

Finally, the no fuel surcharges policy is a genuine differentiator. Many programs — particularly those involving European carriers — tack on $300–$600 in surcharges that gut your redemption's net value. HawaiianMiles charges no fuel surcharges on Hawaiian-operated flights. Your 7,500 miles covers the flight. Taxes and fees on interisland tickets are minimal, often just a few dollars. What you see is what you get.

Go to hawaiianairlines.com and use the 'Book' tool, selecting 'Reward Travel' as your travel type. Enter your route — for example, HNL to OGG (Honolulu to Kahului, Maui) or HNL to LIH (Honolulu to Lihue, Kauai). Plug in your desired travel date and search. You're looking for economy award space priced at 7,500 miles. Availability on interisland routes is almost always wide open — this is one of the best availability scores (5/5) of any sweet spot in this guide series, but it costs nothing to confirm before you transfer.

If you don't have a HawaiianMiles account, create one at hawaiianairlines.com — it takes about two minutes and is free. Note your HawaiianMiles number. You'll need it for the transfer step.

From Amex Membership Rewards: Log into your Amex account, navigate to 'Membership Rewards,' select 'Transfer Points,' and choose Hawaiian Airlines HawaiianMiles as the destination. Enter your HawaiianMiles number and the number of miles you want to transfer (at minimum, 7,500 per person you're booking). Transfers process in 1–2 days.

From Bilt Rewards: Log into your Bilt app or biltrewards.com, navigate to 'Redeem,' select 'Transfer to Airline Partner,' and choose Hawaiian Airlines at 1:1. Same 1–2 day transfer window.

From Marriott Bonvoy: Use this only as a last resort due to the 3:1 ratio. Navigate to Bonvoy's transfer portal and select HawaiianMiles. Allow up to 5 days.

Once your miles land (check your HawaiianMiles account balance), return to hawaiianairlines.com, log in, and re-run your award search. Select the flight you want, confirm the 7,500-mile price, and proceed through checkout. Taxes on interisland awards are typically just a few dollars — no fuel surcharges apply.

HawaiianMiles opens its booking window 330 days out. If you're planning a Hawaii trip far in advance and have specific flight times in mind, you can search and book early. That said, given the excellent availability on these routes, booking 2–4 weeks out is usually fine.

This is rare for interisland routes, but if it happens, try: searching adjacent dates, looking at different departure times on the same route, or checking alternate routing (e.g., OGG to LIH instead of HNL to LIH directly). Interisland availability doesn't fluctuate the way transatlantic business class does.

Let's make this concrete. You're planning a two-week Hawaii trip for two people. You've booked your Honolulu arrival flight separately, and now you need to connect the dots between islands: Honolulu (HNL) to Kahului, Maui (OGG) mid-trip, and then Maui (OGG) to Lihue, Kauai (LIH) before heading home.

The cash price check: Pull up hawaiianairlines.com and look at what these tickets retail for. On a typical mid-trip travel day, the HNL→OGG segment is priced at $189 per person. The OGG→LIH hop runs $149 per person. For two travelers, that's $676 in cash — before you've bought a single plate of shave ice.

The points price: Each segment costs 7,500 HawaiianMiles per person in economy. Two passengers, two flights: 30,000 HawaiianMiles total, plus roughly $10–$20 in taxes and fees across both bookings. No fuel surcharges.

The CPP calculation: You're replacing $676 in cash spending with 30,000 miles. That's 2.25 cents per point — well above the 0.8–1.2 cpp you'd expect on typical HawaiianMiles redemptions, and solidly within the 1.3–3.3 cpp sweet spot range for this redemption.

What the experience looks like: Hawaiian's interisland product is no-frills — these are 20-to-40-minute flights on Boeing 717s. You won't get a meal or premium service. But you will get a reliable, on-time carrier, clean aircraft, and the undeniable satisfaction of hopping between two of the most beautiful island destinations on Earth without opening your wallet at the gate.

For the ChooseFI traveler, the win isn't the in-flight experience — it's the mental accounting shift. You budgeted for interisland flights; now that budget goes to a sunset sailing charter or a snorkeling excursion instead. The points paid for the planes. The cash funds the memories.

Do: Transfer Points in the Right Batch Size HawaiianMiles doesn't allow you to transfer partial miles back out, so calculate exactly how many you need before initiating a transfer. For two passengers on two flights, that's 30,000 miles. Transfer exactly that amount — or a small buffer — rather than dumping your entire MR balance into a program you may not use frequently.

Do: Use Amex MR or Bilt as Your Primary Earning Strategy Since HawaiianMiles are earned primarily through flying, your accumulation plan should center on transferable currencies. The Amex Gold Card (4x on dining and groceries) and Amex Platinum (5x on flights) are elite MR earners. Bilt's no-annual-fee card earning on rent is underused by the ChooseFI community for exactly this kind of transfer.

Do: Search for Availability Before You Transfer This is worth repeating as a pro tip because new points travelers make this mistake constantly. Transfer speeds are 1–2 days for Amex MR and Bilt. Don't transfer points and then discover the flight you wanted is sold out. Always confirm availability first, then transfer, then book immediately once miles land.

Avoid: Using Marriott Bonvoy for This Transfer At a 3:1 ratio, you'd spend 22,500 Bonvoy points for a 7,500-mile award. Bonvoy points are worth approximately 0.7–0.9 cpp on their own best redemptions. The math doesn't hold here — save your Bonvoy points for hotel redemptions.

Do: Consider the Merger Context Hawaiian Airlines is in the process of merging with Alaska Airlines, and HawaiianMiles may eventually transition into Alaska Mileage Plan. Pay attention to program announcements. This could change transfer partners, award pricing, or program structure. The current sweet spot exists now — book it while the program operates under its current rules.

Avoid: Waiting for a 'Better' Redemption on These Miles HawaiianMiles are a limited-use currency. They're excellent for interisland and mainland-to-Hawaii flights, but they don't transfer to other airlines and don't unlock international business class sweet spots. If you've got miles in this program, use them for exactly what they're designed for — Hawaiian flights — rather than letting them sit hoping for a better opportunity that may never come.

Do: Book Multiple Segments in a Single Trip If you're doing a true multi-island itinerary, every interisland hop is 7,500 miles. Three islands means two hops — 15,000 miles per person. Plan your island sequence to minimize backtracking, and book all segments at once once your miles transfer.

Make multi-island trips affordable with the right points strategy

Most visitors to Hawaii stick to one island because interisland flights add $100-$400+ per person to the trip cost. By using points for these short hops, you unlock a fundamentally different Hawaii experience — island-hopping from Oahu to Maui to the Big Island to Kauai without the airfare costs stacking up. This is a multiplier strategy: you are not just saving on one flight, you are enabling an entirely different type of trip. Combining a points-funded mainland-to-Hawaii flight with points-funded interisland hops creates a nearly free (in cash) multi-island Hawaiian vacation.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Decide which islands you want to visit and in what order. The most common combinations are Oahu + Maui, Oahu + Big Island, or a three-island itinerary. Map out how many interisland hops you need so you know the total points required.

Check Hawaiian Airlines (7,500 miles each way), Southwest (variable, typically 4,000-8,000 points), and United (5,000-7,500 miles) for each interisland segment. Southwest often offers the best flexibility with no change fees and no blackout dates.

For Hawaiian Airlines, transfer Amex Membership Rewards. For Southwest, earn Rapid Rewards directly or transfer from Chase (transfer to Southwest is currently limited). For United segments, transfer from Chase or use Turkish Miles&Smiles for even lower pricing.

Book each interisland hop as a separate one-way award. This gives you maximum flexibility to mix airlines and optimize pricing per segment. One-way awards have no penalty compared to round trips on these short routes.

Align your interisland hops with your arrival and departure flights. Arrive on one island and depart from a different one (open-jaw booking) to avoid backtracking. For example, arrive Honolulu, hop to Maui, depart Maui to the mainland.

Hawaiian Airlines has the most extensive interisland network and offers the most daily frequencies. Southwest Airlines also operates key interisland routes (Honolulu-Maui, Honolulu-Kona, Honolulu-Lihue). United flies select interisland segments as well. Each airline has different award pricing and transfer partner access.

Hawaiian Airlines interisland awards typically price at 7,500 HawaiianMiles each way. Southwest varies by cash fare but generally costs 4,000-8,000 Rapid Rewards points each way for interisland hops. United interisland segments can be booked for 5,000-7,500 miles using various Star Alliance partner programs.

Yes, especially when booking multiple hops. A family of four making two interisland hops at $150 each way would spend $1,200 in cash. Converting that to points frees up significant cash for accommodations, activities, and dining. The per-point value (1.5-2.5 cents) is reasonable, and the trip flexibility gained is substantial.

A popular strategy is to fly into Honolulu (Oahu), hop to Maui for beaches and Haleakala, then continue to the Big Island (Kona) for volcanoes and snorkeling, and optionally finish on Kauai for dramatic scenery. Each hop is 30-60 minutes. Allow 2-3 days minimum per island.

This redemption was built for families and couples planning a multi-island Hawaii vacation — full stop. If you're visiting multiple islands (which most Hawaii first-timers and repeat visitors do), you're already mentally budgeting for interisland flights. This sweet spot simply redirects that cash budget back into your pocket and replaces it with points.

Families get a 5/5 Family Friendly score here for good reason: availability is wide open, booking is simple, and the economics scale beautifully. Four people, two hops = 60,000 miles to cover potentially $1,200+ in interisland airfare. That's an extraordinary displacement of vacation cash.

Beginners are explicitly welcomed by this redemption's design. There's no partner airline complexity, no fuel surcharge math to calculate, no routing rules to decode. You search on Hawaiian's website, you transfer points, you book. The 5/5 Beginner Friendly and Easy to Book scores reflect that this is genuinely one of the simplest award redemptions you can execute.

Minimum points needed: 7,500 HawaiianMiles per person per segment. For a solo traveler doing two hops, that's 15,000 miles. For a family of four doing two hops, that's 60,000 miles.

This is NOT for: Travelers who don't have an Amex MR or Bilt account and no path to earning HawaiianMiles quickly. It's also not ideal for travelers who only need a single interisland flight — the opportunity cost of setting up the transfer relationship for 7,500 miles may not be worth it unless you're already accumulating MR points for other redemptions.

This redemption earns a **Beginner** rating — and it genuinely deserves it. In a world of waitlists, fuel surcharges, routing rules, and phone-only bookings, Hawaiian interisland awards are refreshingly clean. **What makes it easy:** Award availability is consistently excellent (5/5). The booking portal is functional and user-friendly. There are no fuel surcharges to calculate. Miles never expire, so there's no pressure. You can complete the entire redemption — from transfer initiation to confirmed booking — in about 48 hours. **The one genuine friction point:** Earning HawaiianMiles isn't as straightforward as earning Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex MR. Hawaiian doesn't have a widely-used co-branded credit card for most people's everyday spend. This means you're dependent on transfer partners, and the Amex MR and Bilt paths are your primary options. If you don't have either, this redemption becomes harder to access. **Tip 1:** Start with an Amex card that earns Membership Rewards — the Amex Gold is the ChooseFI community favorite for everyday earning. Once you're accumulating MR points, you have a direct path to Hawaiian via a 1:1 transfer. **Tip 2:** Always search award availability before transferring. It takes 30 seconds and protects you from the one mistake that could derail an otherwise smooth booking. **Tip 3:** Don't overthink the merger situation. Hawaiian and Alaska remain separate programs today. Book what's in front of you. If you can earn Amex MR points, you can execute this redemption. It's the perfect first award booking for a ChooseFI member who wants to see how the system works without risking complexity.

Interisland awards are the key that unlocks multi-island Hawaii vacations without the stacking airfare costs that keep most travelers on a single island. At 7,500-10,000 miles per hop, the points cost is modest, and the trip transformation is significant. Whether you use Hawaiian Airlines miles, Southwest Rapid Rewards, or United partner programs, the strategy is the same: let points handle the short hops so your cash stays in your pocket for experiences. Combined with a points-funded mainland-to-Hawaii flight, interisland awards make a multi-island Hawaiian vacation one of the most achievable aspirational trips in travel rewards.

#9010. I Broke My Leg Training for a Marathon. The Warning Signs Were There All Along.

Here’s what I missed—and what every runner should know.

When people find out I broke my leg in several places, the first question they ask is, “How did it happen?” I wish I had a great story to tell, but here’s the truth: I broke it slowly, over many miles, as I trained for a fall marathon.

After running the London Marathon this year, I took a few weeks off to recover before I started training for Chicago. I planned on following a 16-week training plan, but because I had taken some time off, I slowly began building my base back up three weeks before the official start of my plan.

Everything went great to start. The hip pain that ailed me in the winter disappeared and my legs felt fresh. I ran a few 4-milers to gauge my fitness level, and I was shocked when I almost scored a personal best. After the second 4-miler, I felt a slight pain in my shin. I’ve had shin splints before, so I thought nothing of it. After a few more weeks of consistent running, though, the pain grew so severe that I pulled back on my running to let my shin heal.

After a month of never-ending pain, I went to the doctor for an expert opinion. After a round of X-rays, the doctor told me the issue was probably shin splints and that I could slowly return to running. I asked whether it could be a stress fracture because the pain felt more intense than a normal shin splint, but was assured my leg was fine.

Three days later at a concert at Red Rocks Amphitheater in Colorado, I turned to say hi to a friend and felt a pop. I immediately knew that I broke my leg. A rod, plate, and seven screws later, I’m now sidelined from running for months, if not longer.

Turns out, I probably did have a stress fracture–but they are hard to detect on X-rays. In fact, Runner’s World published this a story the week before my injury that details how stress fractures are “notoriously tricky to diagnose.” Our story also goes through the five stress fracture warning signs you need to pay attention to. And looking back, I checked off every box, from discomfort with activity to pain that increased throughout runs.

As runners, we know our bodies, and we know when something isn’t right. I regret not getting a second expert opinion on my leg pain. That’s my biggest takeaway from this ordeal. If something feels off, investigate it and ask a lot of questions. Don’t be afraid to be annoying. Trusting your gut is better than being holed up with a broken leg.

I know I will come back stronger than before. Not being able to run makes me appreciate it so much more. Looking back at my previous training blocks, I also know that going forward, I am going to make smarter choices. I should have added more mobility and strength training into my plan to help me reduce my injury risk. Right before sustaining my injury, Runner’s World released the comprehensive Guide to Strength Training program, and I had started completing–and loving–the six follow-along workouts provided in the guide. I can’t wait to get back to them when I’m healed.

If you’re looking to sidestep injury before it sidelines you, we have plenty of member-exclusive programs and tips to help you stay healthy. Use our Guide to Strength Training to build resilience and power as a runner, plus dive into our programs for mastering the 5K, half marathon, and marathon to learn how to train properly–and injury-free–for your next race.

Aly is the Director of Content Hype at Runner’s World. She started running over a decade ago and has run 8 marathons, plus hundreds of shorter distance races. When she isn't running, she loves watching reality competition shows, reading and curating the perfect Taylor Swift playlist.

#9009. The Best Triathlon Suits of 2026, Tested by Real-World Triathletes

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Best tri suits of 2026 rated and reviewed based on 10 criteria. (Photo: Triathlete)

Men's 2XU Light Speed React Sleeved Tri Suit

Women's 2XU Light Speed React Sleeved Tri Suit

When you look good, you feel good – and when you feel good, you race great. It’s no surprise, then, that when triathletes gear up for race day, they spend hours looking online for the best tri suit.

Indeed, in our 2025 Triathlete Community Survey, 88% of respondents said aesthetics were at least “somewhat” important, with 38% saying they wouldn’t wear what they felt was an “ugly” kit.

But a great triathlon suit is more than good-looking – ideally, it also needs to fit well, carry your nutrition stash, provide an aero- and hydro-dynamic advantage, and protect the tender bits from chafing.

We’re asking a lot of tri suits these days, but the industry has stepped up to the challenge. Legacy brands like Zoot and Coeur, as well as newcomers Ryzon and Tri-Fit, have made it possible for triathletes to find not only a suit that meets their practical race-day needs but also shows off their own personal style.

With so many options available, we asked the Philly Tri Club and Triathlete contributors to help with real-world testing of the top triathlon suits of 2026. The 150-strong club is all about creating an inclusive training community, and club members in a variety of shapes and sizes put tri suits through the paces, wearing them through workouts and races and making note of what works and what doesn’t in their triathlon kit reviews. Here’s what they had to say about the best triathlon suits of 2026.

In our 2025 Triathlete Community Survey, we asked readers what brands of triathlon apparel they had in their closets. Though more than 20 brands were represented, the top six are familiar names in the industry.

Pockets: 2 back pockets, 2 svelte front pockets, 1 neck ice pocket

The Regna Elite Trisuit offers a custom fit via an app that completes an AI-powered body scan for a fit based on your unique features. For the ultimate test, we tasked Triathlete contributor Jon Dorn and his wife Heather with testing it out. Jon stands at 6’6” and is self-described as very slender. His wife is 5’3” “buxom, and more powerfully built,” according to Jon.

“I’ve finally found a tri suit that doesn’t chafe my ass or distract me as various sensitive parts start smarting,” said Jon.

Heather noted that the suit was a 95% perfect fit, though the midsection was slightly loose. As someone who doesn’t fit into the “one-size-fits-most” size structure, she was still quite pleased. “This is the best my undercarriage has felt in a tri kit in years,” she reported after a four-hour training ride.

Ultimately, the pair found that the price tag is the biggest deterrent and only really justifiable if you’re someone who doesn’t fit into a standard tri kit well.

If you’re looking for a budget triathlon suit for a sprint or Olympic triathlon that won’t chafe, the 2XU Core Tri Suit is a safe bet. It lacks adequate padding and pockets sizable enough to carry enough nutrition for long-course training or racing, but at the $200 price point, it’s a rare find for short-course racing.

It’s light on compression if that’s your preference and when it comes to breathability, the suit was disappointing, so ideally plan to wear it in more forgiving weather, as our tester found that it trapped heat and sweat more than other comparable suits.

Our tester found it hard to criticize anything about this suit because it fit snugly and comfortably. While she doesn’t normally wear sleeved tri suits, she was pleasantly surprised by how thin and breathable the fabric on these sleeves was, to the point that she forgot the sleeves were even there.

The tri suit has ample compression, especially in the core. The one detractor is that this suit only comes in black or black and white, which is a little generic and not as fun as some of the other options on this list. User beware, too: our tester noticed a bit of color leaking when handwashing the suit. Consider wearing the suit for shorter training sessions or wearing a belt with additional fuel, as the two back pockets are medium-sized and diagonally aligned.

Pockets: 3 back pockets, 2 inner front pockets, 1 neck ice pocket

When it comes to tri suits, it’s the little details that make a brand stand out. In this case, Tri-Fit’s attention to pockets – six in total, including one explicitly for holding ice on your neck during hot races – is reason enough to consider the Vortex for a long-course race.

Testers liked the fit, fabric choice, design, pockets, and overall feel, noting that it looks great with small logos, lightweight fabric, and comfortable chamois padding for shorter events. The chest zips up tightly, preventing wind trap, and performed well during rides and runs.

However, there was substantial drag in the water, and the vent holes under the arms caused chafing – vented fabric would be preferable, as would slightly more compression on the legs. In all, however, the Tri Fit feels premium, and with a few minor design tweaks, could quickly become a favorite tri suit.

Pockets: 1 lower-back channel pocket, 1 neck ice pocket

This tri suit performed adequately in the heat, thanks to the use of smart temp technology, which dials up evaporation from the skin to the air as body temperature rises. The super-thin and light chamois also mitigates heat well, especially on long rides, and strategically-placed airflow channels on the shoulders and back help things feel cool and fast on the bike.

However, the top zipper rubbed against the chest, causing discomfort during running and biking. It also chafed at the neckline due to the lack of a zipper cover. Testers liked that it fit well, but disliked that the zipper needed a fabric cover and that the white top was see-through, especially when wet coming out of the swim or sweating on the run (women testers noted their sports bra was visible while wearing the suit in a race).

At $125, Black Bibs brand has created a budget-friendly triathlon suit that stands out in a market full of offerings $300 or more. But “budget” should not be conflated with “cheap” here – the suit fits well, provides exceptional compression, and is a classic style (men’s and women’s one-piece colorways include a solid black as well as a black bottom half with navy, burgundy, or white uppers). Openings for the legs and arms use silicone “power bands” to keep the suit secure throughout a workout or race, and no chafing was reported. The suit also proved extremely durable both on and off the race course, holding up through dozens of laundry cycles without shrinking, pilling, or splitting seams.

The initial impression of the chamois was mediocre, but improved with subsequent use and resolved itself after several rides. Testers reported drag when swimming, with the neckline sagging, and recommended use with a wetsuit. Dislikes included poor moisture wicking, especially in the upper body, and unusually high rear pockets.

Unlike some tri brands, where women’s suits are simply a smaller version of the men’s, Coeur tri suits are designed with a woman’s physique in mind, from the contours of the suit to the women’s specific seamless chamois. Testers also liked the supple fabric and one-piece design with a full front zipper and high-rise short beneath, allowing for breathability and extra roominess in the torso.

This tri suit performed exceptionally well on the swim and run, but some chafing was experienced on the bike – chamois cream is recommended. The arm openings run slightly small, so athletes with muscular arms should size up or opt for the sleeveless version. Luckily, Coeur offers a variety of competitively-priced women’s tri suit configurations in matching colorways: sleeved, sleeveless, sports bra/shorts, aero tops, and tri tops with built-in bras.

Testers liked the sleek, minimalist, and professional appearance of the monochromatic Arise tri suit, as well as its stretchy, comfortable, and “slippery” feel that allowed for movement and flexibility without chafing. It remained comfortable even when wet, ran true to size, didn’t create unnecessary drag, and worked well with other clothing. This tri suit generally performed well across all conditions and disciplines, with no reported poor performance or chafing.

However, a dime-sized hole appeared in the left armpit after two wears, which was surprising and disappointing, given the suit’s $335 price tag. Testers also wished the back pocket was deeper and had multiple compartments.

Pockets: 1 rear pocket, two side pockets, 3 interior pockets

Zoot has been a mainstay of triathlon apparel for more than 40 years, and for good reason – users recognize the balance of form and function present in many of its products. The suits, designed by endurance athletes, for endurance athletes, come in a variety of designs, including flashy patterns and colorways.

The latest offering from Zoot, the Ultra Tri P1, performed well during swims in the ocean, bike rides on a trainer and outside, and runs outside. Testers liked its comfortable and true-to-size fit as well as built-in UPF 35 sun protection fabric.

However, the pockets were not very big, making it difficult to carry proper nutrition during training rides or runs – testers recommended wearing the suit for short-course racing or long-course events only if nutrition on the course is plentiful. The zipper was also annoying and rubbed a bit, requiring multiple adjustments while running.

Overall, however, the suit was rated as “top-notch” for comfort, breathability, and weight.

#9008. How to Master the Run/Walk Method: Improve Your Pace and Recovery

Boost your speed, increase your fitness, and enhance your recovery with a run/walk training approach.

To pick up your pace, hit new distance milestones, or snag your next race PR, you may not need to train faster or longer. Instead, the smartest training strategy for hitting your next running goal could be harnessing the power of walking.

Runners of all abilities have used the run/walk method to improve their training, recovery, and race-day performance for decades. Working brief and intentional walk breaks into your runs is a proven plan for sustainable training, and is great for all runners—from newcomers just getting started to veterans with years of racing and miles logged on their watches.

In the Runner’s World guide, How to Master the Run/Walk Method: Improve Your Pace and Recovery, we’ll teach you the ins and outs of the run/walk training strategy, along with the health and fitness benefits that can come from incorporating walk intervals into your runs.

In How to Master the Run/Walk Method: Improve Your Pace and Recovery, we’ll teach you:

The run/walk method is as straightforward and simple as it sounds. Instead of running nonstop, you’ll incorporate short, planned walk intervals into your run, alternating between running and walking throughout your session.

The training strategy was pioneered by the late Jeff Galloway in the 1970s. Galloway, a member of the 1972 U.S. Olympic team in the 10,000 meters, began coaching a group of beginner runners to finish a 5K and 10K and realized that adding walk breaks into their training runs helped them finish their miles feeling strong and confident. He had his athletes follow the “huff and puff” rule, meaning that whenever they began to strain their breathing on a run, they would take a brief walk break.

By the end of the athletes’ 10-week training block, they all not only made it to their respective finish lines, but did so injury-free—and had fun along the way. Hence, the run/walk method was officially born.

“Working to run nonstop for 30 minutes or for an entire half marathon or a 50K ultra is an impressive feat,” says program host and certified personal trainer Carissa Galloway. “But with the run/walk method, runners have the ability to run faster and go farther. They can best fatigue and avoid injuries by incorporating precisely planned walk intervals.”

Walk intervals can vary in length, but most advanced run/walkers almost always incorporate 30-second walk durations into their runs. It’s the magic number that gives your heart and legs a chance to recover from your running portions, and return to your run pace feeling strong.

There’s proof in the research when it comes to the effectiveness of the run/walk method for stronger, pain-free running.

One study of recreational runners completing a marathon found that those who followed the run/walk method reported significantly less muscle pain and fatigue after finishing their race. Of those run/walkers, less than 5 percent of them reported extreme exhaustion after the marathon, compared to more than 40 percent of those who ran continuously.

Another study conducted in Australia in 2024 asked participants to complete a 12-week run/walk program with three 30-minute sessions each week. Of the participants, those who said they had chronic lower back pain reported significantly reduced pain and disability.

But the upsides of adding walk breaks into your runs go beyond reducing both post-race and persistent pain. The run/walk method can also help you:

One of the biggest myths about the run/walk method: It’s a strategy reserved for new or slow runners. That’s far from reality. Using run/walk doesn’t automatically make you slower than other runners, and any level of runner can use the strategy.

Many run/walkers find that walking for short periods helps them pick up the pace on the running portions, and their overall speed quickens. That’s because short bouts of walking during your run can help your cardiovascular system recover and make picking up the pace easier during the run portions. You may even notice that you feel more energized and have the strength to cover longer distances using the run/walk method.

And while it’s certainly a smart training strategy for runners logging their first miles, the run/walk method can help advanced athletes boost their efficiency, pick up their speed, and even conquer longer distances they never knew were possible. Advanced run/walkers may even effectively use the strategy to hit an ambitious performance goal on race day—like running a Boston Marathon qualifying time or a big personal best.

“Whether you clock an average nine-minute mile running nonstop, or you do it by taking walk breaks, you can still finish a marathon in under four hours,” Galloway says. “You’ll just use a different method to get there.”

Ashley is Editor of Content Hype at Hearst’s Enthusiast & Wellness Group. She is a former collegiate runner at UNC Asheville where she studied mass communication. Ashley loves all things running; she has raced two marathons, plus has covered some of the sport’s top events in her career, including the Paris Olympics, U.S. Olympic Trials and multiple World Marathon Majors.

#9007. What Is the SuperHalfs Series? Inside the Popular Half Marathon Challenge

All the information you need, including race dates, registration and course details, and how to prepare for racing abroad.

According to the 2026 Running USA Global Runner Survey or more than 11,000 runners, the half marathon is the most popular race distance. Not only that, but almost half of those runners would be happy to travel more than 500 miles for a good half marathon (and marathon). This might be why the SuperHalfs, a European series of six races through Lisbon, Cardiff, Prague, Berlin, Valencia, and Copenhagen, have become so popular.

These races are not neighborhood events, but international spectacles, and they are difficult to get into. A few of the courses, including Copenhagen (2014), Cardiff (2016), and Valencia (2018), have even hosted the World Athletics Half Marathon Championships. Dubbed “a super series for the ordinary runner,” according to Mark Janik, CEO North America of Sports Tours International, the SuperHalfs are perfect for runners who want to combine racing with travel.

While the early 2027 races are sold out, you can start planning for the autumn 2027 and 2028 races. No rush, though, as you have a lifetime to complete all six races and, once you do, you’ll earn more bling—a seventh medal. If you’re ready to set some international race goals, we have the training plans you need to get to the start lines of these extraordinary competitions.

Date: March 7, 2027 (Sunday)Location: Almada, PortugalNumber of Runners: 35,000Time Limit: 3 hours

A favorite course of many elite runners, racers enjoy views along the River Tagus and journey over the 25 de Abril Bridge, once the longest suspension bridge in Europe and a twin of the Golden Gate Bridge in San Francisco. This race is the only time when pedestrians can cross, says Sadie Lowell, JetSetting_Runner, who has helped runners plan their international runcations.

Although Lisbon is a hilly city, the course is flat, and typically serves up nice weather, as Portugal’s capital city boasts about 300 days of sunshine most years. It is also famous for record-setting runs including in 20216 Jacob Kiplimo from Uganda broke the world record—again—during this race with a time of 57:20.

The lottery for this race typically opens in June. Follow the race on Instagram for updates!

Date: April 3, 2027 (Saturday)Location: Prague, Czech RepublicNumber of Runners: 17,000Time Limit: 3 hoursREGISTER

Organizers of the Prague Half Marathon, with a theme of “all runners are beautiful,” may have been inspired to create that phrase because the race course itself is considered so lovely. The sights include castles, rivers, bridges, and historic parts of Prague. For the 13.1-mile course, runners will complete a few loops and turnarounds, with the race starting at Bubenské Nábřeží, Holešovice and ending at Jan Palach Square in the Old Town of Prague.

The idea for the SuperHalfs was born in Prague by Czech creator, Carlo Capalbo, and the series is managed by RunCzech. It’s a truly international event: More than half of the runners who participated in 2025 were from other countries.

The lottery for this race typically opens in August. Follow the race on Instagram for updates!

Date: April 4, 2027 (Sunday)Location: Berlin, GermanyNumber of Runners: over 42,000Time Limit: 3:15 hours

This is the largest of the six races, and, throughout the half, you’ll run past many of Berlin’s most iconic landmarks starting with the Victory Column monument in the center of the Tiergarten district. If you’re lucky, you might also spot a glimpse of Checkpoint Charlie as you make your way through the course. The race ends with a celebratory run through the Brandenburg Gate before reaching the finish.

After the race, celebrate your success with delicious German pretzels—the salt is good for rehydration!

This lottery usually opens in April, with results announced in June. Follow the race on Instagram for updates!

Date: September 19, 2027 (Sunday)Location: Copenhagen, DenmarkNumber of Runners: over 45,000Time Limit: 3 hours

Located in the heart of Copenhagen, the course takes runners through the historic inner city as well as the city’s charming and colorful bridge districts. The race prides itself on being a party filled with music from DJs, bands, and choirs. It also features high-energy cheering sections called “Power Zones” designed to energize you through the miles. And if you were lucky enough to snag a bib for 2026, you’ll be in for a treat because Copenhagen is set to host the 2026 World Championships.

The 2027 lottery for this race will likely open in March. Follow the race on Instagram for updates!

Date: October 3, 2027 (Sunday)Location: Cardiff, WalesNumber of Runners: over 28,000Time Limit: 4 hours

One of the smallest cities in the series, Cardiff, the capital of Wales, is 150 miles west of London. On the half-marathon route, runners travel past Cardiff Castle, the Principality Stadium, Civic Centre, and Cardiff Bay—all favorite tourist spots.

The race is known for its cheering sections and you may hear: “Pob Lwc!” or Welsh for “Good Luck!” as you’re running through the course.

While smaller than the other cities that are part of the series, this half marathon began in 2003 with only 1,500 people and now is part of the world stage of running.

The lottery for this race is usually open from through October. Follow the race on Instagram for updates!

Date: October 24, 2027Location: Valencia, SpainNumber of Runners: 25,000Time Limit: 2:45 hours

While you’ll run through the center of this Spanish city, the roads are wide so you don’t have to worry about overcrowding or slowing down. On course, you’ll see the Torres de Serranos, one of the 12 gates that formed part of the ancient city wall built at the end of the 14th century, along with the city’s famous murals, created by local artists.

Valencia is on the east coast of the Iberian Peninsula on the Mediterranean Sea, so the views of the water as you run to the finish are spectacular—and so is the food you get to indulge in afterward. (This is where paella was invented after all!)

You can register for this race just a few weeks after it’s over, typically in early November. Follow the race on Instagram for updates!

Unlike driving to an American city for a half, if you sign up for a SuperHalf race, you do need to handle more details to make sure your travel and race go smoothly.

While all of the races are in major cities with international airports, you can also travel with a company, such as Sports Tours International. They create group schedules that include multi-day hotel stays, race briefings, escorted trips to expos, some walking tours, shakeout runs, and, most importantly, race registration (which can fill up quickly!).

Whether you travel independently or with a group, it’s smart to fly in at least 48 hours before your race, Lowell tells Runner’s World. “This way you will have a buffer to pickup your bib in case of flight delays or cancellations. Many races don’t allow pick up on the morning of the race,” she explains.

You’ll also want to account for jet lag. “If you typically struggle to adjust your sleep cycle, plan to run the race on the last weekend of your trip,” Lowell says. “If you are able to adjust quickly, you can plan for running the race on your first weekend and exploring the rest of the trip.”

Once you’ve arrived, take Lowell’s advice and keep track of your eating and drinking prerace. “It can be easy when you are in a new city to forget about all the carbs you need to consume and all the water you need to drink,” she adds. “I always recommend stopping at a local grocery store and picking up some food to eat the morning of your race.”

While it may not be a selling point, keep in mind that many of these city streets are old—Lisbon was established in 1200 BCE—and weren’t designed for runners. At times, large crowds may run on narrow roads. While the courses are flat and fast, and most of the running is on large boulevards, you may have to be cautious on cobblestone streets. Of course, this is a small price to pay for an athletic adventure in a picturesque location.

Donna Raskin has had a long career as a health and fitness writer and editor of books and magazine articles. A certified run coach who has practiced yoga for many years, she also loves to lift weights, dance, and go for long walks with her hound dog, Dolly.
