#8971. Triathlon News, October 2026: Ironman Crashes, NYC Tri Returns, Middle East Racing

Tim Heming highlights the biggest news in triathlon in October 2026. (Photo: Triathlete)

In October, the triathlon world turned its eyes to the Big Island for another epic edition of the Ironman World Championship, but that didn’t stop the rest of the multisport world from serving up its usual mix of drama, debate, and headline-grabbing news.

From analyzing the sparse participation numbers at New York’s long-awaited race return to tackling safety, transparency, and course caps following a scary collision on the Queen K, October delivered plenty of food for thought. And, as always, contributor Tim Heming is here to digest it with you.

The first line of Sarah Wassner Flynn’s article about the return of the iconic New York City Triathlon, published earlier this year, reads: “For more than two decades, the New York City Triathlon was one of the sport’s most iconic races. Debuting in 2001, it quickly became a bucket-list event for age-groupers and pros alike.”

The piece previewed this year’s race return, renamed the Big Apple Triathlon, under new ownership of Alpha Win, formerly known as HITS Endurance, with Tommy Struzzieri taking over the company from his father, Tom.

Alpha Win, based in Saugerties, New York, is no novice when it comes to race hosting. They have put on over 200 races, but making a success of this one offered the sternest test of their credentials to date.

Held on October 10, the day when most eyes in the triathlon world were focused almost 5,000 miles west on the Big Island of Hawaii, would it prove enough of a draw to justify the set-up costs of a swim in the Hudson River, a bike up the closed West Side Highway, and a run through Central Park?

Since its halcyon days, the event has been beset by problems, with participation tumbling from a peak of almost 4,000 during its time as part of the Life Time Fitness Series in 2010. In 2024, it was canceled by new owner Supertri before registration even opened, with organizers saying they couldn’t find a suitable date. It didn’t return in 2025 either, which, given Supertri’s focus on producing stylish, short-course events in major urban areas, had to be a worrying sign.

“We’re just trying to bring back something that athletes have been asking for,” Struzzieri said in March, noting that numbers would be capped at 2,500. If that felt optimistic, a New York Post piece on the eve of the event recounted its troubled history and asked: Is this time the charm? stating that around 1,300 athletes were expected to start, with prices ranging from $350–$650.

The results, however, show fewer than half that number: only around 600 finishers across all formats, the lowest the event has seen since it began in 2001. “Every year that there’s an issue with this event, it hurts the event the following year,” Scott Nilson, Supertri’s U.S. general manager of events, told us in 2024. Perhaps this year it will be the simple economics of numbers.

Registration for the 2027 event is now open with early-bird pricing (including processing fees) at $548.90 (Olympic distance) and $383.90 (sprint distance). Triathlete reached out to Alpha Win for comment.

For the majority, the Ironman World Championship is a day of celebration and achievement. It’s a once-in-a-lifetime experience, the ultimate triathlon dream. For Trish Byron, that dream turned into a nightmare.

Byron was struck by a male cyclist from behind almost 30 miles into the bike leg, leaving her with seven fractured ribs, a broken collarbone, a punctured and partially collapsed lung, a concussion, a laceration requiring stitches, and extensive road rash.

It’s understood the cyclist stopped and spoke with volunteers before continuing the race, but Byron’s daughter Cassie Anne put out a plea on Facebook for more information, saying: “We’re hoping to gather firsthand accounts, identify the cyclist involved, and better understand what happened.”

Accidents happen, but the incident raises questions about transparency when serious collisions occur during races. Should such incidents be publicly reported, both to demonstrate that appropriate safety protocols and follow-up procedures have been followed and to help triathletes better understand the risks involved in signing up?

Cassie Anne’s post received a response from Judy Daggett, who said: “This exact scenario happened to me on the bike about mile 85, causing me to crash also. The guy who hit me kept going. Another athlete helped me to my feet.

“I immediately had double vision and said, ‘Yes, I need help,’ but there was no one around. I managed to get back on the bike and ride to T2, praying my vision didn’t completely leave.

“When I got there, they took me by ambulance to the ER for a CT of my head, thinking I could possibly have a brain bleed. Thankfully, I did not, but I also have fractured ribs, a hip and shoulder injury, and a concussion.”

Daggett went on to say she’d reached out to Ironman but was yet to hear from them, stating it was her first DNF in 30 years and that the “men were so aggressive, they need to let them go first”.

Her final point relates to the questions raised about the scheduled swim start waves that interspersed the men’s and women’s age-group divisions in Hawaii, whereas previously, the men had been started earlier in one cohort, followed by the women.

It also brings into focus the broader question (that has continued to surface since the announcement of the return to one day of racing) of whether Ironman should cap numbers on the course for both fairness and safety reasons.

While it might seem that Trish Byron’s family shouldn’t have far to go to find answers, as Anna Grosz, who also responded to the post, explained, it might not be that simple: “I provided medical support for the race. We are bound by patient confidentiality laws. You should reach out to Ironman through official channels. The medical director may be able to communicate directly with the affected athlete, but course volunteers cannot do so.”

Triathlete has contacted Ironman for comment.

Championship season is not quite over in the world of triathlon. The T100 Tour still has three events on the calendar, with Dubai and Saudi Arabia in November ahead of the T100 World Championship Final in Qatar. The action in the Middle East will also continue with the 2026 World Triathlon Multisport Championship in Abu Dhabi.

The headlines will be the professional races over 100K where Hayden Wilde looks to be the odds-on favorite to retain his title, and it’s wide open on the women’s side. But there is also shorter-distance racing and representative age-group competition throughout.

Despite conflict in the region and the cancelation, postponement or relocation of other major sporting events, particularly in Saudi Arabia, both World Triathlon and the Professional Triathletes Organization are, for now, proceeding as planned. That’s perhaps to be expected, with contingency decisions often left until the last possible moment. But if the events do go ahead, it will be interesting to see how much appetite international athletes have for traveling to the region.

Conversations around weight can be a sensitive topic: triggering to some, frustrating to others, and almost irrelevant to others. And Susan Kitchen’s article on why we shouldn’t be concerning ourselves with post-race weight gain will no doubt grab the attention of athletes who might have concerns about how they can be heavier after doing all that exercise.

While Kitchen spells out the reasons here (which, spoiler alert, can be perfectly natural as your body recovers), it also made me think that perhaps the concern shouldn’t be how much you weigh, but why, in the days following an incredible endurance feat, you’re not off celebrating somewhere, rather than hopping on the scale.

You may not find an answer as to which is better, but there is plenty we can learn from Jordan Blanco’s roundtable discussion with triathlon legends Flora Duffy and Jan Frodeno when it comes to their appreciation for the pinnacle events in our sport – including that the 2008 win in Beijing was Frodeno’s first-ever elite victory!

But if there is one takeaway, then it’s probably that following your heart is the first step, and the financial rewards will follow. Doing it the other way around might just be a little tougher.

What do we learn from the Kona bike mechanics recounting tales from the Big Island?

Number one: That most of us should probably invest a bit more time in understanding how to fix our own bikes.

Number two: That whatever daft mistake you’ve made, it won’t be the dumbest thing they’ve seen (one athlete rolled up with two front wheels and no back, another with two back wheels and no front).

Number three: If you do have a problem, get to the mechanics early (the day before race day was the busiest).

And number four: Have a little patience. “That’s really the hardest part of Ironman week – managing athletes’ timeline expectations,” Taylor Bushong, a traveling race mechanic working out of Bike Works Kona, told Sara Stover. “Managing the unrealistic ‘can you just’ requests. The understanding of the level of the request seems to be outside the scope of recognition.”

But while being a bike mechanic sounds like a thankless task, it has some upsides. The real kicker, featuring five carbon wheels and the town’s dump, is cleverly left until the final line.

Some charitable sporting endeavors fall flat while others just fly, and often there seems to be no logic as to which cause will capture the public mood.

Thankfully, for Ethan Hunger, the idea to complete a world-record number of super sprint triathlons within 24 hours to raise money for his local food bank in Bellingham, Washington, really took off.

If ever there was a classic case of nominative determinism, then this is it. Hunger v. Hunger actually started following the COVID pandemic, but as Travis Mundell found out, this year’s challenge was the most ambitious yet, helping push the initiative’s total fundraising beyond $1.2 million.

It’s life-affirming to see such dedication in action, not just from Hunger, but from the community that rolled out to support him, where putting all the proper procedures in place so the record could be ratified by Guinness reads as more grueling than all that swimming, biking, and running.

There’s probably not much more that needs adding to one of the most dramatic Ironman World Championship races in living memory. Having written a reaction piece on how the house (in this case, the Big Island) always wins versus the gambler, I’ve reflected more on how it just seems such a difficult race to get right. My first thought: If the pros can’t do it (see the DNF files here), what chance do the mere mortals have? Follow-up thought: Nobody racing here could ever be described as a mere mortal anyway.

#8970. Here’s How to Train From Now Through the New Year to Maintain Your Hard-Earned Marathon Fitness

A run coach and an exercise physiologist break down the weekly mileage and workouts you need to preserve your speed, strength, and endurance.

You’ve spent months training for your fall marathon, so the thought of losing that hard-earned fitness after race day probably stings. But at the same time, you can’t simply continue logging miles and workouts like you’re in race mode. Trying to stay razor-sharp year-round can lead to injury and burnout; your body needs rest after training for peak fitness.

So, instead, put your marathon fitness on ice. Freeze the adaptations you’ve gained and the endurance you’ve built. Then, you can pick up where you left off on, say, January 1, or whenever it’s time to lock back in for a spring marathon.

If you train right in the weeks between now and the new year, you won’t feel like you’re rebuilding fitness from scratch. Instead, you’ll preserve the key aerobic, muscular, and endurance adaptations you’ve worked so hard to develop.

To do that, we explain the minimum miles you need for maintenance and how speed, strength, and cross-training keep you in prime condition. Expect to return to race training feeling well-rested, confident, and ready to tackle another marathon cycle this spring.

In the first two weeks immediately following your marathon, you’ll want to focus more on rest and easy time-based jogging. Once you’ve recovered, however, you can return to tracking your miles more closely.

The bare minimum mileage you’ll need to maintain will vary from runner to runner, Heather Milton, CSCS, lead exercise physiologist at Primary MD and cofounder of Master My Run, tells Runner’s World. Much of it depends on how many miles you regularly put in over the weeks of your marathon training cycle.

“Science does not give us an exact number of what percentage of your marathon volume to decrease to that still allows you to maintain the same amount of aerobic fitness,” Milton explains. From her coaching experience, however, she’s found this number is likely around 50 percent of a runner’s typical weekly mileage.

David Hall, an RRCA- and USATF-certified run coach and founder of Running Coach CT, agrees. When planning his athletes’ schedules for the off-season, he looks at their typical running volume during marathon training and reduces their weekly mileage to no less than half. Every fourth week, however, mileage can drop to as low as 20 percent of their average to help facilitate recovery.

“A runner who was running 60 miles per week during their marathon build could definitely cut that in half,” Milton says. Or, take a runner who averaged around 40 miles per week. This individual could reduce their weekly mileage to 20, add in some cross-training, and expect to maintain much of their progress.

In fact, Milton adds, every runner can benefit from incorporating more of those cross-training sessions in the off-season. “Other forms of exercise can decrease the repetitiveness of the running motion and help you develop more well-rounded fitness, so I do prefer more variety from cross-training in the down-season,” she explains.

At the same time, Milton wants people to do the exercise they enjoy and, of course, runners love running. “I have to be reasonable about what a runner is willing to do and what keeps them healthy while they’re doing it,” she says. If you want to keep running four days per week in the off-season, that’s still workable—with one important caveat: You need to prioritize strength training.

When you’re in the thick of marathon training, running is your main focus. So while you’re still doing strength work during this time, it mostly helps maintain the strength you already have, rather than increase it, Milton explains. The off-season provides an ideal time to really build up and strengthen your muscle mass and bone health as much as possible.

Each week, Milton says to aim for two to three resistance training sessions that focus on heavier weights with a low to moderate number of reps. (You can do more than three weekly sessions as long as you’re not working the same muscle groups two days in a row.) This sets you up for a stronger return to your spring training cycle because it helps improve running economy, your overall neuromuscular health, and your fast-twitch muscle fibers, which help power you through fast bursts of running or hill climbing.

“Plus, when you start training for your next marathon, you’ll be in a stronger position to increase your running volume again because you’ve strengthened all of the areas of your body that were impacted by your previous race, which can help prevent injuries,” Milton adds.

During the off-season, you certainly don’t need to run every day to maintain your fitness. In fact, you can preserve key fitness markers—such as your VO2 max—with as little as three workouts per week.

“The goal is to maintain at least three to four aerobic days per week to maintain your fitness level,” says Milton. You can opt to run as little as once per week, as long as you continue to cross-train on the remaining days, she adds.

Aim for 30 to 60 minutes of whichever aerobic exercise you most enjoy—hit the gym for the elliptical or indoor pool, or get outside for skiing and cycling.

Similarly, the number of running days per week for Hall’s athletes varies, but many have success with three because it allows more time for strength and flexibility work. He also adds a second rest day to the schedules of his runners who typically train six days per week during a marathon block. But in both cases, consistency is crucial—you don’t want to go a week without doing anything. “Do something every other day at a minimum to stay active,” Hall says.

One of your runs each week should be a bit longer than the others, but it doesn’t need to match the lengths of your true marathon long runs. Milton typically recommends a long run between five and 13 miles, depending on the individual’s training volume.

If you don’t want to worry about tracking mileage in the off-season, that’s fine, too. Running for time instead of miles provides the same endurance benefits, Hall says. Around four weeks postmarathon, his athletes will typically start with one-hour long runs. “Then, they’ll go up to 75 minutes, then to 90 minutes, and then maybe up to an hour and 45,” he explains.

Over several weeks, this gradual progression sets his runners up with a solid base to build from when they start their spring marathon training. “But don’t push the pace,” he emphasizes. “These are easy, conversational efforts.”

Whether you run for time or miles, make sure you’re not increasing either too quickly. “Keep the same rules in mind as when you’re building mileage in marathon training,” Milton says. “Aim to increase by no more than 10 percent each week.” Recent research suggests that, to reduce injury risk, you can apply this rule to the distance of any single run, as well.

What does this look like in practice? Let’s say a runner is doing five aerobic sessions per week, which includes about 20 miles of running. Two are cross-training days and the remaining three are running days. They might choose to run three to five miles one day, five to seven miles another day, and then five to 13 miles for their long run. You also don’t need to increase distance as quickly as you would in marathon training, Milton explains.

Over three weeks, she says a runner might balance their mileage as follows:

Week 1: 4 miles, 6 miles, 10 milesWeek 2: 5 miles, 6 miles, 9 milesWeek 3: 3 miles, 7 miles, 11 miles

In the four weeks immediately following your marathon, don’t worry about fast workouts or hitting paces, says Hall. During those first two weeks postrace, he advises his athletes to go for 20- to 30-minute daily walks. In the third and fourth weeks, he reintroduces easy running and a touch of speed.

“The general rule I apply is: no hard running for the number of days that’s equal to the number of miles in the race. So for a marathon, we’re talking about 30 days of walking and conversational effort running—maybe dipping into tempo pace a bit—but certainly nothing above lactate threshold.”

After that time, Hall says runners can start to add back intensity. In fact, he encourages it, suggesting you incorporate either a 20-minute run at threshold pace or an interval session for the same amount of time. He also recommends alternating one mile at your threshold pace, followed by one minute of easy jogging or brisk walking, until you reach 20 minutes.

“Training at lactate threshold pace can make conversational effort feel easier and can help you run faster while still remaining mostly in an aerobic zone,” Hall explains. In other words, your body adapts so running at any pace starts to feel like it requires less work.

Another way to get in some speed during the winter season? Sign up for a holiday race like a Turkey Trot or Jingle Bell Jog, he says. “It can get boring if all you do is train. Racing a 5K keeps the interest alive and lets you put in a hard effort.” Keep in mind, though, you did just run a marathon, so you don’t need to race all out or cross the finish line with a PR.

According to both Hall and Milton, the golden rule that will help you maintain your hard-earned gains is consistency. Once you’ve recovered physically and mentally from 26.2, get back into a routine that keeps you moving. “Doing something is always better than doing nothing,” Hall says—because you can lose 8 percent of your VO2 max in four to six weeks if you pull the plug on activity completely.

Similarly, you’ll want to avoid “stop-and-go” training. “If you’re running two to four days per week, keep running two to four days per week, every week—within reason, because life gets in the way sometimes,” Milton says. But running 30 miles one week, doing nothing for three weeks, and then trying to get back into it can lead to a real struggle, she adds.

As long as you do your best to stay consistent—and don’t stress when the holidays, travel, or other engagements inevitably interfere—you’ll find your fitness quite close to where you left it after your fall marathon. All that’s left for you to do? Thaw it out with a fresh marathon training cycle this spring.

Morgan is a gear editor who has been with Runner’s World since 2017. She started as an intern ghostwriting The Warmup, a bygone version of the daily RW newsletter. Now, she tests and reviews anything you might find on runners’ feet-from crew socks and compression boots to carbon-plated super shoes.

A lifelong runner and shoe geek, Morgan has been chasing the perfect pair of kicks since she joined her grade school cross-country team. Since then, she ran as a Division I walk-on for the cross-country and track & field teams at the University of Delaware, where she studied English and Biology. She has one full marathon under her belt, and has raced more halfs and 5Ks than she can count.

#8969. 7-Minute Yoga to Practice While Sitting at Your Desk

Yoga while sitting at your desk can be a simple way to soothe physical tension during the work day. This practice was created by instructor Laia Bové, who has taught students of all levels for more than a decade.

If you spend a lot of time hunched over your desk, you already know that it’s important to break the stagnation of long hours in front of your computer screen. But sometimes the time you think you’ll have to release the tension in your neck, shoulders, and upper back—likely before or after work—disappears due to other responsibilities, distractions, or just plain exhaustion.

This 7-minute yoga practice was made with the idea that you can sneak in a little yoga during work. These stretches target the most common areas where tension and aches arise when sitting at a desk and act as a quick reset. By the end of the seven minutes, you’ll feel a lot looser throughout your upper back and maybe even a little more ready to take on the rest of your day.

You can do this sequence between tasks, meetings, or calls, or after you power off your laptop and before you move on to other activities. You don’t need any special clothes or equipment—in fact, you don’t even need to get up from your chair.

Sit in your desk chair with your feet planted on the floor. Exhale and lower your chin toward your chest. Inhale and lift your chin toward the ceiling. Repeat that a few times.

Next time you exhale and lower your chin toward your chest, keep your chin lowered as you turn your head toward the right, as if you were drawing your nose toward your right shoulder. Take a breath here, then return to center with your chin still lowered. Then draw your nose toward your left shoulder. Return to center, then lift your chin to neutral.

Clasp your hands and rest them lightly behind your head. Point your elbows toward the sides of the room to prevent your hands from placing too much pressure on your head. Inhale as you lift your chest and draw your elbows slightly behind your chest, if possible, and slightly arch your back in a Cow Pose variation.

Keeping your hands where they are, exhale as you round your back, bring your elbows toward each other, and draw your navel toward your spine in a seated variation of Cat Pose. Repeat another round of this seated Cat-Cow variation.

Keeping your hands clasped behind your head, exhale as you lean toward the left, feeling a stretch along your right side. Inhale and return to center. Exhale as you bend toward the right, feeling a stretch along your left side. Inhale and return to center, then release your arms.

Place your fingertips on your shoulders and point your elbows toward the sides of the room. Draw your elbows toward each other in front of your chest as if you want them to touch, then lift them to point toward the ceiling, then point them toward the back wall, and then point them at the floor, moving in a large circular motion. Continue drawing elbow circles as many times as you like. Then switch directions.

Exhale and tilt your head toward the right, drawing your right ear toward your right shoulder. Inhale and return to center. Exhale and tilt your head toward the left, drawing your left ear toward your left shoulder. Repeat a few times.

Reach your arms out to your sides in a T shape, then cross your arms and wrap them around your chest as if you’re giving yourself a big hug. Take a few breaths here in Eagle Arms variation. Then repeat with the opposite arm on top. Release your arms.

With your arms relaxed at your sides, draw your shoulders up toward your ears and squeeze your muscles as tightly as you can—maybe you even scrunch the muscles in your face. Take a big breath in, then release your shoulders down and relax the muscles you were tightening. Repeat one more Shoulder Squeeze.

Take a big breath in through your nose and out through your mouth. Repeat as many times as needed until you’re ready to resume your day.

#8968. The 10 Best Running Shoes for Wide Feet and Big Toes

Don’t subject yourself to cramped feet—these running shoes are the comfiest and roomiest.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

I’m four miles out on my run when I feel angry blisters forming between my toes because they’re overcrowded in my shoe’s toebox. Add that to a long list of annoying things going on with my feet: mild plantar fasciitis, black toenails, gnarly calluses that make me ashamed to wear sandals. I am a card-carrying member of the wide-foot club, yet I’ve resisted wide-width running shoes for years. Mostly because around the time I found I had wide feet (over 15 years ago), the only colors available in wide-widths were black, white, or gray.

Today, running shoes for wide feet have become more accessible, more visible, and less boring. Perhaps with the dawn of foot scans at specialty running shops, store owners and brands are finally realizing just how common wide-footed runners are—and why it’s so important runners stop squishing their feet in standard-sized shoes.

I’ve run 28 marathons and vet all kinds of gear, from sports bras to smartwatches, as RW running reviews editor. For research, I visited Aardvark Sports Shop, a local run store in Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, to get the lowdown on running shoes for wide-foot runners from Aardvark Footwear Lead Trainer Kate Egging. Egging, a former RW wear-tester, has worked at Aardvark for four years and is a lifelong wide-foot runner, like myself. I also spoke with A. Stacie Page, PT, DPT, of Johns Hopkins Running Program at Johns Hopkins Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation, who discussed the risks of wearing too-narrow shoes and how this can affect running performance.

Besides gear expertise provided by our staff, we also have a team of 300-plus local shoe testers who log at least 100 miles per pair of running shoes. They provide valuable feedback on fit, feel, and ride to help us determine the best trainers, ensuring our selections are all-inclusive. We also enlisted the help of Egging, because she gets to try on shoes at Aardvark and help runners make footwear decisions.

Compared to the Brooks Ghost, the Brooks Glycerin is broader in the midfoot area, resulting in a more accommodating fit for wider foot shapes. The new triple jacquard knit also provides a stretchier upper that houses wide feet.

The midsole foam provides a supportive, high-energy-return ride stacked at 38 mm in the heel. Brooks added 2 mm of DNA Tuned in the forefoot. What you get is more balanced cushioning throughout the shoe and a lower heel-toe drop.

I’ve worn the Glycerin 23 for base miles and long runs. My feet fit securely in the shoe thanks to the padded border on the interior of the heel collar. The softness underfoot and overall cozy fit make the Glycerin 23 a preferred everyday shoe in my testing pile and one I can depend on when I’m scheduled for hours on the road, according to my training plan.

Shop Men’s at brooksrunning.com | Shop Women’s at brooksrunning.com

It was a tough choice for Senior Editor Pavlína Černá, when she had to choose a shoe to wear for a 75K march south of Prague in the Czech Republic. Her decision: the On Cloudmonster 3.

“The signature CloudTec sole absorbs the impact of my steps like it’s a tiny trampoline that pushes me off right away and rocks me forward, doing half the work of running (or walking) for me,” she said in her shoe review (link below). “The toebox is wide and slightly stretchy, accommodating my foot as it swells over time.”

At Aardvark, Egging noted how On’s shoes have a surprisingly wide but secure fit. Several of our testers also praised the shoe for its roomy toebox.

The shoe has a Speedboard to promote propulsion. The source of its high rebound comes from its Helion foam and CloudTec system. We liked the overall comfort of the shoe on walks, long hikes, and daily runs.

“[The shoe] is super comfortable, excellent cushioning, nothing pinched rubbed or anything,” said tester Dave Brattley. “Definitely, the best pair of shoes that I have had the chance to run in.”

One thing to note: The shoe is only available in standard size. But we found the broad platform and lacing system make the Cloudmonster 3 accessible for both wide- and narrow-foot runners.

Shop Men’s at on.com | Shop Women’s at on.com

What? A Nike shoe on our Best Running Shoes for Wide Feet list? Expecting the brand’s usual narrow fit when I got my pair of Vomero 18s to test I was shocked how accommodating the fit felt wrapped around my wide feet.

Nike updated the lasts of its popular franchises—the Vomero, Structure, and Alphafly—basing the wider foot shape on women’s feedback. Turns out both women and men liked the end result.

The shoe is mega plush with 46 mm of ZoomX and ReactX foams, making it an ideal pick for long runs. The ride is soft and responsive, like a Brooks Glycerin or Saucony Triumph—but with PEBA.

“I really enjoyed how incredibly comfortable the Vomero 18 was,” said Editorial Assistant Michael McDonough. “Once the shoes were broken in, the sheer volume of cushion made longer runs much more enjoyable and pain-free. They helped me increase my mileage without hurting my feet, which has been an issue for me in the past.”

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com

The Gel-Kayano 33 introduces a new stability system: FluidSupport. Replacing the 4-D Guidance system, FluidSupport involves the dual-foam midsole—FF Blast Max and FF Blast Plus—working in tandem with the shoe’s geometry to help guide your form when you need it. The shoe is more flexible with FluidSupport, despite the 40 mm of beefy cushioning.

The shoe only comes in standard size, but it offers plenty of space for runners with high insteps, along with a snug fit in the midfoot area. I found the shoe to have ample toe room. My wide feet didn’t feel squeezed nor did my instep feel any pressure on my runs. Running in the Gel-Kayano 33, you won’t have to stop to loosen the laces.

Our wide-foot testers shared similar feedback. “I like the upper; the collar has lots of cushion that didn’t irritate my ankle bone,” said Lorenzo Molina. “The lacing system was smooth and the overall fit is great because my foot fits better in a wider shoe.”

Shop Men’s at amazon.com | Shop Women’s at amazon.com

Just about everything about the Guide 19 is accommodating. It preserves the same soft, cushioned feel as its predecessor with the same unobtrusive stability tech for, yes, guiding erratic running form.

CenterPath tech lends stability with higher sidewalls and a broader base. The Pwrrun midsole provides max-cushioning, making the Guide 19 a terrific long-run and recovery shoe of choice.

One tester gave the trainer his highest rating because of “its strong comfort, support, and cushioning, and the fact that it had no major weaknesses.”

“I was lucky enough to test this shoe’s predecessor, the Saucony Guide 18, and I enjoyed that shoe immensely for the same reasons,” said our tester, Dave Block. “But I think this model has even more cushioning and softness.”

Shop Men’s at saucony.com | Shop Women’s at saucony.com

The Torin 9 showcases several updates that make the daily trainer an even more welcoming intro to zero-drop shoes. The 28 mm stack height houses the brand’s P35X foam, with a dense core and soft carrier that softens landings without masking ground feel.

“I generally prefer cushioning that provides protection without disconnecting me from the running experience, and the Torin strikes that balance exceptionally well,” said tester Don Kuntzman. “The cushioning felt evenly distributed from heel to forefoot, creating a smooth, balanced ride that never felt overly soft, mushy, or unstable.”

The outsole has Vibram rubber, making the shoe’s ride tackier and more versatile. Our testers weren’t afraid to traverse onto the trail after hitting pace on the road.

The non-gusseted tongue provides more room for high insteps. Altra’s signature wide toebox is a bunion-prone, wide-foot runner’s dream. No need to worry about rubbing or hot spots.

Shop Men’s at altrarunning.com | Shop Women’s at altrarunning.com

Last year, Egging said the Clifton 10 was a pleasant surprise in terms of fit for wide feet. Unlike the Bondi 9, which has a narrower fit than past iterations, she found the Clifton 10’s sidewalls non-intrusive and the midfoot non-constrictive. The same goes for the Clifton 11. Hoka didn’t narrow the shoe’s fit, and it feels just as comfy and accommodating as its predecessor.

The shoe has Hoka’s Active Foot Frame to cradle your foot and help with stability. This means you can run and walk in the Clifton 11 confidently without rolling your ankles or feeling confined and stiff with extra stability features.

The compression-molded EVA foam isn’t as responsive as other supercritical foams you see in running shoes, but the Clifton 11 still has a high energy return ride that boosts everyday runs, long runs, and run/walks.

Shop Men’s at hoka.com | Shop Women’s at hoka.com

Egging wants everyone to know the Echelon 10 is not like the old Echelons Saucony was known for. Formerly a clunky run/walker for runners who need orthotics, the tenth iteration is lighter and more nimble, yet still orthotic-friendly. The shoe has the brand’s highly responsive Pwrrun midsole, which is the same foam in the Guide 18.

According to Egging, the Echelon 10 is an excellent choice for underpronators, or supinators (when your foot rolls inward less than 15 percent while running), because of its broad base and comfy cushioning.

“The Echelon gets a little bit overlooked because it falls into such a ‘comfort customer’ category,” Egging says. “But if you’ve got that new runner that has a high volume foot, maybe that 4E runner who needs the extra wide, who supinates and they need a broader base, this shoe is very runnable.”

If you are having issues with other trainers or are a new runner with specific needs, don’t discredit the Echelon 10. It could be your ticket to a great ride

Shop Men’s at amazon.com | Shop Women’s at amazon.com

Brands tend to make super shoes more tapered in the midfoot, like the spiked shoes on a track. But the Rocket X 3 has an accommodating, broad platform that you could slide an orthotic into.

The shoe has dual-density PEBA foam and a winged carbon plate to promote propulsion. The upper is single-layer engineered mesh, which allows for breathability over the course of a sweaty, foot-swelling marathon. It was tester Shane Houghton’s favorite feature.

“The mesh upper is a great part about Rocket X 2,” he said. “When you tighten the shoe it stays securely in place and wraps around your foot perfectly. And it’s so airy and breathable because the holes in the netting are so big. There is no chance of your feet getting hot in these shoes no matter how tight you’re wearing them. I appreciated the padding around the heel. It was nice to have that there when a lot of racers don’t.”

The Lone Peak 9+ offers both a comfy fit with a roomy toebox, providing ample room for toe splaying. “Fit and comfort is something that the Lone Peak 9+ has dialed in,” says Rip Cantelmi, who previously tested the Lone Peak 7 and Brooks Divide 5. “Laced up, the foot feels relaxed, strong, and sensitive. I have observed that the shoe is wide enough to accommodate toe spacers if you use them. The padding around the collar remains optimized for comfort and flexibility. Heat management remains positive.”

The Altra Lone Peak 9+ has an Altra Ego midsole, which provides just enough supportive cushioning as well as some ground feel, which testers like Cantelmi appreciated.

“Ground feel is something that many trail shoes ignore for the pursuit of comfort in the form of high-stacked foam, but the Lone Peak 9+ finds the perfect balance of cushion, protection, and feel,” says Cantelmi, who describes the shoe’s cushioning as neither minimalist nor marshmallowy.

Shop Men’s at altra.com | Shop Women’s at altra.com

Misconceptions About Wide-Foot Runners and Shoes

“I’ve had my feet measured before; I don’t need to do it again”

Getting your foot measured is not a once-and-done kind of deal. Your foot size changes throughout your life, due to aging, work, and having children. “Sometimes when people get pregnant their feet sizes change dramatically,” says Page. “An injury could also cause an arch to drop if you don’t have that same muscle activation.”

She references a study on incorrectly fitted footwear published in 2018, which found a large proportion of the population was wearing the incorrect size shoe and how this can be associated with foot pain and foot disorders. Her recommendation is simple: get a comfortable shoe that fits properly.

Another reason to have your foot scanned: Some runners may think they have a wide foot when in actuality they have a high arch or instep. “That’s when they need a shoe measuring that high profile,” says Egging.

“I’ve worn this shoe forever; the newest version will fit the same”

“I think it might be even more important for a wide-footed runner to revisit a run specialty store for a fit because the models as they update, don’t always fit the same,” says Egging.

The Hoka Bondi 9, for example, fits narrower than the previous iteration. This is because of Hoka’s sidewalls which are built up to hug your foot, which can result in a tighter fit for wide-foot Bondi lovers.

Altra also requires some probing. Even though the brand is known for its accommodating footshapes and roomy toeboxes, some Altra shoes can fit narrower in the midfoot due to updates. Upper “upgrades” to look out for in any kind of shoe when you’re a wide-foot shopper are gusseted tongues, which can make the fit tighter due to more material on the instep, and overlays.

“Getting black toenails is a rite of passage”

Black toenails are not a badge of honor. Egging is an ultrarunner and she’s never lost one toenail because she received a proper shoe fitting early in her run career. Other signs of needing to get refitted and change your shoe size: numbness, tingling, Achilles tendonitis, and plantar fasciitis.

“Movement is good!” Egging says, when runners are concerned about a little looseness in a road shoe. “A lot of plantar fasciitis in wide-foot runners is coming from that arch being crunched by tight-fitting shoes.” (Trail shoes are a different story; you’ll want a more secure hold around your foot.) Tightness and constriction can also negatively affect your performance. That kind of discomfort, Page warns, can change your running pattern and lead to pain or injury.

When it comes to choosing running shoes, you want some wiggle room. If you see bruising, blood blisters on the tops of your toes, or experience toe curling, you probably need a wider toebox—this also includes runners with hammertoes, bunions, bunionettes, and Morton’s neuroma.

With your bare foot, step on a blank piece of paper. Outline your foot with a pen or pencil. Use a ruler to measure the widest part in inches of your stencil horizontally (across the ball of your foot); be aware you’ll need a wider toebox if you have bunions or bunionettes. Write this number down and refer to the men’s or women’s chart to find your width

Related: How to measure your feet: A guide for runners

What can I do when the shoe I want to buy isn’t available in wide?

If you’re a bra wearer, you may have heard the term “sister sizes.” Shoes also have sister sizes. For example, I wear women’s 5.5 in street shoes, but most of my running shoes are 6.5 because they’re the standard width (B). I size up for foot swelling (it’s recommended to size up your running shoes) and size up again for width. I’m actually a size 6, C width in women’s running shoes.

It’ll take several try-ons to get the right feel and the right shoe, but it can be possible to find a women’s B or men’s D size shoe if there are no wides available, or wide if your foot is extra wide. Women can also pivot to a men’s size, but be forewarned: men’s shoes tend to run longer and have more space in the heel area.

“Socks are super, super important,” says Egging. “I think people neglect that. The price point is frightening at first. You’re like, $18 for one pair of socks? That’s insane! But eight years later when you still have that same sock and that six-pack you got at T.J. Maxx has come and gone in the meantime.” She recommends Injinji, Blister Resist, and Balega.

At RW HQ, we’ve been testing Wide Open, a company that specifically designs socks for wide feet—and that’s been a game changer. Instead of getting blisters in between my toes or second-guessing the wide toebox of an Altra or Topo Athletic shoe, I’ve discovered just how much socks can affect your run like Egging says.

What racing shoe options are there for wide-foot runners?

Wider width options for racing shoes are still a rarity. I’ve found through personal experience that the New Balance SuperComp Elite v6, Hoka Rocket X 3, and Hoka Cielo X1 3 have the most accommodating lasts compared to other super shoes, which taper in the midfoot resulting in narrower fit. A major thing to consider is that your feet swell over time as you run, especially on a hot day. Consider sizing up, but take into consideration most racing shoes are unisex, so they may run longer or be wider in the heel.

Amanda Furrer, Editor, Running Reviews, studied journalism at NYU and writing at Emerson College. She has reviewed gear and covered other topics in the running space for almost 10 years. Since 2013, she has consecutively run the Boston Marathon. She also has a master’s degree in gastronomy from Boston University and was formerly a professional baker for two years before hanging up her apron.

And, you probably want to live not only a longer life, but also a healthier one.

If so, you don’t have to look very far to find claims about how to improve—no, “optimize”—your health.

Want to reverse chronic disease? Extend that youthful glow? Live to 115… or forever? Lots of fitness influencers, authors, and podcasters will tell you how to do it.

#8965. The 67-Year-Old Who Raced Two Full Ironmans a Week Apart

Mary Mitchell won her age group in Kona and eight days later raced Ironman California, where she also won her age group. Here's how she did it. (Photo: Mary Mitchell, FinisherPix)

Fresh off a sixth-place finish at the Ironman World Championship in Kona, American professional triathlete Sam Long recently took to Instagram to ask his followers a question. Should he race Ironman Florida on November 7, or give himself another two weeks to recover and race Ironman Cozumel on November 22?

Long wants to secure his qualification for the 2027 Ironman World Championship early, but the question of how quickly to return to racing after Kona is a serious one. Among the responses to his post were plenty of suggestions that he take the extra recovery time and race Cozumel instead.

After all, Kona is no ordinary Ironman. Its combination of heat, humidity, unpredictable winds and exposed terrain takes a major physical toll, even on athletes who have spent their careers preparing for those conditions. Racing another Ironman just four weeks later is ambitious enough. What about racing one eight days later?

For 67-year-old Australian age-grouper Mary Mitchell, that was precisely the challenge.

On October 10, Mitchell won the women’s 65-69 age group at the Ironman World Championship in Kona, finishing in 13:11:46. Eight days later, she lined up at Ironman California in Sacramento, where she crossed the finish line in 11:32:45, more than 90 minutes faster than her Kona performance.

And she won her age group again. Even more remarkably, her husband, Andrew, 66, who had also raced in Kona, joined her in Sacramento and won his age group too.

What began as a somewhat improbable endurance experiment ended with three age-group victories between them.

The idea wasn’t actually Mary’s. Earlier this year, Mary and Andrew traveled to Morocco to spend time altitude training in the Atlas Mountains with a friend. During the trip, their friend floated an intriguing challenge. What would happen if a bunch of athletes in their 60s attempted two full-distance Ironmans a week apart?

“He persuaded us that it would be a good human experiment to do, to see whether, at our age, you could do two Ironmans in eight days, and what would that be like?” Mitchell explains.

The plan was for all three to qualify for Kona, race the World Championship, and then travel to Sacramento for Ironman California the following weekend.

There was just one problem. Their friend subsequently suffered a knee injury and withdrew from the experiment. But Mary and Andrew had already committed. Their flights and accommodation were booked and the race entries paid for.

“We thought, well, we might as well go,” Mitchell recalls. “How bad can it be?”

They also had the encouragement – or perhaps bad influence – of American friends Jill and Dougin Walker, serial Ironman competitors who have completed around 100 Ironmans apiece.

“We’ve fallen in with a bad crowd,” she jokes.

For Mitchell, who has completed around 30 Ironmans since her first in 2004, racing twice in eight days was uncharted territory. The closest she had previously come was roughly a month between Kona and Ironman Malaysia.

But Mitchell also had another reason to make the most of Kona.

Mitchell had previously won her age group at the Ironman World Championship in 2019. Since then, however, her attempts to return to the top of the podium had been repeatedly derailed.

In 2022, she was hit by a car while riding on the Queen Ka’ahumanu Highway just 10 days prior, preventing her from starting the race.

In 2024, at the women’s World Championship in Nice, she developed food poisoning the night before the race and abandoned roughly 140 kilometers into the bike.

Then in 2025, she returned to Kona, only to discover that what she initially believed to be a cold was COVID. She struggled throughout the race and eventually withdrew on the run.

“I had three years of thwarted attempts to do the World Championship,” she says.

Heading into 2026, Mitchell and her husband had decided this would be their final Kona appearance. They wanted to experience other races and destinations rather than continue returning to the Big Island.

And for much of the race day, Mitchell’s final Kona appearance looked unlikely to deliver another world title.

Mitchell had hoped to swim around 90 minutes, but the ocean conditions and what she admits was insufficient swim preparation conspired against her. She eventually emerged from Kailua Bay in 1:57:06.

“I had an appalling swim,” she says. “I hadn’t done enough long swimming, didn’t have enough endurance, just because swimming’s not my favorite thing.”

By the time she reached transition, Mitchell had effectively written off her chances of winning: “When I stood up out of the water, I thought, a competitive race is off the table now.”

Rather than chase positions, she decided to enjoy what she believed would be her last Ironman World Championship. Her mantra became simple: “Look after yourself and just keep chipping away at it.”

Despite the heat, wind, and particularly oppressive humidity, Mitchell began making steady progress through the field. She completed the bike in 6:38:10 and started the marathon feeling surprisingly good. She settled into a sustainable pace, making sure to take in adequate fluids and calories at every aid station.

With her husband, Andrew, also competing, there was nobody on the sidelines feeding her information about her position. It wasn’t until she reached the top of the Energy Lab, with roughly 12 kilometers remaining, that an acquaintance delivered some unexpected news.

“She said, ‘You’re first and running faster than anyone else in your age group.’ And I’m like, ‘What? No, come on.’”

Mitchell completed the marathon in 4:23:23, the fastest run in her age group, to secure her second age-group world title.

Ordinarily, the next few days would have been devoted to celebrating, recovering and enjoying the satisfaction of a long-awaited victory. Instead, she had another Ironman looming.

Following the Kona awards dinner and a celebratory glass of wine, Mary and Andrew flew to Sacramento, arriving on Monday with less than a week remaining before their next race.

There was no elaborate recovery protocol, no special preparation, and definitely no attempt to squeeze in additional fitness.

“We rode our bikes for an hour to an hour and a half along the river trail a couple of times, which was really nice,” Mitchell recalls.

The rides were deliberately easy, simply turning their legs over while enjoying the scenery and wildlife. She also completed a couple of short runs no longer than 30 minutes or demanding.

Her only swim was a brief dip in the river to test the water temperature and a new wetsuit, purchased after her previous one split during a 70.3 race in Leipzig, Germany, earlier in the trip.

More surprisingly, Mitchell wasn’t experiencing any crippling muscle soreness she remembered from her earlier Ironman days.

“It’s strange. They sort of ached, but they didn’t actually feel sore,” she explains.

She believes advances in running shoe technology have made a meaningful difference to how her legs feel after an Ironman. She raced in “super shoes” but suspects recovering from back-to-back marathons would have been considerably harder in the shoes available a decade ago.

Still, there was plenty of uncertainty. When asked whether she questioned the wisdom of attempting another Ironman, Mary laughs: “Oh, I thought about that just about every day.”

“If they’d had a half [Ironman] race, I probably would have dropped down to that distance.”

She reasoned that California’s current-assisted, wetsuit-legal swim would be far less demanding than Kona’s ocean swim. The flat, relatively straightforward bike course also appeared manageable.

But the marathon was another matter entirely.

“My big concern throughout the whole week was the run. Can you do two marathons in eight days with having raced in Kona with the conditions that are notoriously one of the more difficult races that you can do?”

Mitchell had trained specifically for Kona and made no adjustments to prepare for the double. Whatever happened in Sacramento would simply happen.

As expected, the California swim was a very different experience. Thanks to the river current and wetsuit, Mitchell emerged from the water in approximately 55 minutes, effectively halving her swim time from Kona.

But the bike wasn’t entirely without incident. Early in the ride, Mitchell developed significant pain in her quadriceps muscle and her shin. By the end of the first 90-kilometer lap, she was seriously considering pulling out.

“I was thinking, should I stop? It’s really quite sore,” she recalls. “Am I causing damage?”

She decided to continue to the next aid station and reassess, knowing she could stop at any point. Eventually, the pain subsided.

With no expectations, and already holding her Kona qualification for the following year, Mitchell approached the rest of the race with an unusually relaxed attitude. She chatted with volunteers, stopped when necessary, and enjoyed the atmosphere.

“I was just chilled the entire race because I didn’t have anything to prove,” she explains.

The marathon, her greatest concern, proved surprisingly manageable. Rather than experiencing the crushing fatigue she had anticipated, Mitchell found herself settling into a rhythm. The crowds were enthusiastic, the aid stations welcoming, and she passed the kilometers chatting with other competitors.

Her marathon time, 4:23:30, was almost identical to the one she had run in Kona eight days earlier. When she crossed the finish line in 11:32:45, she had not only completed the experiment but had also won her age group again. Andrew had done the same.

“To our astonishment, we both won our age groups,” Mitchell says.

Perhaps even more surprising was how they felt afterward.

“When we first started this sport, you do an Ironman and basically couldn’t walk for three days. Getting up out of a chair was really difficult and painful.”

This time, within 24 to 48 hours, both felt remarkably normal.

Mitchell discovered triathlon in her 30s, partly because Andrew was already involved in sport and she was tired of being left at home while he trained. She bought a cheap bike, started entering local short-course events and quickly fell in love with the sport and its community.

Her first Ironman came in 2004 at Busselton in Western Australia. Like many newcomers, she initially assumed it would be a one-off experience. More than two decades later, she’s still going.

Now retired and living in Adelaide, Mitchell trains up to 20-25 hours per week during her biggest blocks. She has worked with a coach for many years and increasingly recognizes the importance of strength training and nutrition, particularly in preserving muscle mass as she ages. Around five years ago, she also began working with a sports dietitian to improve her fueling, gut training, and overall nutritional approach.

But Mitchell is quick to point out that endurance sport doesn’t consume her entire existence. She enjoys good food, wine, socializing, reading and traveling with Andrew. And while she is competitive, she says curiosity is an even greater motivation.

“I just want to see how far I can push myself,” she explains.

Since retiring, Mitchell has challenged herself to do “at least one thing each year that takes me out of my comfort zone.”

Last year, that meant racing Patagonman in Chile, confronting her dislike of cold water by jumping from a ferry into a freezing cold fjord to start the race. This year, it was the Kona-California double. Next year, she’s already entered the 100-kilometer Tarawera ultramarathon in New Zealand.

For Mitchell, the biggest reward of the double wasn’t another age-group victory. It was discovering that, at age 67, she could still surprise herself.

“I think it resets your mind. It resets your thinking about what your body can achieve. And what mentally you can achieve,” she reflects.

The experience also reinforced what she loves about triathlon: the places it takes her, the friendships it creates, and the opportunities to challenge assumptions about her own limitations.

“It’s taught me that you’re stronger than you think you are, mentally and physically.”

Would she ever attempt two Ironmans in eight days again?

“No. Absolutely not. There’s no need to repeat the experiment!”

For all the satisfaction of the achievement, Mitchell admits she would have liked more time to savor her second Kona world title. Instead, almost immediately, she was packing up and preparing to race again.

“It would have been nice to just chill and enjoy it a little bit more,” she explains. “Have a couple more glasses of wine, soak it in.”

But the experience did change one thing: Despite initially declaring that 2026 would be their last Kona, Mary and Andrew have both accepted qualifying slots to next year’s World Championship.

#8964. The Best Black Friday Running Shoe Deals Are Here—Save on Brooks, Asics, Saucony, and More

These Black Friday deals include daily trainers, stability shoes, and marathon racers.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Editor’s Note: Prices and availability are subject to change. Check your size—and maybe a different color—to see if it’s in stock.

From Brooks to Asics to Saucony, these running shoes are on sale now at amazing discounts for Black Friday. Now’s the perfect time to score all kinds of trainers for early winter runs and races. Many of these shoes are on our best running shoes list and are discounted by up to 48 percent.

And when we say there are good deals, we mean it. Right now, Black Friday is giving us amazing running shoe sales. You’ll find favorite daily trainers and marathon racing shoes. Everything you need is here: If you’re a beginner looking for a shoe with Goldilocks cushioning—here’s your guide to point you in the right direction and help you save big.

These shoes are available in limited colors and sizes, so race there fast!

The GlideRide Max is a whopping 53 percent off. It’s pumped with FF Blast Max and FF Blast Plus midsole foams for a max-cushioned ride with smooth toe-off, thanks to Asics’s Guidesole tech.

“This is an awesome shoe—one of my favorites I’ve ever tested,” said Senior News Editor Theo Kahler, who trains at 6:30 pace. “It’s got a lot of plushy comfort without feeling clunky or slow. The ride is one of the best I’ve gotten from any daily trainer. It’s also a very soft shoe—not necessarily in the foam, but the insoles and collar are very soft and comfortable.”

Truly, the Endorphin Pro 4 is my personal favorite marathon shoe. The fit isn’t compressive like the Nike Vaporfly 4, and the ride isn’t as volatile as the Nike Alphafly 3 (or, for that matter, the Saucony Endorphin Elite 2).

Layers of Pwrrun PB and Pwrrun HG foam provide high rebound and support over hours of road racing. The Speedroll rocker profile encourages fast turnover.

“The Saucony Endorphin Pro 4 is a great upgrade in the Endorphin Pro lineup,” said tester Greg Jaindl. “I have worn all previous versions of the Endorphin Pro line, and this version is a great update without changing what works too much.

I think the best part of the shoe is its snappy, responsive ride! Saucony has nailed the smooth transition with its Speedroll technology. The Pro 4 also makes sure to put enough cushioning in the shoe that you’re protected for longer distances, but not making it too squishy that you lose out on the energy return.”

Just as popular as the Ghost, the Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 is a top-rated trainer that we’ve included in our Best Running Shoes and Best Walking Shoes guides. It’s a go-to trainer for runners looking for a softly cushioned shoe that provides stability when you need it. The guide rails system is the brand’s holistic support tech; dense foam located on the medial and lateral sides of the shoe acts as bumpers to help with knee and ankle alignment.

“My favorite feature of the shoe is the ride,” said tester and overpronator Peter Vuong. “It’s very smooth, has the right amount of bounce, and transitions from heel to toe very nicely. It might be one of the best shoes I’ve ever worn in terms of the ride.”

Think of the Clifton 10 as your go-to everyday trainer. The shoe has an accommodating fit (wide-foot runners didn’t feel squeezed) and a bouncy ride. Whether you’re a new runner or following a run/walk marathon training plan, the ClifTEN is your cushioned companion, delivering a high-rebound ride in a max-cushioned package.

“The Hoka ClifTEN is probably one of the most comfortable shoes I have run in,” said Assistant Commerce Photo Editor Saba Ahmed. “From the roomy and cushioned midsole area to the cushioned arch support, these are a pair of shoes that you can truly go run in right out of the box. As a wide shoe wearer, I felt the wide sizing was accurate and felt no discomfort in the mid area and felt plenty of flexibility by the toes.”

The Tecton X 3 is a super shoe for trail runners and ultrarunners. It’s prepped for gnarly terrain with its grippy Vibram Megagrip outsole, protective gaiter-style collar, and resilient Matryx quick-dry upper.

The shoe has carbon-fiber winglets in its midsole to provide stability on uneven surfaces and propulsion.

“This is a GREAT shoe, it has many unique features that will help train and ultimately race,” said tester Mike Parmer. “Starting with the built-in sock to protect your ankle while running and the aggressive cushion. Compared to other Hoka trail shoes, these are by far the best and lightest shoe I have tested.”

At 46 mm, the Hyperion Max 3 is a towering super trainer with responsive PEBA DNA Gold foam in its midsole. We like it for marathon training or even racing (as long as you’re not an elite who must follow 40 mm or less stack-height guidelines).

“I love the Hyperion Max: This shoe is a great training shoe for getting those long miles in with tired feet. It takes the pounding out when running on roads; it really absorbs the impact well and also feels easy to push the faster miles as well,” said tester Ricky Snyder.

The Arahi 8 was included in our Gear of the Year buying guide. Hoka truly updated the cushioning and flexibility of the shoe, righting the wrongs of the previously stiff and firm seventh iteration.

New to the Arahi 8 was the H-Frame support system, an H-shaped midsole component that helps stabilize your ride. The brand also added 3 mm of foam in the heel. The result is softer landings, especially for heel strikers.

#8963. I Wish Yoga Studios Would Stop Trying to Sell Me on Their Teacher Training Programs

Los Angeles-based yoga instructor Ramoni Overton questions whether a common trend across yoga studios is negatively affecting students. Overton is the creator of the YouTube channel Yoga With Ramoni.

I was brand new to yoga when I first experienced a teacher training sales pitch at the end of class. I had stood up after Savasana feeling pure bliss, practically floating off my mat. But suddenly the instructor was pedaling the studio’s upcoming yoga teacher training (YTT) to the entire room. I was surprised, but I mostly brushed it off, assuming it was a one-time thing.

But then it happened a second time. Then a third. And a fifth. After I heard the exact same sales pitch multiple times, my post-class high vanished before I even made it to the front door. It was replaced by a single thought. “Seriously? Again?”

This experience isn’t unique to me—it’s been happening to many other yoga students. And, in my opinion, it’s a reason why some of them might quietly not return to class.

As a yoga teacher for four years and a yoga student for nine, I’ve noticed that most students aren’t coming to yoga to build a second career. They already have full days and packed schedules. They’re coming to yoga to unwind, decompress, and experience a single hour in which the outside world completely disappears.

At the same time, I understand the reasons behind the post-class YTT pitch. Yoga studios have bills to pay, and YTT is one of the more reliable revenue streams in a business that runs on thin margins. But when studios push their instructors to pitch constantly (and when some instructors receive commission for every sign-up), the pressure is on. The yoga teacher who was supposed to hold space for you is now knowingly or unknowingly working a sales quota. That changes the energy of a studio, whether anyone admits it or not.

And it adds up to something that’s bigger than one annoying moment. Seemingly everywhere else in life, we are constantly being sold something. Ads interrupt us while we’re watching TV, listening to podcasts or the radio, and scrolling through social media. Yoga was supposed to be one of the few places that wasn’t also a marketing funnel.

Studios don’t need to stop sharing information about their YTT offerings. But they do need to stop treating every student on the mat as a sales lead. There are so many ways to share training info without disrupting the post-class quiet. A simple flyer at the front desk, an announcement on the studio schedule, or a free information session for those who are genuinely curious. Let people come, flow, and leave in peace.

If the training is enticing, students will ask about it on their own. You won’t have to sell them on it.

#8962. The Brooks Launch 12 Helps You Run Fast—and Save Big

This affordable trainer has racing shoe DNA.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

The Launch 12 is cushier than a racing flat but can handle hard workouts on the track and on the road. The affordable trainer—a bargain buy for $120—won’t break the bank, but it doesn’t feel cheaply made. The Launch has that Brooks touch; the comfy fit that securely locks your foot inside an airy mesh upper.

We included the Launch 12 in our Best Affordable Shoes guide because it’s an excellent choice for runners wanting a designated trainer for fast days. It’s also a sweet, cheaper lower-stacked alternative in a sea of towering, high-cushioned models.

For the runner who says the Brooks Ghost is too bulky and boxy, the Launch 12 could be your sole mate.

I’ve added track workouts to my training this year after finally overcoming my fear of the dreaded all-eyes-on-me oval. It’s fun to go balls-to-the-wall in today’s super trainers and high stacks during speed sessions, but I sometimes desire a more grounded, minimally designed trainer to really test my fitness. The Brooks Launch 12 is that shoe.

Finding out there’s DNA Flash v2 foam in the Launch 12 is like finding an Easter egg in a movie. It’s a callout to the Hyperion Elite 4, Brooks’s premium racing shoe model. The shoe originally had nitrogen-infused DNA Flash v2 foam to pump up your ride before switching to DNA Gold (PEBA, baby) in the Hyperion Elite 5. But it can’t be ignored that DNA Flash v2 was a form of Brooks’s original super foam.

This gives the shoe a firm, snappy ride with plenty of padding for shock absorption. It’s not max-cushioned, and certainly not super trainer height at 35 mm, but it packs plenty of support for hard and long efforts.

“Typically, I’m a fan of the middle ground when it comes to trainers,” said Content Hyper Editor Ashley Tysiac. “I like to have a shoe with enough cushioning that I feel like my feet are supported, but not too much that I feel like my feet are being weighed down by bricks. This shoe was a pleasant break from some of the heavier, maximalist trainers that I’ve tried in the past couple of years. It’s a lightweight shoe that provides a firm ride.

“There’s not a ton of give to the shoe or spring in its step, but I didn’t mind that. The firm, easy ride was something I could enjoy on regular runs, long runs, and even some runs with faster-paced segments in the middle.”

The Launch 12 is built like a track shoe with its narrow, streamlined last. Tester Ricky Snyder said he had no issues with the fit, saying everything was “perfect, no hot spots or cramping in the toe box, no hard or rubbing plastic parts.”

However, Tysiac—and I—found the Launch 12’s midfoot a wee too snug.

“I wasn’t a huge fan of the lacing system,” she said. “No matter how many times I loosened and re-laced my shoes, it always felt too tight through the midfoot area, causing some noticeable discomfort.”

As a runner with wide feet, I couldn’t agree more with Tysiac. Compared to Brooks’s Hyperion 3, which also has DNA Flash v2 foam along a knit upper that hugs your foot, I felt the Launch 12 was much narrower and constrictive. The Hyperion 3 costs $20 extra, and speaking from experience, it could be worth the spending if you have wide feet like mine.

The Launch 12 is a shoe for runners looking to find a cheaper alternative to the more costly speedwork ones on the market, but it’s also for runners who miss shoes pre-super foam. The shoe may have an older midsole version of Brooks’s special sauce, but the ride takes you back to simple days, when a firmly cushioned trainer was all you needed to get in a run.

“I took out the Brooks Launch 12 on a variety of runs, including regular runs, regular runs with pickups in the middle, and long runs. Perhaps the shoe’s best feature that stands out is how light it is, providing a ride that doesn’t feel too bogged down. They felt light enough to rip off some faster-paced fartlek segments during the middle of a regular run, but still supportive enough to make it through a longer run.”

For $120, you’ll find a trainer that can take on multiple workouts. The Launch 12 is a good deal for the runner looking to save.

#8961. How to Master the Run/Walk Method: Tracking Your Intervals

Proper tracking and workout structure can lead to success using this training technique.

Whether you’re aiming for a 16-minute or 8-minute mile pace, utilizing a balanced run/walk interval structure makes for more efficient workouts, better fitness progression, and stronger race performances.

It’s not necessarily how fast you’re going, but the intention behind your intervals that dictates your training and racing success with the run/walk method. Your walk breaks shouldn’t feel like a casual stroll through the park, nor should your run intervals translate to an all-out sprint effort. With the Runner’s World program, How to Master the Run/Walk Method, you’ll learn how to best manage your efforts, organize your intervals, and track your sessions.

From nailing your interval durations to finding your preferred training tracker, you’ll discover how to implement the run/walk method consistently into your routine—and start seeing results in your fitness and race performances.

In Runner’s World’s How to Master the Run/Walk Method: Tracking Your Intervals, we’ll teach you:

While you can use either time or distance to log your run/walks, we recommend starting with time-based intervals, especially if you’re new to running or the run/walk method. You’ll split your running and walking intervals into specified periods of seconds or minutes, rather than distance logged.

If you’re using a training plan such as Runner’s World Start Running or Run Nonstop plan, you’ll gradually increase your run time while shortening your walk time until your walk breaks disappear altogether. But with the run/walk method, you’ll always have walk breaks built in, and you’ll adjust your run interval based on your current goal or race pace.

Notice that no matter your overall pace, you can allot 30 seconds of walking. It’s an ideal interval duration for reaping the recovery benefits of walking without significantly affecting your pace.

As your pace increases, the larger your run-to-walk ratio will become, translating to more time spent running. For example, you may run for two minutes and walk for 30 seconds to hit a 9-minute mile, but when your goal is to shoot for an 8-minute mile, you’ll run for longer (four minutes) to hit a quicker pace.

Instead of focusing on a specific number or pace, use feel to guide your walk intervals. Be intentional with your walks, keeping them brisk but allowing your heart rate to drop and your muscles to enjoy some recovery. Your walk effort should feel significantly less intense than your run portions.

“I tell my runners you should be walking not like you’re looking for sharks’ teeth on the beach or cracks in the sidewalk. You should feel like you’ve got someplace to be, but you shouldn’t get into the race walking motion that you would see in the Olympics,” says Chris Twiggs, chief training officer at Galloway Training.

As you get faster as a walker, you’ll take some of the pressure off of having to run faster to stick with your goal pace. You may also notice more efficient transitions from walk to run, and vice versa, as you improve your speed.

Because run/walk sessions require meticulous tracking, you’ll want to use an interval timer for optimal results. Your smartwatch or fitness tracker may have interval capabilities, but an interval timer is the best tool for accurately structuring your run/walks. Set your run/walk ratios on the timer before your workout, and attach it to your jacket or waistband. The timer will buzz to alert you during your workout when it’s time to run or walk.

If you’re logging your workouts on a fitness tracker or app like Strava, don’t worry about pressing pause during your walk intervals. Keeping the clock going during your entire workout gives you a more accurate representation of your effort, which makes tracking your fitness progress clearer. After each session, write down your total distance, interval ratio, and how you felt during the workout to measure both your objective and subjective progress.

The last component to consider before heading out the door? Shoes. Lace up a pair of comfortable and supportive shoes to power your run/walk workouts. While most run/walkers should rely on run shoes that transition smoothly between intervals, your shoe choice depends on your preferences and experience. Find your ideal shoe by consulting our run/walk shoe guide, curated by Runner’s World gear experts after putting a variety of models through extensive wear testing.

“The main things to look for [in run/walk shoes] are cushioning, support, and durability,” says Carissa Galloway, RDN, certified personal trainer and race commentator. “If you’re just starting out, a shoe with higher stability is important.”

Ashley is Editor of Content Hype at Hearst’s Enthusiast & Wellness Group. She is a former collegiate runner at UNC Asheville where she studied mass communication. Ashley loves all things running; she has raced two marathons, plus has covered some of the sport’s top events in her career, including the Paris Olympics, U.S. Olympic Trials and multiple World Marathon Majors.
