#8945. Inside Sullivan Middaugh’s Balancing Act Between Off-Road Dominance and LA 2028

There are few races Sullivan Middaugh would like to target more than next year’s XTERRA World Championship in New Mexico. However, if everything goes to plan, there’s only a slim chance he’ll be on the start line to defend his title.

That’s because Middaugh is part of an exciting crop of American men trying to help the Project Podium program live up to its name at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. And with an increasingly crowded triathlon calendar, the timing doesn’t quite work.

The challenge is that the 2027 XTERRA World Championship weekend in Ruidoso falls between the World Triathlon Championship Finals in Hamburg, Germany, and another top-level race in Weihai, China. Both are part of the rebranded T50 Championship series.

Not only could these events prove critical in helping the U.S. secure three men’s spots for Los Angeles – the host nation is already guaranteed two – but Hamburg could also present an opportunity for Middaugh to stake his claim to one of those places.

He can’t afford to let up. It’s still early in the Olympic qualification cycle, but the U.S. currently has eight men in the top 50 of the Olympic rankings, more than any other nation, with Middaugh the fourth-ranked American at 31st overall.

But while the focus will understandably shift toward the work of coach Parker Spencer’s Project Podium squad, which splits its time between Tempe, Arizona, in the winter and Park City, Utah, in the summer, XTERRA will never be entirely out of mind.

After all, it’s the discipline that put the Middaugh family on the triathlon map, and never more so than earlier this month, when Sullivan claimed his first full-distance XTERRA world title, younger brother Porter finished seventh, and father Josiah, at 48 years young, placed sixth.

Three members of the same family, spanning two generations, finishing in the top seven of a World Championship race is a remarkable feat, with few obvious parallels across elite sport.

The achievement was even more special because it had been 11 years since an American man last won the event. That was Josiah, in 2015. Before him, you have to go back another 15 years to Michael Tobin’s victory in 2000.

“No, I haven’t heard anything quite like that,” Sullivan confirms. “And especially having my dad in the race is pretty incredible!”

More than the result itself, it’s the opportunity to continue racing alongside his father that Sullivan appreciates.

“Following in his footsteps is pretty awesome,” he continues. “Every year he says he’s gonna retire, but I don’t know. It’s been pretty awesome to be able to continue to train and race with him. I grew up just following him on the XTERRA circuit and going to races and watching him. I never really thought we’d be racing together.”

Sullivan’s success also made up for his defeat by Reed Legg at the North American Championship earlier this year. Legg’s victory interrupted a Middaugh dynasty that has seen Josiah win 15 U.S. elite national titles and Sullivan dominate the more recent championship era.

And it was made all the sweeter by the XTERRA World Championship’s return to the U.S. after four years in Italy.

“I put it on my calendar and kept it in mind all year,” Sullivan says. “It was a race at altitude, which I grew up at, and so I felt like it was a good opportunity. Grindstone Lake, where we swam, is at 7,000 feet and the course got up to maybe a little bit over 8,000 feet. But at home in Colorado, my house is at like 7,500 feet, and you can only really go up from there. So, the six or seven weeks leading in, I went home and trained with dad because I knew it would be a big advantage if I could be fully acclimatized.”

While Porter, who also trains with Project Podium, finished seventh, Sullivan believes his younger brother might have mounted a stronger challenge had he not been racing at the Under-23 World Championship in Spain.

Sullivan skipped that race to sharpen his mountain biking skills, although it didn’t prevent an early spill on the bike.

“Yeah, I overcooked the corners a little bit on the first couple of turns in the single track section,” he explains. “It wasn’t a bad spill out, but I kinda had to slam on the brake, go off the trail, tip over and get up quick. My bike computer fell off, which wasn’t a big deal, and maybe a blessing in disguise to not worry about power and just focus on effort.”

Sullivan had an almost four-minute lead heading onto the run and extended his advantage with the day’s fastest 10K split, but at no point did he feel comfortable.

“I didn’t really get any splits and thought that no lead was safe on the run. I just tried to give it full gas, focusing on pushing the climbs and rolling the downhills because I knew they’d be coming.”

Among the athletes trying to hunt him down were two very familiar faces – Porter and Josiah – and there was a brief moment of family camaraderie as their paths crossed on the course.

“I just focus on myself for the most part, but it reminds you that they’re also out there battling. I saw them running together, so that was pretty cool because I knew they’d be pushing each other. We were all pumped, gave each other a high five, and that was pretty much it.”

There were plenty more high fives and hugs at the finish, where Sullivan’s mom, sister, and grandparents were also in attendance.

While this was Sullivan’s first full-distance XTERRA world title, he had previously won the Short Track World Championship in Molveno, Italy, in 2024.

In recent years, short-track racing has typically taken place a couple of days before or the day after the main event, although it wasn’t on the schedule in Ruidoso.

“It’s like a three or four-minute swim, maybe a 15-minute bike and a seven-minute run,” Sullivan says, with distances depending on the course layout. “It’s all under 30 minutes for the most part, so more intense and a little bit different, and you can’t make as many mistakes. I think it suits me because I’ve spent a lot of time training for sprint distance draft-legal triathlons. I really enjoy it.”

While XTERRA might be seen as a distraction from road triathlon, Sullivan believes it complements his efforts elsewhere.

“It helps me with my skills for the draft-legal stuff as well. I look to people like Flora Duffy and Hayden Wilde who were able to do well at both, and think they’re an example for me.”

For the next 18 months, the priority will be collecting Olympic qualification points, with the window having opened in May.

Sullivan has already recorded top-10 finishes at World Triathlon Cups in Huatulco, Mexico; Edmonton, Canada; Rio de Janeiro, Brazil; and Asunción, Paraguay. He also competed at the Americas Triathlon Championships in Antofagasta, Chile, finishing 11th. He now heads to Chile for two more World Cup races, in San Pedro de la Paz and Iquique.

While USA Triathlon hasn’t officially released its selection policy for Los Angeles, Sullivan expects the Olympic test event in July 2027 and the World Championship Finals in Hamburg to be key races. He anticipates that a top-eight finish, combined with being the leading American, could be enough to meet the automatic selection criteria.

But first, he needs to secure starts at the biggest races. “Spots keep flipping, so it’s gonna be pretty tough,” he adds. “I’ve been mostly focusing on the World Cup level, which is the step below the World Championship Series, but as my swim develops, I’ll try and focus more on the World Championship Series because that’s the level you need to be at in the Olympics.”

The higher the level, the more critical the swim becomes. “If you’re the best swimmer, you can be in the race up until the run, but if you don’t have a good swim, you may never even be in the race,” he explains. “The swim sets you up for a good day to get in the right bike group, but you also need to be able to run well off a hard bike. That’s something XTERRA helps me with.”

Sullivan admits that bridging the gap in the swim is his biggest immediate challenge, but he also knows he’ll need a blistering run to compete at the very top.

“Especially with Alex Yee and Hayden Wilde, it is just getting faster and faster,” he says. “You need to be an elite runner if you want to be on the podium, and that means hitting sub-14 minutes sometimes in the 5K and sub-29 minutes occasionally on the 10K. Right now, I’m in the low 14s and around 30, maybe a little under depending on the course.”

If he can get there, it will be with the help of Project Podium. Established in 2018, Project Podium is funded by USA Triathlon, corporate sponsors, and private donors, including longtime benefactors Dr. Bill Warren and his wife Lynne. Based at Arizona State University, the program provides promising American male triathletes with coaching, scholarships, and financial support as they pursue Olympic ambitions.

Sullivan, who graduated with a degree in biomedical sciences in August, has enormous respect for coach Spencer, who he says also understands his passion for the trails and why XTERRA should remain part of his program.

“I love mountain biking, and so it’s good for me to be able to kinda go in and out, but I think that as the Olympics get closer I’ll have to take a slight step away from XTERRA, but we’ll see.”

Finally, if Sullivan’s Olympic dream does come to fruition, could there be more than one Middaugh on the U.S. team?

“That’s definitely a big ask, but would be amazing. I don’t know if it’s on the cards for ’28, but maybe for ’32 it could be more plausible. I think we both have the ability to get to that level if we stick with it, and when I see Porter in the race, we don’t really need to say anything. We just understand what we need to do.”

#8944. Salomon Aero Blaze 4 Grvl GTX Review: Built for Wet, Gritty Miles

The waterproof Gore-Tex upper and grippy lugs handle sloppy gravel—and slick floors during long shifts.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

The Salomon Aero Blaze 4 Grvl GTX is technically a gravel running shoe, and it excels in that arena. It’s also becoming an absolute cult favorite among nurses, techs, and other healthcare workers who spend 12 hours on slick floors and want something wipeable, grippy, and weather/other substances-tough. Personally, I tested it on the one surface it was born for: wet, gritty, cursed early-morning gravel that always tries to murder me. Tough luck, gravel gods. I’m still alive.

The Gore-Tex of the Aero Blaze 4 Grvl GTX is the cold, wet, ugly-conditions sibling in Salomon’s trail running gravel lineup. It’s a boss of a gravel trainer that shares its midsole, outsole, drop, and stack with the standard Grvl running shoe; the difference is that Gore-Tex upper, which trades some airflow and a little weight for weather and moisture blocking power. If you train through damp autumns and slushy winters, like I do, the GTX is 100 percent what you want. If you run mostly in dry, warm conditions, save the $20 and some sweat and take the regular version.

When it comes to the Aero Blaze 4 Grvl GTX, the lugs make the shoe. At 2.5 mm, the lugs aren’t the aggressive, mud-clawing teeth you’ll get on a mountain shoe. They’re short, chevron-shaped, and made of Contagrip rubber that gives you enough hold without digging, and they’re short enough that road-to-trail is totally doable.

I ran them at Shirley Chisholm Park in Brooklyn, which is a landfill-turned-park full of gravel hills. The conditions were damp, slippery, and gloomy. I took them out in the early morning, with loose stone over wet packed base. It’s weather that makes you wonder why you’re there and not at the TJ Maxx across the highway. But, even as a Maxxinista, I settled in fast and happy because the lugs gripped like they were made of sticky tack. My uphills weren’t tripping me up and pulling my toes under my knees, and the downhills didn't turn into a gravel slide. They have just enough give and flex in that rock-protected sole to keep my wobbly body upright, in spite of what gravity would want me to do.

Short lugs also mean less trapped debris and more contact area, which is why the grip carries over to hard, wet surfaces. That’s a big part of the healthcare-worker love: it’s a grippy sole that doesn't feel like a clunky work clog or like you’re rounding in cleats.

The optiFoam² midsole sits in the moderate-cushion zone. It’s soft enough to take the edge off a long shift or a long run, and firm enough that it doesn't feel mushy on uneven stone. It’s not quite a Goldilocks for all situations, but where it works it sings. The 8mm drop is traditional and calf-friendly, so it suits people who are on their feet all day.

It’s not terribly responsive overall, but somehow, in spite of that, it feels fast on gravel, especially on the trickier uphills, where you lose a lot of oomph in most hybrid shoes. It has a nice “settle into your stride” ride feel that gives you a lot of pep for the price. It’s not a racer, but I could see myself racing in them.

The weather in the mornings was, for a period of time, frankly, unholy. My feet stayed dry and comfortable the entire time. My body: not so much. The Gore-Tex membrane handles puddle splash, wet grass, and gravel dust (read: concrete) without seepage, and the upper is easy to wipe down, which is the second reason it’s popular in hospitals and clinics: spills, splashes, and grime aren’t likely to be permanent.

The trade-off is the standard Gore-Tex trade-off: it’s just less dang breathable than a mesh upper, so it runs warmer. Fit-wise, it’s a standard width suitable for most runners—save for those with a really wide midfoot—with a secure, wraparound lockdown.

There’s a quirk to gravel nobody chats about, but I obsess over—the aforementioned concrete situation. The quickLace neo bungee system is great for quick, adjustable fit, but wet gravel dust can dry on the bungee and basically cement it in place. The laces get stuck.

The fix: wet them down a little. A bit of water de-cements the dust and the system moves freely again. Rinse your shoes after dusty runs and you’ll never notice.

Here’s where I must be honest about the limits. This is not the shoe for flat, slabby rock or highly technical trails. The lugs are too shallow to bite into loose, steep, or rooty terrain, and the sole isn’t quite flexible enough to conform around rock features. If your trails look like a scramble, look at a deeper-lugged trail shoe instead.

And it looks good doing it. The number of these I see on chic New Yorkers in my office is wild. But, the important bits, like the abrasion-resistant upper, hold up to gritty, scuffy use, and the reflective details are aces for dark early-morning starts.

Is the Salomon Aero Blaze 4 Grvl GTX waterproof? Yes. It uses a Gore-Tex membrane, so it’s waterproof and wind-resistant.

Is it a trail shoe or a road shoe? It’s a hybrid gravel shoe. It’s at home on gravel, fire roads, and mixed paths, but it isn’t designed for technical, rocky trails.

Are Salomon Aero Blaze 4 Grvl GTX shoes good for nurses? Many healthcare workers swear by the third version and are grabbing the fourth for the grip. It’s easy to clean and moisture-resistant.

GTX or standard Grvl? Pick the GTX for wet, cold conditions. Pick the standard version for dry, warm weather and better airflow.

The Aero Blaze 4 Grvl GTX is a stylish, abrasion-resistant, grippy gravel shoe that doubles as a great on-your-feet-all-day option. It’s not a technical trail mistress, or a trail racer, and it isn’t trying to be. For gritty gravel, fire roads, and messy mixed terrain in lousy weather, it’s one of the best new choices around.

#8942. 15-Minute Beginner-Friendly Yoga, No Flexibility Required

Taylor Lorenz—known online as Taylor’s Tracks—is a certified yoga teacher with more than 800 hours of training in vinyasa, hatha, and yin yoga. Here, she guides you through a practice suitable for any experience level with yoga.

No matter how long you’ve been practicing yoga, returning to the basics is always beneficial. This yoga for beginners practice features a flow full of repeating shapes, including forward bends, side stretches, and gentle twists, all supported by modifications and props, if needed, to ensure that the poses work for any body, regardless of how flexible or inflexible you might be.

Listen to your body, breathe slowly, and enjoy the flow.

Keep two yoga blocks or block-like props (think: thick books) close by. These can help you access poses that your body might otherwise object to so that you can still benefit.

Begin kneeling in Thunderbolt Pose. If this doesn’t feel comfortable for your ankles or knees, slide a block beneath your sit bones to minimize the pressure. If it’s still uncomfortable, you can skip this pose.

Come onto your hands and knees with your shoulders over your wrists, hips stacked over your knees. With your next inhalation, lower your belly, lift your chin and chest, and arch your back in Cow Pose.

Exhale as you round your back and tuck your chin in Cat Pose.

Repeat Cat and Cow 3 times each, moving with the pace of your breath.

As you round into your last Cat Pose, tuck your toes and sink your sit bones back toward your heels.

Shift your shoulders forward over your wrists. Keep your toes tucked and with your next exhalation, lift your knees away from the mat and reach your hips up and back in Downward-Facing Dog. Think of your body being in an inverted V shape.

Feel free to bend you knees as much as you need to for the pose to feel comfortable along your hamstrings and lower back. You can also place blocks underneath your hands.

Stay here for 3 cycles of breath, pedaling out your feet by bending one knee and straightening the other, and then switching. You can also sway a little from side to side or simply stay in stillness.

Walk your feet toward your hands to come into a Standing Forward Bend. Relax your neck and let your head hang. You can let your hands dangle or rest your fingertips on the mat.

You can also place a block beneath each of your hands. You might want to bend your knees slightly to ease the strain on your hamstrings or lower back.

Inhale and start to lift your chest slightly, bringing your fingertips to your shins and lengthening your spine in Halfway Lift. Keep the back of your neck long and stare straight down at the mat. You can also keep your fingertips on your blocks here.

Inhale to rise as you come to standing, sweeping your arms out toward the sides and overhead. Bring your hands together at heart center in Mountain Pose.

With your next inhalation, reach your arms back toward the sky. Grab your left wrist with your right hand and guide your left wrist up and over to the right in a Standing Side Bend. Feel the stretch along your left side body.

Inhale as you come back through center and exhale as you twist toward the right, with your left arm reaching forward and your right arm reaching toward the back of the mat. Gaze toward the right.

When you’re ready, come back through center before repeating Standing Side Bend and Standing Twist on the opposite side.

Inhale to come back through center, exhale to Standing Forward Bend.

With your next exhalation, step back to Downward-Facing Dog.

From Downward Dog, step your right foot between your hands. Lower your left knee to the mat and sweep your arms overhead in Low Lunge.

Use our right hand to grab hold of your left wrist again, guiding it up and over in a side bend while keeping your balance in your Low Lunge. Press through your right foot and your back knee to help find steadiness.

Inhale as you come back through center and exhale as you twist toward the right, with your left arm reaching forward and your right arm reaching toward the back of the mat.

Inhale both arms back to center, palms facing forward. With your exhalation, bring your hands to the ground or to blocks on either side of your front foot. Start to straighten your front leg, sliding your right heel away from you and flexing your right foot in Half Splits.

You can keep your hands underneath your shoulders or slide them forward closer to your feet for a more intense shoulder and side body stretch.

With your next inhalation, come back through Low Lunge. Exhale, Downward-Facing Dog.

Reach your left leg to the sky and repeat the following poses on the opposite side:

Step toward the front of the mat and fold forward in Standing Forward Bend.

Inhale, reaching your arms up and overhead with your big toes touching or hip-distance apart. With your exhalation, reach your arms alongside your head and sit your hips back in Chair Pose.

Keep your arms high and begin to draw your left knee toward your chest, foot flexed. With your exhalation, step your left foot back into a High Lunge.

With your right hand, grab your left wrist, and reaching up and over toward the right side.

Inhale to come back through center. Exhale to open your arms toward the right, left arm forward, right arm back.

Inhale to reach both arms toward the sky. Exhale to straighten the right leg, hinging at your hips and folding your chest toward your right leg with your back heel lifted in a less intense variation of Pyramid Pose. Bring your hands to the mat to frame your front foot, your shin, or blocks on either side of your foot. Take 1 full breath here.

When you’re ready, step your left foot up to meet your right in Standing Forward Bend.

Inhale, reaching your arms up and overhead. With your exhalation, keep your arms high and sit your hips back in Chair Pose.

Repeat the following poses on the opposite side:

Gently land your knees to your mat and move through hands and knee into a seated position. Bring the soles of your feet together and let your knees fall out toward the sides in Bound Angle Pose. If this feels too intense, slide a blocks beneath each knee for extra support.

Stay here, or round your spine and walk your hands forward as you bring your chest toward your toes. Let your body find where it wants to be rather than force the shape. Take 5 breaths in your chosen position.

When you’re ready, move through a seated position to come all the way onto your back in Savasana. Feel free to add blocks beneath your knees for extra support.

Stay here for 3-5 minutes or as long as you’d like.

Push yourself upright to a comfortable seat. Bring your hands together at heart center, bow your head, and thank yourself for showing up on your mat today.

#8941. What Happens When Grief Derails Your Triathlon Training

Rachel Olson wins 2026 Ironman 70.3 São Paulo after struggling to train through the grief of losing her mother in November 2024. (Photo: Romulo Cruz/Ironman)

In late September, Rachel Olson crossed the finish line first at Ironman 70.3 São Paulo, nearly 10 minutes ahead of her nearest competitor. The race, by her own admission, was “not spectacular” for the longtime pro triathlete. But the support that followed was. The crowd embraced her, and athletes and fans who had followed her story cheered a little louder, as though they knew what it took just to get her to the start line.

Because in the months after her mother Janis died in November 2024 of liver disease, Olson could barely bring herself to work out. She did not want to disappear from triathlon. But she’d go to the pool and just sit on the edge and cry. She’d hop on her bike and feel a sudden urge to turn around. Running, always an easy way to manage big emotions, became a chore.

Then her body began to rebel: digestive issues, mysterious inflammation, bone-deep exhaustion, muscles that wouldn’t recover.

“My body was basically screaming at me that something was wrong, like it was constantly fighting something,” said Olson, 35, who lives in Boulder with her fiancé, fellow pro triathlete Andre Lopes. “Your mind is telling you to process, and your body is telling you to slow down.”

For endurance athletes, the instinct after a loss is often to train through the emotional pain. The adage goes that exercise helps with grief: Get outside, move your body, clear your head. Sometimes it does. But for Olson and many others, the very thing that once gave life structure can become one more demand on a body and mind already stretched thin.

“Grief doesn’t just live in the mind. It’s in the chest, in the restlessness, in this low-grade energy that has nowhere obvious to go,” said Kenza Haddock, president and co-founder of Oceanic Counseling Group in Murrells Inlet, South Carolina. “Endurance sport can tip from processing grief into outrunning it, using exhaustion to stay ahead of the feeling rather than move through it. It can just leave you more numb.”

Plenty of endurance athletes have turned grief into a mission. In August 2026, Matthew Hollingham, a 25-year-old doctoral student at Penn State, created an “Arctic Circle to Africa” triathlon in memory of his late fiancée Lovisa Arnesson-Cronhamre, who was killed in a hit-and-run while jogging on campus. Over 61 days and 3,545 miles, he swam in a lake above the Arctic Circle, ran a marathon a day for 37 days, and cycled just over 110 miles a day for 23. He raised more than $40,000 for two charities and kept her memory present.

Others have taken similar routes; at the 2026 London Marathon, Laura Coleman-Day, a 33-year-old mother from Lincolnshire in the U.K., went viral for changing into her wedding dress and running the final miles in it as a dedication to her late husband, Xander.

This kind of public mission can be cathartic, says Hilary Bucell, a psychotherapist and lecturer at Columbia University.

“Engaging in something like triathlon can become a ritualized space where the recognition of the loss is welcomed and at the same time, the sport’s necessity for present moment awareness also helps athletes acknowledge new life experiences continuing now beyond the loss,” she said.

Of course, racing to honor a loved one doesn’t erase grief — it just gives you a place to put it. It can also offer a healthy distraction from the deep ache of a devastating loss.

Some aren’t able to navigate their grief in such a public and profound way. There are those like Olson whose grief hits the body hard enough to derail training. In 2023, Gustav Iden, the 2022 Ironman World Champion, ended his season early to heal and regroup after the death of his mother, revealing “it was very emotional, and it was hard to find joy in training after that.” (He returned to racing about a year later.)

As one of her mother’s main caretakers, Olson spent two years before her death flying to her hometown in Texas for doctor’s appointments. Triathlon took a backseat: She parted ways with her coach and scaled back her training. Even when she did have time to work out, anxiety followed.

“I would think, ‘Am I going to be out on a bike ride and get a phone call saying she’s in the hospital? Are things going to go downhill?’”

After Janis died, that anxiety turned physical. Olson was never diagnosed with one specific issue, but testing showed elevated inflammation markers and low ferritin, requiring an iron infusion.

“Ultimately, I think my body was responding to trauma. It felt like I had an illness,” she said. “Trying to perform in a body that felt completely foreign to me was incredibly difficult. I didn’t understand why my body wasn’t doing what it had done before.”

Research suggests that grief can affect the body as well as the mind. The National Institutes of Health (NIH) lists impaired immune response and increased mortality from heart disease, especially in older, widowed patients, among the physical complications. The effects may vary, as not everyone experiences the same physical response.

Part of the explanation may lie in how the brain processes the loss of a loved one through interconnected systems involved in emotion, threat detection, and the regulation of stress hormones. Grief can flood the body with inflammatory signals. and increase cortisol, the steroid hormone produced by the adrenal glands that regulates the body’s response to stress.

“Grief is a neurological event that impacts your ability to learn and remember things, attend to things, and impacts your mood,” said Wilfred van Gorp, a Manhattan-based board-certified neuropsychologist. “Losing someone keeps your amygdala on high alert and elevates cortisol. It impacts you in your body as well as your mind.”

Grief and stress can also disrupt communication between the brain and the gut, which may contribute to everything from irritable bowel syndrome to acid reflux to ulcers, according to research.

For Olson, whose stomach swelled within days of her mother’s death, that brain-gut link was obvious.

“Only two days after [she passed], I woke up, and my stomach was distended about five inches. And then I kind of exploded in inflammation weight,” she shared. “Trying to get that down is not an easy process.”

Still, Olson pushed on. She’d qualified for her first Ironman World Championship slated for about 10 months after Janis died. She wanted to race there to honor her mom. She also didn’t want to lose her identity as a triathlete. Her training “wasn’t even close” to peak levels. In Kona, her stomach rebelled on the bike. After vomiting for three hours, she pulled out soon after starting the run.

“I held onto triathlon so tightly even though my body wasn’t ready. My mind wasn’t ready,” Olson said. “I kept pushing because I wanted it so badly. I attached too much weight to needing training [and racing] to go well and needing something in my life to be OK. Looking back, I realize I didn’t have to be OK.”

After Kona, Olson took a break. She focused on her other jobs as a triathlon coach and as a sales rep, and on envisioning what her wedding to Lopes could look like without her mom.

“I decided I wasn’t going to think about triathlon for a couple of weeks,” she shared. “If I still wanted it afterward, great. If I didn’t, that was OK, too.”

Spoiler: She still loved it. With the fog lifted, Olson saw a different future in the sport, starting with a new coach, Kasper Pedersen, who could build a sustainable load and understand her fragile state.

“I looked for a coach who understands that life happens,” said Olson. “Kasper is great at helping me push my boundaries, but he also knows that I may need to go at my own pace.”

They’re keeping her training volume relatively low as she re-establishes a baseline and repairs her frayed central nervous system.

“I really wanted to make my body and mind think, ‘This is fun. This is helping us,’ rather than setting off alarm bells every time I went out,” Olson shared. “There are still days where I have to take some time off. … Grief really is a roller coaster. But overall, we’ve done a really good job of figuring out what is working.”

Talking about it helps, too, though it doesn’t come easily. Olson describes her grief as a “cloud over her personal life,” and opening up about it has cost her: One friend drifted away, unable to understand what she was going through. Olson wonders if she was simply too much to handle. Still, she finds solace in speaking out, and in being a voice for others who may be grieving alone.

“As athletes, we want to put difficult things in the back of our minds and keep going,” she said. “But I’m glad I can be a voice for other people who are going through the same so they feel less alone than they think they are.”

If her recent win in Brazil is any sign, Olson is rounding a bend toward healing, with an approach to triathlon (and life) that’s less about control and more about leaning into the process, however unpredictable and messy it may be.

“I feel like I’m a different person than I was before [my mom died]. It will always feel like a part of me has been ripped away. But I also know that there’s literally no pain that hurts as bad as what I went through,” she said. “So I’ll keep telling myself, ‘Yes, I can do this thing.’”

#8940. The beliefs these Master Health Coaches had to unlearn (and you might too)

For example, in Motivational Interviewing, an effective communication style used in coaching and counseling, there is something called the “righting reflex.”

The righting reflex is the instinct to help or “fix” a client, as well as give them directions on how best to change. Often, the righting reflex is particularly strong in people who really, really care.

Sounds like a great instinct to follow if you’re a coach, right?

Motivational Interviewing describes how this (beautiful, well-intentioned) instinct to help can actually hinder a client’s progress.

That’s because when we swoop in to fix, correct, or steer, clients often do the exact opposite of what we’re hoping for: They dig in and get defensive.

Push someone the “right” way and, paradoxically, they’ll start advocating for the very habits they came to you to change. You end up being the one arguing for change—which leaves them to argue against it. Everyone walks away a little more frustrated, and the client feels more stuck than ever.

Instead, great, experienced coaches learn to get curious instead of corrective. (They might even encourage the client to explore not changing!)

That’s just one example of an upside-down skill that separates a good coach from a masterful one. But it’s certainly not the only example.

We asked some of Precision Nutrition’s most seasoned PN Level 2 Master Health Coach Certified coaches a simple question:

What’s something you were sure about early in your career that you later had to unlearn?

Their (honest, and sometimes humbling) answers are below, plus the wiser way forward they adopted, and are now sharing with you.

Our first lesson to unlearn comes from PN in-house coach Jeremy Fernandes, PN2-MHC.

With over 14 years of coaching experience, Coach Jeremy is known for his friendly, comfortable, “talk to me like I’m your buddy” coaching style. Which is ironic, because as you’ll see, he started off his career leaning heavily on a rigid structure that was actually pushing clients away.

At the beginning of my career, when I’d been a personal trainer for a year or two, I had a friend ask if I offered nutrition coaching. And my first move was: Here are all of the forms. And when I say “all of the forms,” I mean all of them—I probably sent this person 20 pages to fill out.

Three weeks later I had to hunt them down, and we ended up filling them out together—which took two and a half grueling hours.

If not for those forms, we could have started actually coaching, like, 20 days earlier.

Not long after, another friend showed up at my door with this white-hot intensity: “Tell me what to do, I’m ready,” they said. And I immediately dumped a metaphorical bucket of ice water on them with those darn forms. It was radio silence after that.

The problem was that I was operating like my sole job was to extract information from a person and then solve the mystery—as if I had some advanced pattern recognition about you that you didn’t have about yourself.

And unfortunately, I kept on that terrible path for a while.

What finally prompted a change was going through the Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification.

Going through that course, I saw there was a better framework—one that doesn’t rely on me robotically extracting information.

I learned to let the client take the lead, and then just listen and maybe ask a few good questions. And it works so much better—for everyone.

Now I work from the assumption that my client knows themselves better than anyone. One of my most valuable questions is simply:

“What have you tried before, what did you like about it, and what didn’t you like?”

When I let people take the floor, they nail the really big stuff more often than not—in a way my paperwork and my detective work never facilitated.

Honestly, the forms were me projecting professionalism, because back then I didn’t feel like a professional. My identity as a coach never felt natural until after L2. Now, just letting someone talk feels like coaching. We start with a connection, and then I just let them fill in the gaps.

The next lesson to unlearn comes from PN Director of Community Engagement and in-house coach Kate Solovieva, PN2-MHC.

With over 16 years of coaching experience, Coach Kate is known for her honesty and incisiveness. She has a way of dropping realness on her clients that may first feel like a shock, but ultimately ends up getting her clients to the heart of the matter much faster. But one hard truth she had to face was her own.

You know the story: You reach the healthy weight, the habits lock in, and the weight just stays stable on its own. You hit “save” and move on with your happily ever after.

At least most of the time. It’s true, some goals really are like that. If you want to run a marathon, you can pick a race date, follow a training program, show up to the start line, run it—and then you never have to run again and you will still have achieved that goal. That’s a real destination; you cross the finish line once and check the goal off.

But weight loss, muscle gain, body recomposition, building a habit of movement or eating well—those aren’t like that. Especially when the goal means working against a chronic tendency, like a predisposition to high blood pressure, or to hating exercise, or to living in a larger body than you’d prefer.

Those goals come with a pretty good amount of ongoing and intentional maintenance—daily, weekly, monthly. There’s no save button.

This realization didn’t come from one single client or one moment for me. It came through a collection of observations, including observations of myself. But once I saw it, it changed how I coach.

I realized that if there’s no real finish line, then my job is to manufacture finish lines along the way. That way, my clients continually feel like they’re accomplishing something satisfying.

I take the big goal and break it into something specific and daily—and then I insert smaller outcome goals into the journey.

For instance, someone going from sedentary to wanting to lose 100 pounds is facing a huge goal, full of behaviors and identities they’ll have to grow into. So along the way, we might set a goal of running a single mile without stopping. Strictly speaking, that doesn’t have much to do with the bigger goal—but it also has everything to do with it. It’s checkable. Achievable. Ideally it’s also something they’re a little excited about: fun, interesting, maybe even a little scary, but still within reach.

Because here’s the thing: It’s very hard to motivate the human brain to work out three times a week for the rest of their life to “get healthier.” “Being healthy” isn’t tangible, it’s not immediate—you can’t feel that far-off outcome in your body.

But striving towards a fun, achievable goal in the next three to six months? That’s real. It also builds in structure, and provides those little spikes of motivation—the hit of dopamine you get from working hard at something and actually accomplishing it.

Health isn’t something we ever fully “accomplish” or check off. So we have to give ourselves these little concrete goals along the way that we can feel and see and be delighted by.

The next lesson to unlearn comes from PN content creator Azul Corajoria, CPT, PN2-MHC.

With over nine years of coaching experience, Coach Azul’s coaching fingerprint is empathetic, relatable, and endlessly encouraging.

While these traits always came naturally to her, for a long time, she thought she had to adopt an opposite style to help certain clients (and herself) to “get back in line” when habits didn’t go as planned.

Early in my coaching career, I thought that if someone wasn’t following through on what they said they would do, it’s because they needed more structure or just to get their “head in the game.”

I couldn’t understand why someone would invest in coaching and then not do the things we planned.

It was especially confusing because most of my clients had “discipline.” They were successful, responsible, hardworking people who showed up for their jobs, families, and everyone else in their lives.

Meanwhile, I was also “disciplined” in many areas of my life—yet I also struggled with eating well and exercising consistently.

At this time, I felt this lack of consistency was my fault, and went straight to being really angry at myself. I thought I was just missing the “perfect something” (the perfect workout, the perfect diet) to help me change, so I’d just move from thing to thing, but each one would bring fresh disappointment.

I was incredibly frustrated by this cycle, and my response was to get stricter and harsher with myself.

It’s hard to say when it all changed. It wasn’t an overnight epiphany; it was a culmination of years of getting curious, being open to different methods, like the Body Positivity Movement and Intuitive Eating. I dove into self-compassion and positive psychology research, and I went through the PN Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification.

I applied everything I learned, and I noticed that the more open and curious I was, the better my clients responded. Slowly, that turned into the realization that the more open and curious I was with myself, the better I would respond.

I stopped binge eating. I started enjoying exercise more. I took more career risks.

I learned that when we can respond to a setback with curiosity instead of punishment, we’re much more likely to stay engaged. When I allow myself to be disappointed by an action, take responsibility for it, and remain on my own side, I feel safer reflecting and taking risks. The more I do that, the more likely I am to achieve the things I want.

Sometimes the most helpful thing we can teach a client (and ourselves) is not how to push harder or “just be more disciplined.” It’s how to make a mistake, remain on our own side, and keep going.

Because self-compassion is not the opposite of accountability; it’s often what makes accountability possible. (I call it “compassionate accountability.”)

None of us will ever be the “perfect” coach, and we don’t have to be. The more human I’ve allowed myself to be, the better relationships I’ve had with my clients. My biggest goal as a coach is to create an environment my client feels safe to come back to with not only their wins, but their losses. The safer they feel being honest and open with me, the safer they’ll feel to try new things—and over time they’ll build the confidence to do it themselves.

The next lesson to unlearn comes from PN in-house coach and Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification instructor Dom Matteo, PN2-MHC, NBC-HWC.

With over 16 years of coaching experience, Coach Dom stands out for his non-judgemental attitude and excellent listening skills. For Dom, these traits are relatively inherent, but they’ve also been carefully developed and honed, in part by letting go of what he calls the “coach’s ego”—the assumption that he already knew what a client’s success should look like, and that he was the one who got to keep score.

I took that stated goal at face value, and treated whatever number they gave me as the measuring stick, as the most important thing to work towards.

But then, I’d see a client struggling to do their actions even 50 percent of the time, and I’d think: ‘This person is never going to be happy, because this won’t get them to the goal weight they told me they wanted.’

Remember, I assumed the number was the real goal.

However, again and again, those same clients would turn out to be genuinely happy with their progress, not because they hit their exact goal, but because they felt so much better about themselves and their lives.

What I learned is that the stated outcome was almost never the true goal for many of them. When they said ‘lose 50 pounds,’ what they really meant was: I want to feel better. And being consistent even half the time, over a year, netted results they were thrilled with. Because they felt better. They felt different.

So the thing I had to let go of was my own scorecard. Who am I to tell a client that what they’re doing isn’t good enough, if they’re happy with how things are going?

My new definition of progress became less about approaching a specific final number and more about another question: “Am I a little better today than I was yesterday?”

These days, I spend time up front helping a client build what we call a “wellness vision.” We clarify their values, and what success actually looks and feels like to them.

Then, instead of assuming I know how to measure their progress, I’ll ask: “How will you know if this is helping? How do you want to measure success?”

The result is that even a client who’s fixated on the scale can see other signs of progress long before the scale actually changes. And often, those other signs are the things they really wanted to change in the first place.

It turns out the most useful thing I can provide isn’t a judgement about whether a client is succeeding. Instead, it’s to help them determine and notice their own success, by their own measures.

The next lesson to unlearn comes from PN in-house coach and Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification instructor Jason Bonn, PN2-MHC, NBC-HWC.

With over 18 years of coaching experience, Coach Jason’s clients describe him as patient, observant, and deeply dedicated. He has a knack for spotting a client’s potential—though as you’ll read in this story, Coach Jason learned that getting too focused on a specific version of that potential sometimes kept him from seeing other ways his clients could grow and thrive.

For me, progress felt like a puzzle to solve: I’d play with adjustments to exercise volume or intensity, calorie or protein intake, eating more slowly, eating to 80 percent fullness, all the fundamental stuff.

But then, because of one client I still think about, I began to shift how I thought about “progress.”

He was in our PN coaching program. He lost 40 to 50 pounds in his first six months—which was great—but then everything stalled.

We tried adjustment after adjustment for the next two and a half years. We added more protein, more cardio, and worked through his particular peccadillo, eating corn chips at night. But none of it moved his numbers.

What got me was that he kept showing up anyway: three straight years, re-enrolling each time, even though the scale had plateaued.

That told me something was working for him—it just wasn’t something I recognized yet.

In his third year, we stopped looking only at the gym and his diet, and started looking at his whole life. He was a landscape painter, so we built his practices around that instead: make a sketch or work on a painting daily, anything that sparked some joy or interest. Within a couple of weeks, he was getting on his bike and riding out to further places for different scenery to paint.

In part because of this client, I’m now a lot more cognizant of coaching the whole person, and considering their Deep Health. Weight and performance numbers are just one piece of a much bigger picture that includes relationships, emotional wellbeing, and what someone finds meaningful.

I’ve also stopped zeroing in on “problem” behavior.

I try to understand a person’s life overall—not just the behavior I’ve been hired to help with—because there’s a connectedness to it all, and behavior tends to emerge within the context of someone’s life.

I’ve also stopped treating the coaching relationship as a means to an outcome and started treating it as the main thing—the sun that everything orbits, the glue that holds it all together.

That client kept coming back for three years because the relationship mattered to him. By the end, I’d stopped thinking I was failing him. The weight loss was such a small part of the success. The relationship was the bigger piece.

Coaching mastery isn’t about stockpiling more information. (Your clients can Google information or ask a chatbot, and so can you.)

It’s about developing the judgment to know when to use what you know, when to set it aside, and when the most helpful thing you can do is nothing at all, except be there.

But that kind of judgment is hard to build alone; it takes practice, expert feedback, and a few humbling moments with real clients—which is exactly what the PN Level 2 Master Health Coach Certification is designed to offer.

With enough practice, self-awareness, and the right training, you can gain the wisdom and skill of the above coaches.

But the best coaches, it turns out, are defined less by what they know than by what they’ve been willing to unlearn.

Ready to move from competent to truly masterful—in 20 weeks?

#8939. A Frightening Encounter on a Dark Road Nearly Took Night Running From Me. This Year, I’m Taking It Back.

I N THE DARK, the headlights cast a distorted version of my silhouette on the industrial building to my left as the vehicle makes its way past me. I’m running along an otherwise desolate road, not far from my house. The car comes to a halt at the stop sign about 300 feet in front of me—and idles. My legs instinctively slow down, my body reacting before my mind has a chance to catch up. I quickly calculate what to do next. There are no side streets I can turn into—I either have to run past the car or turn around, which would add a few miles to my run that I’m not ready for. Maybe the driver is just checking his phone, I tell myself.

But the broad-shouldered man with a long graying beard at the wheel is waiting for me with the window rolled down, his arm resting in its frame. He starts shouting before I can make sense of the situation: What do I think I am doing, running in the dark? Am I trying to get killed? My body tenses, anticipating the man’s possible next move. He has daughters my age, he continues, and he’d kill them if they did that. Could I at least carry this with me, he roars, throwing a key-chain alarm to my feet, then driving off before I have a chance to react.

I sprint the last half a mile home, propelled by anxious energy. My inability to focus only fuels my confusion; so does the blue egg-shaped alarm in my trembling hand that I don’t have a clear memory of picking up but am holding nevertheless. I try to replay in my head how it got there—and why. I have reflective bands on both my arms and my ankles, so drivers can spot me. I use my phone’s light to illuminate the ground in front of me whenever I need to.

The next day, I don’t run outside in the dark. Too cold, I convince myself when I step on the treadmill I hate so much in my apartment complex gym. Too rattled, is what I am unwilling to admit. Because do I have any right to feel that way when technically nothing happened to me? The stranger, in the end, didn’t hurt me.

Still, something changed on the road in the dark.

With every rhythmic thump the belt makes, I am less determined to keep going. My mind can’t handle the monotony. I start skipping days when I cannot make it out for a daytime run. At some point over the next few weeks, the key to the gym falls behind the shoe rack, and I don’t even notice.

THE LIKELY DIAGNOSIS is seasonal affective disorder. It could also be winter blues, but that one is milder and more temporary. My somber mood and low energy seem constant. For most people, it passes by spring, my therapist says. What helps? For one, exercise! But at that point, my couch’s cushions have resigned to accepting my body’s indentation as their new shape.

By the time spring comes, my fitness is at odds with my enthusiasm for the prolonged daylight, and I end up with shin splints. I spend the rest of the year trying to heal and return to form.

I don’t forget about the gray-bearded man. In fact, I share the story, framing it as a silly encounter. “Would you believe that?” I say with a forced smile.

“That’s not okay,” my friends and coworkers answer with their words as much as their faces.

My feelings start morphing from self-blame into anger. What should have been clear to me from the beginning dawns on me slowly: Vigilance is important, but the solution to a stranger’s concerns about my safety is not to instill more fear in the name of “protection.” Women running at night are not the problem. We’ve long ago dismantled the patriarchal notion that men should be our protectors when, in fact, they often pose the danger.

And so when the clock falls back an hour at the start of November, I’m determined not to fall back into a cycle of seasonal depression and injury.

BY MID-DECEMBER, it’s dark by 4:30 p.m. I wrap my torso in color-changing LED tubes. Today I pick emerald. As I descend the trail that clings to the bank of the Delaware River, the historic cantilever bridge that crosses the water comes into view, itself wrapped in green color-changing lights. I smile for no other reason but that we match.

I run up a semicircle road where, for a moment, the world is reduced to cones of warm yellow glowing from vintage streetlights. My chest lamp illuminates just enough ground in front of me to fit my next two steps. Beyond that, I trust that my feet remember what my eyes cannot see.

The darkness has a way of taming my unruly mind. The stillness mutes my whirling thoughts, a nearly impossible achievement among the hectic noise of daylight. It’s the closest I come to meditating, to understanding what it means to be present. It doesn’t matter where the road leads or how long is left of my run; it’s only here and now. The quiet is mostly disrupted by my own two feet. They take turns striking the ground, but their thuds meet in the echo that reverberates off building walls before getting swallowed up by the endless nightfall blue encircling me.

How did I ever allow this to be taken away from me?

Someone lingers at the end of the sidewalk in front of me, and I instinctively switch to the opposite side, picking up speed.

The person pays me no mind, looking in the direction of a leash they’re holding, the end of which I cannot make out. The black road becomes deserted again, and I slow my pace. What was born out of necessity has grown into my favorite part of the day. I love this. I need this. This is the world I want to live in.

This article originally appeared in the Spring 2026 issue of Runner’s World.

Pavlína Černá, an RRCA-certified run coach and cycling enthusiast, has been with Runner’s World, Bicycling, and Popular Mechanics since August 2021. When she doesn’t edit, she writes; when she doesn’t write, she reads or translates. In whatever time she has left, you can find her outside running, riding, or roller-skating to the beat of one of the many audiobooks on her TBL list.

That's the magic of this redemption, and once you see it, you can't unsee it. Here's the math that makes the ChooseFI community light up: a round-trip business class ticket from JFK to Madrid on Iberia regularly retails for **$2,500 to $5,000** in cash. At the off-peak Avios rate of **34,000 points one-way**, you're extracting **7.4 to 14.7 cents per point** — a figure that puts this redemption in a completely different category from most loyalty redemptions, where 1–2 cents per point is considered standard. To put that in human terms: if you transferred 34,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards points to Iberia Plus and used them for this booking, you'd be getting a value equivalent to someone handing you a $2,500–$5,000 check in exchange for points that cost you roughly $340–$510 in credit card spend to earn (at a 1% earn baseline). That's not a deal. That's a pricing inefficiency, and it's one that's been hiding in plain sight for travelers who only know British Airways Avios and never discovered Iberia's **separate, more generous award chart**. The FI mindset is about finding asymmetries — places where the value you receive is wildly disproportionate to what you give up. This is one of the cleanest examples in the entire travel rewards ecosystem. You're not gaming anything. You're simply using Iberia's published off-peak pricing to access a premium cabin product that most people assume is out of reach. Your future self, lying flat at 38,000 feet somewhere over the Atlantic, will be glad you learned this system.

Europe in a lie-flat seat for fewer points than most domestic first class awards

Free calculator shows when you could reach financial independence — plus a savings rate tracker, expense audit, and more.

Here's the insight that separates travelers who occasionally use points from those who systematically fly business class to Europe for nearly free: Iberia Avios and British Airways Avios are the same currency, but they operate on completely different award charts.

Most people who've been in the travel rewards world for a while know about British Airways Avios. They know that BA prices awards by distance, and they know that BA is notorious for hefty fuel surcharges that can turn a "free" business class flight into a $700+ fees bill. So they write off transatlantic Avios redemptions as not worth it.

That's the mistake. Iberia — a fellow Oneworld carrier and Avios partner — publishes its own off-peak award chart for flights operated on Iberia metal (Iberia aircraft, Iberia flight numbers). Flights from the US to Madrid, when booked through Iberia Plus (not British Airways Executive Club), price out at 34,000 Avios one-way in business class during off-peak periods. That's the same Avios currency, same points you can transfer from Chase, but priced under Iberia's more favorable structure.

The fuel surcharge situation is also materially better on Iberia-operated flights booked through Iberia Plus than BA-operated flights booked through BA. Taxes and fees are generally moderate — you're looking at a few hundred dollars in fees rather than the $600–$700+ that sometimes plagues British Airways award bookings.

Off-peak windows are specific. Iberia defines off-peak as January through March and October through November. Mark those months. Outside of those windows, pricing steps up, and the sweet spot math starts to erode.

The transfer path is straightforward. Iberia Plus is a 1:1 transfer partner with Chase Ultimate Rewards, and transfers are instant — a critical advantage when you're chasing limited award availability. You search, you find the seat, you transfer, you book. No waiting 3–5 days for points to land and watching the seat disappear.

Marriott Bonvoy is also a transfer partner (3:1 ratio, 1–5 days), but the math there is less favorable and the speed is slower. Chase Ultimate Rewards is your primary earning vehicle for this redemption.

One important structural note: Avios are shareable across BA, Iberia, Aer Lingus, and Vueling accounts — meaning if you've been accumulating BA Avios, you can move them to an Iberia Plus account to access Iberia's off-peak pricing. This opens the door even if you've been building your Avios balance through the British Airways credit card or BA partners. The accounts need to be linked through the Avios household account feature, but it's a powerful tool that many travelers overlook.

Finally, keep the expiry rule in mind: Iberia Avios expire after 36 months of account inactivity. A single small transaction — even buying a few Avios — resets the clock. Don't let your points die quietly in an unused account.

If you don't already have one, go to iberia.com and sign up for a free Iberia Plus account. This takes about five minutes. Write down your membership number — you'll need it for the transfer step. Make sure your name matches your passport exactly to avoid issues at check-in.

Go to iberia.com and select "Book with Avios" in the award booking section. Enter your route (e.g., JFK to MAD) and select your travel dates. Critically, target off-peak months: January through March, and October through November. These are the windows where the 34,000 Avios one-way business class pricing applies.

Search one-way first. Iberia's search tool will show you available Avios seats color-coded by price — you're looking for the off-peak pricing tier. If you see 34,000 Avios for business class, that's your seat. Note the specific flight number and date before doing anything with your points.

Before transferring a single point, click through the booking to see the full taxes and fees. Iberia charges moderate fees on transatlantic awards — generally more reasonable than British Airways — but you want to know the number. Confirm you're comfortable with the cash portion before proceeding.

Log into your Chase Ultimate Rewards portal at ultimaterewards.com. Navigate to "Transfer to Travel Partners" and select Iberia Plus. Transfer exactly 34,000 points (or the amount required for your specific itinerary). Transfers from Chase to Iberia Plus are 1:1 and instant — your Avios will appear in your Iberia Plus account within minutes.

Go back to iberia.com with your Iberia Plus account logged in. Confirm the award seat is still showing (it should be — you moved fast). Complete the booking using your Avios balance. Pay the taxes and fees with a card that earns well on travel or general spend.

Award space on popular routes can be tight. Here's how to improve your odds:

Most airline programs charge the same award price year-round or use dynamic pricing that moves with demand. Iberia is unusual because it publishes an explicit off-peak calendar with fixed lower pricing during specific date ranges. Off-peak pricing applies to the flight date, not the booking date, so you can book an off-peak flight months in advance and lock in the lower rate. The off-peak discount is roughly 50% compared to peak pricing on the same route. This creates a planning advantage for flexible travelers who can target specific travel windows. Combined with the fact that Avios transfer from five major credit card programs, it is one of the most accessible premium redemptions in the loyalty landscape.

Let's walk through a real example so the numbers are concrete.

It's mid-October — peak fall travel season for most Europeans, but squarely within Iberia's off-peak award window (October through November). You've found award space on IB6251, JFK to MAD, departing John F. Kennedy at 10:30 PM and arriving at Madrid Barajas the following afternoon. The aircraft is an Airbus A350-900 — one of the best long-haul platforms in the sky.

The cash price for this flight in business class: $3,200 one-way, as priced on iberia.com for that week. Round trip in business runs approximately $4,800–$6,000 depending on timing.

The Avios price: 34,000 Iberia Avios plus approximately $250–$350 in taxes and fees.

Your CPP on this redemption: With a retail value of $3,200 and a cost of 34,000 points, you're extracting 9.4 cents per point — comfortably in the 7.4–14.7 cent range that defines this sweet spot as exceptional.

Now let's talk about what you're actually getting for those points. Iberia Business on the A350-900 features fully flat seats in a 1-2-1 configuration — meaning every passenger has direct aisle access. No climbing over a seatmate at 2 AM. The seat converts to a fully flat bed of approximately 73 inches. You'll have a personal entertainment screen, noise-canceling headphones, and amenity kit.

Before you board, you have access to Iberia's business class lounge at MAD (on the return) and partner lounges at JFK — typically the Iberia-operated space or a Oneworld partner lounge. The meal service on this transatlantic route reflects Spanish hospitality: proper courses, wine service, and a breakfast before landing.

For a couple traveling together, this redemption costs 68,000 Avios plus fees — a round figure that's very achievable through the Chase Sapphire Preferred or Sapphire Reserve welcome bonus alone. You land in Madrid rested, having slept in a flat bed over the Atlantic, having spent a fraction of what cash passengers paid. That's the FI travel rewards system working exactly as it should.

Do this: Book as close to 355 days out as possible for off-peak dates. Iberia releases award space up to 355 days in advance. The most reliable business class availability appears right when that window opens. If your target is January or February travel, set a calendar reminder for April or May of the prior year and search on Day 355. The seats won't last.

Do this: Transfer Avios from a BA account if you've been building there. If you've been earning BA Avios through the British Airways credit card or BA shopping portal, you don't need to start over. Avios are transferable across BA, Iberia, Aer Lingus, and Vueling accounts via the household account feature. Link the accounts, move the Avios to your Iberia Plus account, and access the off-peak pricing. This is an underused feature.

Do this: Earn points primarily through Chase Ultimate Rewards. The Chase Sapphire Preferred, Sapphire Reserve, and Ink Business Preferred all feed into the same Chase UR pool with a 1:1 instant transfer to Iberia Plus. For this redemption specifically, Chase is your most efficient earning engine. Use the welcome bonus from one of these cards as your foundation — a 60,000–100,000 point bonus gets you most of the way to two one-way business class seats.

Avoid this: Transferring points before confirming award space. Avios are transferred into Iberia Plus and can't be easily moved back or transferred to another program without complexity. Always confirm the exact flight, date, and availability BEFORE you initiate a transfer from Chase. The instant transfer speed from Chase means you can lock in availability quickly — but only once you've verified the seat exists.

Avoid this: Booking during peak periods expecting off-peak pricing. December, July, and August are not off-peak. The 34,000 Avios rate is specifically tied to Iberia's off-peak calendar (January–March and October–November). Outside those windows, pricing increases significantly and the CPP math deteriorates. Don't assume off-peak pricing applies year-round.

Do this: Keep your Iberia Plus account active. Avios expire after 36 months of account inactivity. If you're holding points for a future redemption, keep the account alive with a small transaction — even earning a few Avios through a partner purchase resets the clock for another 36 months.

This redemption is ideal for couples and solo travelers who want to experience genuine transatlantic business class — flat beds, real meal service, lounge access — without the $3,000–$5,000 cash outlay that normally makes that choice feel irresponsible on a FI journey.

This is also an excellent gateway redemption for families with older children who understand that off-peak travel timing is part of the strategy — though booking four or more business class seats requires significant Avios accumulation and tighter award availability.

For the FI community member who's disciplined about earning and has a Chase UR foundation, this is one of the cleanest business class sweet spots available anywhere in the transatlantic market.

This redemption is rated **moderate difficulty** — not because anything about it is technically complex, but because it requires you to navigate a few specific steps that most people haven't done before. **The main challenges are:** 1. **Awareness of the separate Iberia award chart.** Most travelers default to British Airways Avios and never discover that Iberia prices its own flights differently. Once you know this, it's not a challenge — it's an advantage. 2. **Award availability.** Iberia business class award seats on JFK–MAD are genuinely limited, especially as you get closer to the off-peak windows. You're competing with other knowledgeable award travelers. Availability is rated a 3 out of 5 for a reason — the seats are there, but you have to work for them. 3. **Account setup.** You need an Iberia Plus account separate from any BA account, and you need to navigate iberia.com's award search interface, which is functional but not as polished as some other programs. **Three tips to overcome these challenges:** - Search award space **355 days in advance** for maximum selection - Use **iberia.com directly** to search — it shows Iberia-operated availability most accurately - Keep the **Chase UR instant transfer** in your back pocket so you can act the moment you find space If you've ever transferred points to an airline and booked an award flight before, this will feel familiar. If this is your first time, expect to spend an evening learning the process — but the payoff is a flat-bed seat over the Atlantic for a fraction of its cash price. That's worth an evening.

Iberia Avios and British Airways Avios are the same currency and can be transferred between accounts for free. However, Iberia's award chart prices flights on Iberia metal differently than British Airways does. For flights to Madrid on Iberia-operated routes, booking through Iberia Plus is typically cheaper than through BA Executive Club.

No. Iberia's off-peak pricing applies only to Iberia-operated flights. British Airways has its own separate pricing structure through BA Executive Club. For flights to London, you would need to use BA Avios and their own award chart, which does not offer the same off-peak discount.

Yes. Iberia updates its off-peak calendar periodically, and the specific date ranges can shift by a few weeks. Always check the current published calendar before planning your trip. The general pattern of January-March and October-November as off-peak has been consistent, but exact boundaries vary.

Iberia long-haul business class features fully flat seats in a 1-2-1 configuration with direct aisle access on their A350 and A330 aircraft. The seats convert to a flat bed for sleeping. The food and wine service reflects Spanish culinary traditions, including Iberian ham and regional wines. It is a solid European business class product, comparable to Air France or Lufthansa.

Iberia Avios off-peak business class to Madrid is the most efficient way to fly business class to Europe on points. At 34,000 Avios one-way, it costs less than many domestic first class awards. The off-peak calendar rewards flexible travelers with a 50% discount, and the breadth of transfer partners means almost anyone with transferable points can access this redemption. If you can align your European travel with the off-peak windows, this sweet spot delivers exceptional value with minimal complexity.
