#8937. After Training for My First Marathon, I Felt Like My Body Didn’t Look Like the Runner I Thought I’d Become. Experts Helped Me See Otherwise.

Marathon training changed how I saw my body—even when it didn’t change how I looked.

Two weeks out from my first marathon, I looked in the mirror and didn’t see the version of myself I thought I would. There was no six-pack, not even a hint of ab definition. My glutes weren’t particularly sculpted, and I wouldn’t exactly describe myself as lean like many runners I see.

At 5-foot-10, I’ve never been the smallest girl in the room. And while my long legs certainly help me cover more distance, I expected months of marathon training to leave me looking more visibly athletic, with more muscle definition and a physique that reflected just how hard I’d been working. I thought that after months of early alarms, added protein, and steadily increasing mileage, I’d look in the mirror and see a different body type.

Somewhere along the way, I absorbed the idea that a runner’s body should look a certain way. When mine didn’t match that image, I started wondering if I wasn’t training hard enough, if I was doing something wrong, or if my body simply wasn’t responding the way it was supposed to.

As I approached race day, I thought about why I was holding myself to that standard in the first place, especially because I was running the New York City Marathon on behalf of Planned Parenthood of Greater New York, an organization whose work centers on bodily autonomy and compassionate care.

Why was I putting so much pressure on my body to look different when it was already doing something incredible? I realized training for a marathon isn’t just about building endurance; it can also mean confronting the expectations you place on yourself.

So many people have an idea of what a “runner’s body” is supposed to look like, particularly fed by what we see online. When you see the same body type represented over and over, it’s easy to start associating that appearance with athleticism. But running a marathon is an enormous physical undertaking, and there’s no single body type that proves you’re capable of doing it.

Clinical sport psychologist Hillary Cauthen, PsyD, explains that the concept of “a runner’s body” is “largely a socially constructed ideal influenced by media representation, sport culture, and the tendency to associate certain physical characteristics with athletic success.” She adds that distance running has historically been represented by a lean body type, particularly smaller-framed athletes, which can leave some recreational runners questioning whether they fit the mold.

Comparison is a large part of this problem, too, says Cindra Kamphoff, PhD, mental performance coach and founder of the Mentally Strong Institute. “We see elite runners and start believing that’s what we should look like,” she explains.

Marathon training is practically a master class in comparison, making it hard to avoid. You’re tracking your pace, watching your mileage climb, sharing runs on Strava, and seeing what everyone else is doing. It can feel like your body should be changing right alongside your stats.

There’s also a particularly frustrating point of tension for women, who can feel caught between the cultural expectation to be smaller and the athletic ideal of looking lean and strong. Carinthia Bank, LCSW, a social worker who works with runners on body image, describes this as the “female athlete paradox,” in which women are judged against both ideals.

For example, a woman might recognize that building strength and fueling adequately are essential to marathon training, yet still feel pressure to maintain a smaller frame or worry that eating more to support her mileage will change her body in ways she doesn’t want. These competing expectations can shape how women judge their bodies, even as they get stronger and more capable, Bank explains.

Marathon training can also increase the time we spend thinking about our bodies, particularly when we’re experiencing physical or emotional discomfort, Bank adds. Many runners tend to think they’d feel better if their bodies were different, which can lead to judgment and blame toward the body they have.

That’s the trap I found myself in. While I was training for 26.2 miles, part of me was still measuring my progress against an imaginary finish line where I’d emerge with a completely different-looking body. I would accomplish something I’d never done before, like running my farthest distance, yet I was using my appearance to dictate my progress.

Cauthen offers a simple definition to keep in mind: “A runner’s body is not a specific shape or size. It is a body that runs.”

Here’s the thing about marathon training: Your body adapts to the physical demands of running, but those changes don’t guarantee an aesthetic transformation. You might build muscle, experience weight fluctuations, or notice an increase in appetite as your body works to fuel and recover. “Improved fitness does not always result in weight loss or a smaller body,” Cauthen says.

There’s also a practical reason not to make getting smaller one of your goals in marathon training. Kamphoff encourages runners “to focus on fueling for performance rather than restricting for appearance,” reminding us that “you can’t expect your body to perform at its best if you’re constantly trying to make it take up less space.”

Marathon training requires substantial energy, and restricting food to change your appearance can leave you without enough fuel to support your workouts and recovery.

Plus, fixating on your size can affect more than physical performance. “Focusing on getting smaller can distract and discourage us from actions that are helpful to performance and mental health,” Bank says. When you’re preoccupied with changing your body, you can miss out on learning what helps you perform, enjoying the process, and appreciating everything your body allows you to do.

I had to confront the fact that I’d been treating my appearance as a report card for my training. If I was working hard enough, I assumed I’d eventually see visible proof in the mirror. But I realized I can become a stronger, more capable runner without looking the way I imagined I would.

For me, that meant recognizing that the body I’d been criticizing was the same one carrying me through early morning runs and increasingly long distances. My body wasn’t failing at becoming a runner’s body—I’d been expecting it to meet a standard that had very little to do with what I was asking it to do.

I wish I could say that learning all of this made me instantly love every inch of my body, but that wouldn’t be honest. I’m still working on it, and I still have moments when I catch my reflection and wonder why I don’t look the way I imagined I would after months of training. But I’m trying to shift my focus from what my body looks like to what it’s allowing me to do, with the help of these expert tips.

“One of the most important shifts runners can make is moving from body evaluation to body appreciation,” Cauthen says. Instead of asking whether I look like someone who runs marathons, I’m trying to ask myself what my body has helped me accomplish. And the answer is a lot more impressive than whether or not I have visible abs.

As I got closer to race day, I continued to remind myself that I don’t have to look a certain way to feel proud of what I accomplished. My body carried me through months of training, and that’s worth celebrating all on its own.

I’m also learning to give myself a little more grace when my expectations don’t match reality. Bank reminds runners that “human beings usually get uncomfortable when there’s a difference between what we wanted and what we get,” and encourages compassion rather than self-criticism.

I don’t have to ignore the fact that I expected marathon training to change my appearance, but I also don’t want those expectations to overshadow everything else I’ve gained, including running farther than I ever thought possible, learning how to fuel and maintain energy, and showing up for myself.

Cauthen recommends distinguishing between observing a physical change and assigning a negative meaning to it, which has really stuck with me. “Noticing that your legs have become more muscular, your weight has fluctuated, or your clothing fits differently is an observation,” she explains. “Deciding those changes mean you are too big, not fit enough, or don’t look like a runner is an interpretation.” This helped me realize how quickly I can turn a neutral observation into self-criticism.

Instead of jumping to conclusions, Cauthen says it’s helpful to ask yourself a few questions when those negative thoughts creep in. For example, “is this thought based on evidence or comparison?” and “am I evaluating my body based on appearance or how I feel and function?” These questions challenge the assumptions that we tend to make about our bodies.

Kamphoff encourages runners to develop what she calls an “inner coach” instead of listening to an inner critic. One strategy she recommends is to “capture your wins” by writing down three things you’re proud of after training. The idea is to shift your attention from perceived imperfections to the progress you’ve made.

I’m trying to practice this by celebrating the things that don’t show up in a mirror. For example, I’ve learned how to pace myself and keep going when a run gets uncomfortable. “Your body has been showing up for you mile after mile. Make sure your self-talk is showing up for your body, too,” says Kamphoff.

Ultimately, I’m learning that I don’t need to love how my body looks every single day to respect what it does for me. “Body acceptance does not require loving every part of your appearance every day,” Cauthen says. “Sometimes it starts with respecting your body’s needs and appreciating its efforts, even when your feelings about your appearance are complicated.”

I can have complicated feelings about the way I look and still be proud of the athlete I’ve become. And I can show up at the starting line without meeting some imaginary physical standard first.

That’s the mindset I carried with me to the marathon. I ran 26.2 miles for a cause I believe in, after months of training that challenged me physically and mentally. My body didn’t have to look a certain way to deserve that moment.

After all those early mornings and hours of preparation, I finally crossed the finish line, put the medal around my neck, and walked out of Central Park feeling something I hadn’t quite felt throughout training: pride. Not because my body looked different, but because of everything it had just done. I felt so grateful for my legs that kept moving, my strength that carried me through the tough miles, and a body that got me to the finish line without injury.

No, my body may not have looked like the “marathon body” I once imagined, but it was a marathon body. I didn’t need a mirror selfie to prove what I’d accomplished: I ran all 26.2 miles. Honestly, what could be more impressive than that?

Alyssa is a New York City–based runner and lifestyle writer covering the intersection of fitness, beauty, and everyday routines. Currently training for the NYC Marathon, she brings a firsthand perspective to stories on endurance, recovery, and the mental side of running—alongside the real-life habits that support it. Her work is rooted in what’s practical, personal, and worth incorporating into your own routine.

#8936. The Biomechanics of Speed: How Your Form Can Improve Your Pace

This “speedwork” is way more fun than sprint repeats.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Whether you’re lacing up your shoes for a 5K or gearing up for a longer endurance race, if you want to get faster, you have to do both longer runs and speedwork sessions to train your aerobic and anaerobic systems. But for the biggest speed gains, you should also look beyond your cardiovascular fitness and work your… posture?

“People often think of running as a lower body sport, but running is everything going on between your ears and everywhere below,” says Anh Bui, D.P.T., C.S.C.S., a former collegiate runner, doctor of physical therapy, and biomechanics specialist in Oakland, California.

While you probably can’t (and shouldn’t) transform your running form into the stride of, say, Olympians on the podium, you can incorporate tweaks to make your mechanics more ideal for you. And that can help you improve performance, get faster, and lower your risk of getting hurt.

“There’s high variability between everyone’s biomechanics based on how you’re structurally and genetically built,” says Bui. “The key is to optimize movement, not force idealism, and to run efficiently to maximize speed and minimize injury risk.”

Read on for more about how each part of your biomechanics, from head to toe, contributes to your speed—plus a handful of moves to add to your routine that’ll help you pick up the pace.

It’s easier to maintain good posture on a short jog versus a long training run when your body starts to drag. But focusing on staying tall and keeping your shoulders from slumping is an important part of efficient running form—not to mention makes it easier to breathe.

Standing up straight as you run with a slight forward lean helps pull you forward, says Ellen Foster, D.P.T., a doctor of physical therapy, movement quality expert, and running coach in Cincinnati. “I like to encourage runners to sort of ‘fall’ forward from the ankles so that their hips are slightly in front of their feet,” she says. “Just make sure you don’t lean forward by bending at the hips or waist, as that would lead to pushing your hips back and losing valuable hip extension.”

Your arms play a surprisingly big role in picking up your pace. Just try pumping your arms harder next time you’re huffing up a hill and see how much it helps. Here’s why: The motion of your arms and legs are linked. “And our arms act as pendulums to help balance our trunk, as forces travel up our body from our legs,” says Foster. “So, when we swing our arms in a more efficient way, our legs often follow their lead.”

While research on just how crucial the arm swing is to running mechanics is limited (most studies focus more on the lower half of the body), and results offer mixed information, most researchers agree that swinging the arms helps with vertical oscillation (or how much we move upward as we stride), side-to-side balance, and minimizing rotation.

“Anecdotally, I find that arm swing drills can be a good starting place when working on increasing cadence, especially if someone is struggling to increase cadence due to poor coordination,” Foster says. Cadence, or the number of steps you take per minute, often changes depending on the speed you’re running, but experts suggest a quicker cadence can limit overstriding and help with forward momentum.

Sprinters tend to drive their knees up aggressively, about 90 degrees from the ground. That’s not sustainable over longer distances, says Bui, who says distance runners should ideally maintain more like 45 degrees of knee drive.

Why does the position of your knees matter? “Picking up your speed without appropriate knee drive will increase likelihood of overstriding, or landing with the foot far in front of your body,” Bui explains. That can slow you down and increases ground reaction forces—or forces exerted by the ground onto the body, Bui says—and ups your chances of injury.

When considering how your feet play into your form and your pace, a lot of it is about those ground reaction forces. If you reduce the time your feet come in contact with the ground, you can potentially lower the force on your body—and lessen your risk of injuries like shin splints, says Foster.

“When we look at vertical ground reaction forces (vGRF) across time, midfoot striking has a lower rate of vGRF with one smooth peak,” Bui explains. By contrast, heel striking has a longer ground contact time, leading to a higher peak force and greater load on the body. This is because your ankle dorsiflexors (when you pull toes toward shins) can’t efficiently absorb the impact of your foot strike, and therefore, your knee joint takes on extra force, she adds.

Try to pick up your cadence and adjust so you’re striking the ground with your foot underneath your body (rather than out too far in front) to help reduce those forces up the leg. Typically, heel striking accompanies overstriding—which can increase risk of injury from the added load—and upping your cadence can help you avoid it.

Keep in mind that your body needs time to adjust to any changes you make in your form. Also, while your body may take on more force with a heel strike, it doesn’t always lead to more injuries or slower speeds. It’s one piece of the biomechanical puzzle. “Heel striking isn’t inherently dangerous by itself,” Foster says.

To improve your biomechanics, working with a run-form coach or physical therapist with advanced training in motor learning or neuromuscular re-education is hugely beneficial, says Foster. “It’s easy to understand the correct biomechanics, but it’s much more challenging to implement them,” she says.

Although working with one of these pros is ideal, a few exercises you can practice on your own can help you get a jumpstart on improving biomechanics.

Here are five biomechanical drills that focus on different aspects of your form. Do them often (for a few minutes as part of your warmup before every run, for example) to make the movements feel like second nature. Then, when you’re working to incorporate tweaks to your form into your run, don’t try to make several changes all at once; try sprinkling them into your runs slowly, thinking about a single form tweak for 30 seconds once per mile.

Just make sure not to jump in too quickly. All tweaks to your body’s biomechanics should be gradual or you risk the chance of injury, says Foster.

Why it works: This super-quick drill emphasizes balance and stability while firing up your posterior chain, which helps develop a more powerful push-off.

How to do it: Stand with feet hip-width apart. Raise right knee to hip height. In a quick, explosive movement, lower right foot to floor and raise left knee high, then lower left knee and raise right knee to hip height again. Do 5 reps. Rest for 1-2 minutes, then repeat for a second set.

Why it works: Practicing this movement at a quick, consistent pace helps make your arm swing more efficient.

How to do it: Set a metronome app (like Metronome Beats) to a beats per minute that feels in sync with your running cadence; 180 bpm is ideal but dial it back if that feels too quick. Sitting on the edge of a chair or standing with feet hip-width apart, pump arms forward and back to the beat, starting with 10-15 seconds. Do 3-5 sets, resting for about 10-20 second between sets.

Why it works: The plyometric motion of this jump helps prep your tendons to store and release energy quickly. Start by doing the move with both legs, then progress to one leg at a time, recommends Bui.

How to do it: Stand with feet hip-width apart. Keeping legs straight, push off the floor from the ball of feet and swing arms up to jump as high as you can. As soon as you land, jump again. Do 5 reps, jumping as quickly as you can (and minimizing your feet’s contact with the floor). Rest for 1-2 minutes, then repeat for a second set.

Why it works: This quick movement increases tendon capacity, trains your body to absorb load as you make contact with the ground, and decreases the time your feet stay in contact with the ground.

How to do it: Stand on the edge of a step or box about a foot tall. With right foot leading, step both feet down to floor. As soon as left foot hits floor, jump up explosively, pushing off floor with both feet. Repeat for 5 steps. Then repeat with left foot leading the step down. Do 2 sets.

Why it works: This move is really just running, with exaggerated motions that mimic ideal sprinting form—and helps develop speed, power, and explosiveness.

How to do it: On a track or long patch of ground, jog forward with as long a stride as possible. As you move, raise the front knee as high as possible while lifting the back foot (keeping leg straight) behind you. Continue for 10 reps total. Rest for 1-2 minutes, then repeat for a second set.

Recommended Experience: No experience necessary! Anyone can accomplish this training plan.

Get the PlanRecommended Experience: This plan is for a new runner who is just getting back into exercise.

Get the PlanRecommended Experience: For a new runner who has been exercising regularly for at least a year, or someone who has completed a few 5Ks or 10Ks and can complete 6 miles in one workout. This plan peaks at 28 miles in a week with a 12-mile long run.

Get the PlanRecommended Experience: For runners comfortable exercising for at least an hour at a moderate effort. This plan peaks at 32 miles in a week with a 14-mile long run.

Get the PlanRecommended Experience: For a consistent runner used to regularly working out four to five times a week. The plan starts with a 10-mile long run and peaks at 44 to 47 miles a week with a 22-mile long run, helping you average under a 9:10 per mile come race day.

#8935. Essential Yoga Poses That Deliver Serious Knee Strengthening

The thing about practicing yoga for knee strengthening is you typically don’t know you need to do it until there’s an issue. YouTube yoga teacher Yoga With Kassandra takes you through a routine designed to emphasize the muscles that support knee strength and explains how to modify the poses to suit your needs.

Whether you’re wanting to build knee strength to enhance your everyday functionality or you’re recovery from a knee injury and finally at the point where you can practice yoga, you need strengthening exercises that support all the muscles that support and stabilize your knees. Basically, you want to work on the hip adductors, the quads, the glutes, the hamstrings.

The following poses literally work all of the muscles that contribute to knee stability. You’ll also get to play around a little with some dynamic movement and try some balancing exercises that help you understand how to properly engage the muscles that support the knee. Then you can take that awareness into other yoga poses as well as your everyday movements.

Regularly practicing this yoga for knee strength routine will help anyone build knee strength. I know from personal experience just how frustrating a knee injury can be, so if that applies to you, know that the more you dedicate time towards rehabilitating yourself, and the more diligent you are with your practices, the more likely you’ll feel a difference in your ease of movement. And remember that rest is equally as important as stretching and strengthening.

You will need a block or a block-like item for several of these poses. If you experience pain in any of the poses, slowly come out and skip ahead to the next pose. Always consult with your physician or physical therapist prior to introducing new exercises.

Start lying on your back and bring your feet about hip-distance apart and your heels pretty close toward your glutes. Place the block directly in between the inner thighs and squeeze the block as much as you possibly can. Then push down into all four corners of both feet and slowly lift first the pelvis off the mat, then the lower back, and then the mid back in Bridge Pose. The higher you lift, the harder it becomes to squeeze your block, but keep squeezing it anyway. This helps train your inner thighs, or adductor muscles, to contract. Building inner thigh power can also help you become better at balancing poses.

Take about 3 breaths here, pushing down through your big toes. Then exhale and slowly roll down, inch by inch. Move your block to the side.

From lying on your back, lift your right leg toward the sky and straighten it without locking your knee or hyperextending it. Interlace your fingers behind your right hamstrings. Instead of making this a passive stretch, push your leg against your palms as much as you can, and feel your arms resist. Keep pushing, pushing, pushing with your hamstrings. This should be challenging. You’ll also get a little arm workout. Try to keep your lower back neutral and close to the mat. Continue for a few more breaths.

You might find that your leg starts coming a little closer toward your chest, and that’s fine, but don’t force the stretch. Then release and switch legs.

Re-extend your right leg and bring your hands behind the back of your calf muscles. If that means you need to bend a little in your knee, that’s perfectly fine. If you can’t reach that far, bring your hands to the hamstrings again, but shift them closer to the knee, which creates a different sensation. Same thing, you want to push against your hands and resist. Then repeat on the other side.

This is not a yoga pose, but it’s absolutely amazing for your adductors. Grab your block and place it between your inner thighs again. Instead of keeping your heels close to you as in Bridge, walk your feet out so it feels almost as if your legs are almost straight and there’s about 6 inches between the mat and the backs of your knees.

Flex your feet, push your heels down into the mat, and see if you can squeeze your block and lift your hips off the mat. They’re only going to lift about an inch or so and that’s fine. This is an intense pose. You’re gonna feel it in your legs pretty much right away. If you don’t feel it, it’s because your knees are too bent and you need to straighten them a little more. Squeeze your block, push down into your heels, and try to drag your heels toward your shoulders. Hold here for a few more breaths. Then lower and move your block off to the side.

Come into Downward-Facing Dog. Normally I would suggest some Cat and Cow stretches before going into Down Dog, but if you’re recovering from knee issues you might not be able to apply bring your knees to the mat because of the pressure, so consider those stretches optional or take a seated version of them. You’re pushing into the heels here to stretch your hamstrings, lengthen your arms, and lengthen your spine.

Reach your right leg toward the sky in Three-Legged Dog, then step forward toward the top of the mat. Push down into your feet and come up into High Lunge. You want your feet hip-distance apart for stability. It’s find to bend your back knee if that feels more doable. It’s important that your front knee is going in the same direction as your toes and is stacked over your ankle. You don’t want the knee to be swaying to one side or jutting forward in front of your toes.

Bring your hands to your heart and keep your right knee bent and focus on its stability as you tilt your chest forward into a variation of Warrior 3. Keep the knee of your supporting leg bent as you reach your left leg back and find your balance.

As you inhale, push your right leg straight, and then exhale gently as you bend your right knee again. Think of this as almost like a one-legged squat. So inhale, straighten the leg. Exhale, bend the knee.

Continue for several breaths. Keep your right knee pointing straight over the second and third toes. Last one, inhale to straighten and hold here.

From Warrior 3, reach your left leg straight toward the ceiling and bring your chest toward your right thigh in Standing Splits. You might want to bring your block underneath your hands or fingertips.

Then exhale, bend both knees as much as you can, and see if you can bring your knees together to touch, so you’re in a little ball with your left foot hovering above the mat.

Then inhale, open back up into Standing Splits. Look at your right knee and make certain it’s not shifting to the right or the left. Do that once more.

Bend both knees and bring your left foot to the mat with your big toes together and your heels slightly apart in Chair Pose. If this creates tension in your lower back, you can keep your feet hip-distance apart. Rock your weight back into your heels and keep your tailbone reaching back and your thighs hugging the midline as if you were still squeezing that block. Stay here or reach your arms alongside your head.

Lean more weight onto your right leg, and see if you can pick up your left foot and step it back into your High Lunge. Then very carefully pivot the back foot almost parallel to the short side of the mat, keeping your shin and your knee facing the same direction, in Warrior 2. Your right knee is still bending. Squeezing the glutes helps press that right knee open as it points forward. Reach your arms straight out from your shoulders.

To work on strengthening, inhale as you straighten the front leg and bring your hands together in front of you, and then exhale back into Warrior 2 and reach your arms. Repeat several times. The goal is not to rush this but to do it with control. You want to really feel that knee tracking directly over the second and third toes and not wobbling.

Straighten your right leg, being careful not to lock or hyperextend your knees. Then shift forward into Triangle Pose and reach your left arm upward. Draw your left shoulder slightly back as you open across the chest.

From Triangle, look down at the floor and circle your hands to the mat. Step to Downward-Facing Dog.

Repeat these poses on your left side, starting with High Lunge and continuing to Dynamic Warrior 3, Standing Splits, Chair Pose, Dynamic Warrior 2, Triangle, and Down Dog.

From Down Dog, walk your feet to the top of the mat. Bend your knees a little, grab your block, and come all the way to standing. Come into Mountain Pose with the block in between your thighs, just as you did in Bridge Pose. Squeeze the block and hug in toward the midline. You can feel the adductors engage. Plant down firmly through all four corners of both feet.

As you inhale, stand a little taller. As you exhale, continue to squeeze your block as you lower yourself into Chair Pose. Repeat this movement about 5 times, moving slowly and steadily, continuing to squeeze the block. You might need to adjust your block a little.

Slowly fold forward in Standing Forward Bend. If you need to bend your knees, that’s perfectly fine. Even in this fold, can you squeeze your block? Then bend your knees a little more and release your block.

Slowly roll all the way up to standing. Notice how you feel as you attempt the pose, because if you’re still injured, the shape might not be accessible to you, and it’s fine to skip it. Lean onto your right foot, bend your left knee, and catch hold of the inner edge of your left foot behind you with your left hand. Keep your left hip and knee drawing inward toward the midline. So imagine you’re still squeezing your block in between your thighs. That is really important.

Reach your right arm forward. Instead of dipping the chest down and thinking of lifting the leg up, focus on pushing your foot into your palm. You’re not going super far forward in your Dancer Pose. You’re not working on flexibility, you’re working on strength, although you might feel an intense stretch along the front of your lifted quads.

To help with balance, you can always practice within arm’s reach of a chair or a wall so that you can reach out if needed for extra steadiness.

Then release and repeat on your other leg, foot into the right hand.

Make your way onto your belly on the mat. The shape of this pose is very similar to Dancer, so if this isn’t working for you, work on Locust Pose. If you want to do Bow Pose, bend your knees and see if you can catch hold of your feet and imagine you still have the block in between the inner upper thighs. Squeeze in and start to push the feet against your hands.

If you’re not doing Bow Pose, then bring your arms alongside your body, palms facing the mat, and slowly lift your feet and legs and chest off the mat Focus your gaze forward and down to keep the back of your neck long. Hold here or slowly release and then lift several times.

Flip over onto your back. Grab your block, lift your hips, slide your block underneath your pelvis, and just let yourself settle here. Slow down your breath and start to unwind.

When you’re ready, press into your feet, lift your pelvis, and move your block to the side before lowering yourself down. Maybe you draw your knees toward your belly and bring your arms underneath your calves and stay still or rock a little side to side.

Extend your arms and legs, close your eyes, and notice how you feel now as opposed to when you first started this practice. Let yourself settle into this space.

When you’re ready, begin to lengthen your breath and wiggle your fingers and toes. You can reach your arms up overhead, take a big stretch, and roll onto one side. Come up to take a seat, sitting up tall, maybe closing your eyes for a moment.

Thank you so much for doing this knee-strengthening sequence with me. I hope that it gave you some ideas as to how you can strengthen your knees.

#8934. Are High-Intensity Workouts Messing With Your Cortisol?

If you’ve scrolled through social media lately, you’ve probably seen wellness influencers claim high-intensity exercise increases cortisol, the infamous “stress hormone” that, in excess amounts, can lead to fatigue, weight gain, trouble sleeping, high blood pressure, and elevated blood sugar.

Many influencers say to switch to a no-stress, low-sweat regimen. And while low-intensity exercises such as Pilates, treadmill walking, or yoga are valid ways to work out—and serve as excellent cross-training activities for runners—HIIT workouts (like hill repeats, sprint intervals, and tempo runs) are key if you’re training for a race or looking to build speed and power.

But are high-intensity runs actually messing with your hormones, or is the wellness side of the internet spreading misinformation? We’re here to separate fact from fiction.

Cortisol is a hormone made by your adrenal glands, which are located on top of your kidneys and are part of your body’s endocrine system.

“Cortisol helps regulate metabolism, blood pressure, and the immune response, and it makes energy available when the body is under stress—including during exercise,” says Dr. Aysegul Eren, M.D., endocrinologist and medical director of the Adrenal Program at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center.

This hormone rises when your body faces increased physical or metabolic demand, such as exercise, illness, fasting, low blood sugar, or psychological stress, Eren explains. During exercise, cortisol naturally spikes as a way to provide energy to your body so it can perform. Viewed through that lens, cortisol is an important part of your body’s response to exercise and your ability to complete workouts.

“Higher-intensity exercise reliably causes a temporary cortisol rise, generally related to exercise intensity,” Eren says. “This is normal physiology, not something harmful to prevent.”

How long cortisol remains elevated depends on the stressor, according to Dr. Feyza Erenler, M.D., an endocrinologist at Tufts Medical Center. It may be minutes to hours for a brief stimulus like exercise, she explains.

A 2021 meta-analysis of 10 studies on HIIT, published in the Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports, found that cortisol increased immediately after exercise, often fell below baseline about two hours later, and returned to baseline within 24 hours.

“There’s no evidence that a specific number of HIIT sessions causes chronically high cortisol,” Eren says. “The more relevant concern is overtraining—chronic training without adequate recovery—which can lead to persistent underperformance. ‘Too much’ is individual, depending on training load, sleep, nutrition, recovery, and other stressors.”

In fact, research shows physical activity can actually lead to lower cortisol levels. A 2026 study in the Journal of Sport and Health Science found that those who did 150 minutes of moderate- to vigorous-intensity aerobic exercise (50 to 85% of their max heart rate) every week for a year saw a reduction in long-term cortisol levels.

Symptoms frequently attributed to “high cortisol,” such as fatigue, poor sleep, anxiety, or difficulty losing weight, don’t indicate that a person has high cortisol, according to Erenler. “These symptoms are extremely common and nonspecific and can occur for many different reasons,” she says.

Signs of true high cortisol—not the brief, self-resolving spike during exercise—include bruising, muscle weakness (particularly in the upper legs), wide purple stretch marks, worsening high blood pressure or diabetes, and sometimes changes in fat distribution, according to Eren.

If you’re experiencing any of the above symptoms, Eren recommends discussing them with your healthcare provider rather than trying to diagnose yourself with high cortisol all on your own (or with the help of a chatbot). Chronic high cortisol levels that are undiagnosed can cause high blood pressure, diabetes, muscle and bone loss, higher infection risk, and cardiovascular complications.

But rest assured, cortisol disorders are rare. For instance, Cushing syndrome, a condition where you have too much cortisol in your blood for a long period of time, only affects 10 to 15 people per million each year, according to the Endocrine Society. Cushing syndrome is caused by a tumor on the pituitary gland at the base of your brain, not too much high-intensity exercise.

“During exercise, cortisol temporarily rises in response to the physiological stress and then decreases as the body recovers and the stressor resolves,” Erenler says. “In Cushing syndrome, cortisol exposure remains inappropriately elevated over time, and the normal regulatory mechanisms—including the normal circadian pattern and suppression of cortisol production—are disrupted.”

For most healthy people, there’s no need to try to suppress the normal cortisol response to exercise. Instead, the goal should be a sustainable training program that includes adequate recovery, sufficient sleep and nutrition, and variation in workout intensity.

“Don’t worry about the temporary rise in cortisol that occurs with exercise,” Eren says. “It’s a normal part of the body’s response to physical activity, not a sign that exercise is harming you.”

Erenler agrees and says the goal isn’t to eliminate cortisol—it’s to challenge your body appropriately and give it enough recovery to adapt to the stress you’re placing on it.

#8933. How to Master the Run/Walk Method: Train for a 5K & 10K

Learn how to tackle the approachable distances with the power of walk breaks.

You’ve completed your Magic Mile time trials, dialed in your pacing, and tracked your progress with your run/walk workouts. Now, it’s time to hit the starting line!

The 5K and 10K make for perfect race distances for beginner and veteran run/walkers alike. Whether you’re shooting to cross your first finish line or earn that big PR, you can train for and race toward your goals with the run/walk method powering every step.

The Runner’s World guide, How to Master the Run/Walk Method, helps you get to the finish line and cover two of the most popular and approachable distances. Pair our chapter with one of our dedicated training plans to prepare for your first or fastest 5K or 10K yet.

In Runner’s World’s How to Master the Run/Walk Method: Train for a 5K & 10K, we’ll teach you:

For beginners, a 5K or 10K serves as a great introduction to using the run/walk training strategy for race day. It’s an opportunity to get accustomed to pacing, structure your intervals, and follow a dedicated run/walk training plan. Once you’ve nailed your 5K/10K training block, you may find it easier to bump up to longer distances and chase after new race goals.

But even if you’re not a racing newcomer, a shorter, approachable distance can be an ideal place to start with run/walk. You might even race faster with the run/walk method than you did previously when running the entire distance.

The shorter the distance, the shorter the walk break will likely be, especially if you’re shooting for a PR. Use your data from your Magic Mile test to determine your goal pace for race day.

Some crucial benefits of using run/walk for a 5K/10K include:

Weekly Schedule: 3 total run/walk days (1 race rehearsal, 1 speed workout, 1 long run), 1 easy walk day, 3 rest or cross-train daysSample Workout: 6-8 x 400-meter repeatsRecommended Experience: For an experienced runner, who has done 5Ks and/or half marathons or marathons, and wants to use the run/walk method to get faster.

Weekly Schedule: 3 total run/walk days (2 easy runs, 1 long run), 1 easy walk day, 2 strength train days, 2 rest or cross-train daysSample Workout: 30-minute run/walk + strength trainingRecommended Experience: For new runners and those who have been running for three months and are ready to do their first race.

Weekly Schedule: 3 total run/walk days (1 race rehearsal, 1 speed workout, 1 long run), 2 strength train days, 3 rest or cross-train daysSample Workout: 8 x 400-meter repeatsRecommended Experience: For an experienced runner, who has done 10Ks and/or half marathons or marathons, and wants to use the run/walk method to get faster.

With one of Runner’s World’s dedicated 5K and 10K run/walk training plans, you can build your endurance and speed for tackling your race. Spanning anywhere from six to eight weeks, our plans include three run/walk days, two to three rest or cross-train days, and even additional easy walk and strength training days, depending on the plan. Whether you’re a beginner looking to dip your toes in run/walk or an experienced run/walker chasing after a personal best, we have a plan tailored to your goals.

Newcomers embarking on their run/walk journey for the first time can also utilize our Couch to 5K training plan. It’s a 10-week plan with two to three days of run/walk, two days of rest, and two days of strength training, aimed at getting you across your first finish line.

#8932. Tracksmith Created the Blueprint for Indie Running Brands. Can It Survive Without Its Architect?

The Boston-born apparel company enters a new era following the sudden departure of founder Matt Taylor.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

The running journalist Mario Fraioli still remembers the shorts Matt Taylor sent him in 2014, when Taylor was launching a new apparel brand.

Dubbed the Longfellow short, the prototype pair had a button at the waist, they were longer than typical running shorts, and they didn’t have a liner. The idea was, in Fraioli’s telling, that you could go straight from an easy run to a coffee shop and still look presentable. Taylor wanted to know what Fraioli thought.

Fraioli’s reaction? He didn’t love them. The sizing was off for him.

He was, however, intrigued by Taylor’s passion for the apparel and the nascent brand.

“He was super excited,” Fraioli told Runner’s World.

With $35,000 of his savings from a previous endeavor and seed round capital, Taylor launched Tracksmith later in 2014. The initial product line was four men’s items, including those Longfellow shorts and a “Grayboy” T-shirt that mimicked the standard-issue shirt of college athletic departments, plus a spike bag and Meter magazine. Women’s clothing followed about nine months later.

The idea of Tracksmith? Top-quality running apparel for people who were not professional athletes, but trained hard and loved their sport. The names and designs of the products reflected the roots of the sport and Taylor’s reverence for its history.

Frugal runners initially had sticker shock. Tracksmith manufactured its clothing in the U.S., using quality materials, which cost more. But the company was one of the earliest independent running brands selling apparel for serious runners outside of the major shoe companies. Women’s running apparel brand Oiselle had hatched earlier, in 2007.

Tracksmith quickly grew. It added retail locations in Boston and New York, and hundreds of items for sale—including four shoe styles, which were added in 2022.

Now, Taylor has been abruptly pushed out of the company he founded, and industry observers are left wondering if the brand can keep growing without him.

Fraioli, who is now a coach and writer of the Morning Shakeout newsletter, announced the news of Taylor’s departure in his October 13 email, writing that the newsletter would no longer have Tracksmith as a sponsor.

“A big part of my belief in Tracksmith was tied to my belief in Matt’s character, authenticity, and creative vision, and with him gone, I’ve lost confidence in where the brand is headed,” he wrote.

It’s unclear what precipitated the split. Taylor declined to speak to Runner’s World, and former employees were in the dark about the details of his ouster.

Taylor had hired a CEO in January, Jared Carver, a veteran of Converse, to handle the day-to-day operations so he could get back to focusing on the “brand’s vision and creative expression,” according to a company LinkedIn post eight months ago.

In a concurrent post, Taylor wrote: “I didn’t start Tracksmith to be a CEO—I started it to change the way running is presented with the hope of changing how it is perceived. My goals were to build distinct products, tell compelling stories and create a sense of camaraderie, the same you might feel on your cross country team.”

Insiders and one analyst painted a picture of a brand that opened a lane for rival independent retailers to follow suit—and perhaps surpass—Tracksmith. Bandit and Satisfy are two of the brands frequently cited as competitors, especially as the sport has seen enormous growth coming out of COVID.

“Other people have, I think, drafted on their success and made the marketplace more competitive,” said Matt Powell, an industry analyst who is a senior advisor with BCE Consulting. “For any brand, I think it’s hard to stay ahead of the trends, and you never have an unassailable position. Somebody’s always trying to copy you, or do what you do better. That's a big challenge for a small brand.”

It is not known if Tracksmith was profitable, as the company is privately held, and those who were close to Taylor in the company’s early days wondered whether investors and board members were growing impatient. Tracksmith would not talk about the company’s financials or name the members of its board. A Tracksmith representative confirmed Taylor’s exit and that of Matt Pauk, the head of product, who left in August, and offered a statement:

“Matt Taylor, Tracksmith’s founder, has transitioned out of his role with the company and departed Tracksmith. Matt’s unique vision created the Tracksmith we know today, and undoubtedly shaped the culture and business of running. At its core, Tracksmith has always been about people—our team, our partners, the people who push the sport forward, and the runners we serve. These values remain unchanged, and we are confident in our ability to continue building upon the strong foundation established in Tracksmith's 12 years.”

As early employees try to process what happened, they expressed appreciation for what Taylor brought to the industry.

Taylor, they said, was the animating force of the brand. He named the various products after runners in history, and arranged artful photo shoots with athletes in the mist and the mud. His love of the sport was obvious. (He’s still a serious runner. In 2024, Taylor ran the Boston Marathon, at age 47, in 2:43:18.)

Lou Serafini was one of the first employees. Like Fraioli, he didn’t immediately get what the brand was about. At the time, he was working at Heartbreak Hill Running Company before Taylor recruited him to work for Tracksmith.

“I remember being kind of confused,” Serafini said, “not really understanding what they were trying to do. I think most visionary brands have a little bit of that, where it has to be different enough where it makes people kind of scratch their head a little bit.”

Serafini went to Tracksmith’s first Boston Marathon pop-up in 2015, in an empty storefront at 285 Newbury Street, which in 2017 became its permanent home, just blocks from the marathon finish line. (Now pop-ups are a standard part of major marathons with cutting-edge brands; expos are in dreary convention centers, a necessary stop for runners to make to pick up their bibs.)

Serafini’s first job was managing the shop and building a running community there. “That was the first time where I really realized the ethos of the brand,” he said.

When he first started at Tracksmith in 2017, if Serafini saw any runners wearing Tracksmith clothing along the Charles River paths, it was an exciting moment. By the end of his tenure, in 2024, he remembered spotting runners in the brand all over the world.

The best days at Tracksmith always have been Boston Marathon Monday and the Tuesday after. Runners would crowd the shop, pick up a free poster, and get it stamped with their finishing time. “The focus of those days was to sit in the track house and stamp posters and have a 30-second conversation with somebody about how their race went,” Serafini said. In 2018, the year Boston went off in a nor’easter, the Tracksmith headquarters on Newbury became a hospital of sorts for runners trying to get warm.

Two other former employees, in conversations with Runner’s World, echoed Serafini’s assessment of Taylor as a visionary.

One former employee, who asked not to be named, said the committed runner didn’t have much to choose from before Tracksmith, describing the industry’s 2014 offerings as “neon, boring, and not high performance.” Tracksmith took the better products the pros were getting and gave them to amateurs. (And though the price point was initially surprising, these days, in the era of $300 super shoes, it seems reasonable.)

But getting eyeballs on a new business is cash intensive, and Taylor had big, expensive operations, which included stipends for unsponsored Olympic Marathon Trials qualifiers and hosting twilight 5Ks for the fast amateurs looking to run PRs. Real estate on Newbury Street and in Brooklyn does not come cheap, either. A London location that opened in 2023 closed in August.

Without Taylor, does the brand have legs? The fear is that it becomes “performance J.Crew,” preppy running apparel without the investment in the sport.

In response to a question about bolstering the sport, the Tracksmith spokesperson confirmed the company would be continuing with its programming and support of amateur runners through clubs and meets like Tracksmith Stamata, the Twilight series, Hare AC, and the Amateur Support Program. “Nothing has changed or will change there,” the spokesperson said.

But with Taylor’s departure, some see Tracksmith being at a crossroads, caught between funders seeking a return on their investment and fast-growing competition.

“I think a lot of investors, private equity investors, they revere founders and understand that the business that they’re in, particularly one like this, it’s as much of a cultural business as anything else,” said Ryan Eckel, who worked for Tracksmith as the brand president for five years, from 2019 to 2024. “And when you start treating it like it’s making widgets, I think you lose sight [of the culture] and ultimately I think it hurts their investments long term.”

Powell, though, still sees a lane for Tracksmith, especially with consumers who are willing to pay premium prices.

“On one level, I would tell you there's never been a better time to be a small brand, because I think the consumer is looking for unique products,” he said. “But because the consumer is always demanding new and next, that part is really hard for a small brand to execute.”

Sarah Lorge Butler is a writer and editor living in Eugene, Oregon, and her stories about the sport, its trends, and fascinating individuals have appeared in Runner’s World since 2005. She is the author of two popular fitness books, Run Your Butt Off! and Walk Your Butt Off!

#8931. Unlock Your Full Potential by Fixing These Common Triathlon Body Imbalances

Triathletes can face muscle imbalances. These off-season exercises help build proper strength to prepare for next season. (Photo: Brad Kaminski/Triathlete)

Triathlon training is all about repetition, with hours upon hours spent catching and pulling in the pool, turning the pedals on the bike, and turning the legs over on the run. With that repetition comes natural imbalance, with some muscle groups getting overworked while others get neglected (or even weaken with age).

Over time, these imbalances can impact performance directly or indirectly by contributing to injury development. That’s why taking time to identify and address these imbalances now will help keep you healthy in the long run.

By pinpointing areas of weakness or asymmetry early on, athletes can target the stabilizing muscles, improve biomechanical efficiency across all three disciplines, and significantly reduce the risk of overuse injuries that often arise from repetitive strain. Here’s how.

While swimming is generally thought of as the “safest” discipline in triathlon, issues can and do occur, often manifesting as “swimmer’s shoulder.” Swimmer’s shoulder is a bit of a catch-all term for pain in the front of the shoulder that encompasses several pathologies, including rotator cuff issues.

Typically, underlying laxity and instability exist. One factor that can contribute to shoulder problems is a strength imbalance between the shoulder internal and external rotators, with the internal rotators becoming disproportionately strong in comparison to the external rotators. This makes sense, as the shoulder internal rotators are active throughout the catch and pull, working to rotate the arm in and push against water.

But the external rotators still play an important role, as they help to stabilize the shoulder joint, keeping the ball of the joint centered in the socket to help prevent impingement and pain with overhead use and shoulder abnormalities. To decrease injury risk, external rotators should have about two-thirds of the strength of the internal rotators.

The most reliable, valid ways to check this involve specialized dynamometry equipment that measures force. But if you’re just looking to get a general idea, check how many reps of each of the below motions you can do until fatigue.

In this case, the test (lying prone, rotating the back of the arm up) can also be used as an effective strengthening exercise for external rotation. Start with higher reps, lower weights to learn the motion (3 sets of 10-12), then work up to higher weights, lower reps (4 sets of 6-8) to build more strength.

If this position causes pain or is too difficult at first, a side-lying shoulder external rotation is also a good option.

While the incidence of overuse injuries attributed to cycling is generally lower than those attributed to running, they can and do occur, most commonly impacting the knee and lower back. Although singling out contributing factors is difficult, the prolonged posture and muscle activations associated with cycling predispose athletes to overdeveloped quadriceps and an undeveloped posterior chain (glutes, hamstrings, back extensors) and lateral hip muscles.

Cyclists need strong quads – these are the predominant muscle used to power the pedal stroke. But the glutes and hamstrings do assist, so neglecting those leaves some power on the table. Plus, that injury-prone lower back needs adequate strength and endurance to withstand hours spent in a forward-flexed position.

Also, because muscle weakness and tightness often go hand-in-hand, related limitations in mobility throughout the posterior chain limit a cyclist’s ability to comfortably hold more aggressive aero positions. Those quads of steel will only help so much if you’re sitting up to ease back and glute discomfort by the end of a long ride!

The strength and endurance of the posterior chain (and also the lateral hip, which can play a role when it comes to knee pain on the bike) can be checked using a single-leg bridge hold.

The single-leg RDL is a good choice for eliciting both high force and stretch in the hamstrings and strengthening the gluteal muscles, back extensors, and lateral hips. Isolating each leg can also help with side-to-side imbalances.

When it comes to muscle strength and running, the glutes have been frequently implicated as the cause of (and solution to) many issues. But, while the glutes do play an important stability-related role in the run gait and deficits have been linked with injury, the true workhorse of the run gait – the calves – often gets overlooked and under-strengthened.

The soleus (one of the calf muscles) experiences forces of up to eight times body weight and produces up to 50% of forward propulsive power while running. Because the calves insert onto the heel via the Achilles tendon (which acts as a spring during running), the two are linked, with decreased calf strength seen in athletes with Achilles issues compared to healthy controls.

Strong calves can also help to protect against tibial bone stress injuries. Masters athletes lose calf strength (and Achilles tendon stiffness) disproportionately to other muscle groups with age, leading to both a reduction in propulsion and step length and an increased risk of lower leg soft tissue injuries such as strains and tendinopathies. So, when it comes to both performance and helping to guard against many common lower leg injuries, first check the powerhouse muscles below the knee!

Calf strength can be tested with a single-leg calf raise test.

The test here can again be used as the exercise – just load it up!

So, while the different disciplines and repeated motions of triathlon might lend athletes to certain imbalances, not all is lost! Triathletes can make themselves stronger, more resilient, and faster with some awareness and work – so don’t neglect those details.

#8930. How Warrior 1 Can Help Relieve Your Tight Hips and Lower Back

(Photo: Andrew Clark; Design in Canva by Laura Harold)

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about how to do Warrior 1 first appeared in the June 2007 issue of Yoga Journal. Find more of our Archives here.

When you have only a short time for your daily practice, which poses do you choose? Whether you opt for a simple Adho Mukha Svanasana (Downward-Facing Dog), the paired inversions Sirsasana (Headstand) and Sarvangasana (Shoulderstand), or a restorative pose to counter your hectic day, consider including another pose consistently: Virabhadrasana I (Warrior I).

I often sing the praises of this challenging pose to skeptical students who feel that it’s a lot of work without a lot of noticeable benefit, so let me explain my enthusiasm for it. In my work as a physical therapist and yoga teacher, I’ve noticed that many people in our sedentary society have tight hip flexors, which they don’t stretch much, if at all. I’m convinced that short, tight hip flexors are a major factor in many cases of chronic or recurring back pain that so many people experience in the West.

The hip flexors become tight when the hips are constantly placed in a flexed position—think sitting, driving, or sleeping in the fetal position. Like any other muscles, hip flexors will shorten structurally if they are not stretched. However, if you incorporate Virabhadrasana I into your regular practice, you’ll stretch the hip flexors, helping them gradually return to their normal length and easing a source of backaches.

The hip flexor muscles include the iliacus, psoas, rectus femoris, tensor fasciae latae, sartorius, and, in some situations, the short adductors pectines and adductor brevis. All of these muscles (except the adductors mentioned) cross the front of the hip and are active in hip flexion, which pulls the femur (thighbone) and torso closer together. The hip flexes when you perform a sit-up or lift your leg toward your chest while standing. (Each of these muscles has other actions, too, but we’re focusing here on their hip-flexing ability.)

Of the whole group of muscles, the iliacus and psoas are the strongest hip flexors. They are often referred to as the iliopsoas because they both follow the same path and have exactly the same action. Although they have different origins, the psoas originates on the lumbar spine, while the iliacus originates on the inner surface of the ilium, one of the large bones of the pelvis—they come together in the very back of the lower abdomen and run across the floor of the pelvis, over the outer part of the pubic bones on each side, and dive deep through the inner upper thighs to attach to the inner upper femurs.

The iliopsoas is powerful partly due to its size—each psoas is nearly as big around as your wrist—and partly because its position so close to the hip joint gives it excellent leverage. It is such a strong muscle, in fact, that it can influence the tilt of your pelvis and therefore the position of your spine during your daily activities. In other words, when the iliopsoas gets very short and tight, it can pull your pelvis into an anterior (forward) tilt. This type of tilt—when the top rim of the pelvis tips forward and down and the coccyx (tailbone) lifts up—usually puts the lumbar spine into hyperextension, also known as a swayback. (A posterior or backward pelvic tilt happens when the top of the pelvis moves backward, the coccyx moves down and tucks under, and the lower back flattens.)

Strong abdominals help pull the pelvis into a posterior tilt, but you might be surprised to hear that even if you have strong abdominals, a tight and strong iliopsoas muscle can win the battle and tilt your pelvis forward.

A chronically hyperextended lumbar spine puts the lower back muscles in a shortened position, causing them to ache. If the only thing that relieves your lower back discomfort is to lie on your back and pull your knees to your chest (therefore flattening the curve), you might have a hyperextended lumbar. Hyperextension also puts a greater percentage of your upper body weight onto the small facet joints on the posterior aspect of the vertebrae instead of on the solid vertebral bodies and disks, where it’s meant to be.

Enter our hero Virabhadrasana I, which can stretch the hip flexors, correct an anteriorly tilted pelvis, and help decompress your lower back. But remember to focus on practicing it with a strong posterior pelvic tilt. If you don’t, and your psoas and iliacus are tight, they will pull the lumbar spine into hyperextension and you’ll eventually feel lower back compression and pain in the pose.

There are several ways to learn how to hold a posterior tilt, but it’s best to learn the action first before integrating it into the pose. Try this: Stand with your back to a wall, with your heels about a foot away from it and your knees slightly bent. Feel an anterior tilt by moving your frontal hip points (the two bony knobs on the front of your pelvis, each known as the ASIS, or the anterior superior iliac spine) down toward your thighs, your coccyx up the wall, and your lower back away from the wall. To move from an anterior to a posterior tilt, lift your ASIS (hip points) up away from your thighs, take your tailbone down the wall, and feel your lower back move onto or toward the wall.

Now that you’re familiar with the action of a posterior tilt, here’s how to incorporate it into your Virabhadrasana I.

Set up the pose with your back to a wall, right foot forward, left heel pressing into the wall. Place a strap over the upper thigh in the crease of your right hip and hold it down with one hand on each side of the thigh. Be sure to keep your chest lifted and your shoulders down. If you are in an anterior tilt, your hip points will drop down toward or even onto the belt. To counter that, bend both knees a little and strongly lift your hip points up off the strap and into a posterior tilt. With the hip points lifted, gradually straighten the left knee, pressing the heel into the floor but keeping the lift up on the hip points, in order to stretch the iliopsoas across the front of the left hip.

Keep in mind that for most students, when the front knee bends more deeply, up to the ultimate goal of 90 degrees, it’s hard to hold the posterior tilt. If that’s the case for you, try coming only partway into the pose.

You can deepen the iliopsoas stretch a bit more by minimizing the external rotation of the left hip. When you do this, your left knee will turn out less. The iliopsoas is an external rotator, so it will try to reduce the stretch by externally rotating as you do a posterior tilt. To lessen this, be sure to turn your left foot 6o degrees away from the wall. (In standing poses like Warrior II, you turn your foot out more, so that it’s parallel to the bottom edge of your mat.) Once you’ve done that, square your pelvis toward the wall across from you as much as you can by pressing the left inner heel down firmly, lifting the left inner knee, and using the strength of the left leg to help bring the left half of the pelvis forward. You’ll not only deepen the iliopsoas stretch, but you’ll also protect your left knee from a twisting injury.

As your iliopsoas stretches and lengthens, it will pull less on your lumbar spine and pelvis, and you’ll be able to lift your lower back up out of the pelvis, thereby decompressing it and relieving discomfort. You may also notice that your posture, both standing and walking, improves, and you might enjoy a new sense of space in your hips and lower back. And you can rest assured that you’re helping prevent arthritis in your lower back.

I hope I’ve made a convincing case for consistently including hip flexor stretches in your home practice. It’s especially important to work them on sedentary days and before practicing backbends—if you’re stuck in an anterior pelvic tilt, you can imagine the compression in the lower back while you do Setu Bandha Sarvangasana (Bridge Pose), Ustrasana (Camel Pose), or Urdhva Dhanurasana (Upward Bow Pose). When you consider adding Warrior I as your iliopsoas stretch, know that you’re setting the stage for a strong and healthy back in the years to come.
